risk_of_bias.key_concern: The trial was open-label (patients, families, and treating clinicians all knew treatment assignment) with significantly higher discontinuation in the lithium arm (32.2% vs 15.7% risperidone), though independent evaluators were blinded for the primary clinical outcome and weight/BMI/laboratory measures were objectively measured, limiting bias on the weight endpoints specifically.

summary: The TEAM study randomized 279 antimanic medication-naive children and adolescents (6-15 years) with DSM-IV bipolar I mania to open-label risperidone, lithium carbonate (titrated to 1.1-1.3 mEq/L), or divalproex sodium for 8 weeks. Risperidone produced significantly greater weight gain (mean 3.31 kg) and BMI increase than lithium (1.42 kg) or divalproex sodium (1.67 kg) (P<.001 for both comparisons), while weight gain was reported as a common adverse effect in all three groups (69.0% with lithium, 73.2% with divalproex, 95.5% with risperidone).

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: Per the extraction-scope override, only the outcomes central to this weight-gain review (weight kg change, BMI change, and the binary weight-gain adverse-event count) were extracted as the 'primary' outcomes; the trial's own designated primary endpoint (CGI-BP-IM response rate) was omitted per scope. Weight/BMI arm_results are from Table 3's completer subset (n=62 lithium, n=76 divalproex, n=78 risperidone at week 8), not the full randomized n; sample_sizes.per_arm reflects the full randomized n per Table 2. Lithium salt is explicitly stated as 'lithium carbonate' in the Methods. No single maintained mg/day dose is reported for lithium (dosing was titrated to serum level per Table 1), so dose_salt_mg_per_day fields are null; only the achieved mean serum level (1.09±0.34 mEq/L, numerically equal to mmol/L) and target range (1.1-1.3 mEq/L) are reported. Between-group mean differences for weight/BMI were calculated from per-arm means/SDs (paper reported only F-statistics and P values from ANCOVA-type group comparisons, not explicit mean differences); SEs were derived via sqrt(sd1^2/n1+sd2^2/n2). No lithium-vs-divalproex P value was reported in text for weight or BMI, so those effect entries have p_value=null. The binary weight-gain adverse-event outcome (Table 4) had no between-group OR/RR/P value reported, so between_group_effects is empty for that outcome. Total serious adverse events (n=5) and their arm distribution were not broken down per arm in the text.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: Body weight changes were listed as a named side-effect only in the chlorpromazine group's list (21%), with no percentage or count given for the lithium group — the lithium-group side-effect list (dryness of mouth, tremor, lassitude, nausea, vomiting) does not include weight gain, suggesting it was not among the notable side effects in that arm, but this is not explicitly stated as zero. summary: This double-blind, placebo-controlled RCT tested lithium carbonate (titrated to serum levels of 0.8-1.2 mmol/L, achieved mean 1.07 mmol/L) versus placebo in 40 hospitalized children and adolescents (ages 10-17) with conduct disorder and severe aggression over 4 weeks of treatment. Lithium was significantly more effective than placebo at reducing aggression on both the Overt Aggression Scale (p=.04) and the Global Clinical Judgements Consensus Scale responder rate (80% vs 30%, OR 9.3, p=.004). Weight gain occurred in both groups (17/20 lithium vs 16/20 placebo, not significantly different) with the placebo group gaining slightly more on average (1.9±2.7 kg) than the lithium group (1.6±1.7 kg).

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: Weight gain is reported only as an adverse-event frequency count (17/20 lithium vs 16/20 placebo, Fisher exact P>.99) with no threshold specified, and as continuous mean±SD change (placebo 1.9±2.7 kg; lithium 1.6±1.7 kg) in the Comment/Safety Measures narrative text — no per-arm N is separately given for the continuous kg change but it equals the full randomized N (20 per arm) since all subjects completed. Per extraction scope instructions, only PRIMARY outcomes (OAS and GCJCS) are included in the outcomes array; the weight gain continuous and binary AE data are captured in adverse_events.per_arm and derived fields rather than as separate outcome objects, since scope restricts 'outcomes' to primary efficacy endpoints only. CGI responder outcome (14/20 vs 4/20, OR 9.3, P=.004) was omitted as a secondary/redundant global measure per scope narrowing to primary outcomes only (OAS is the specific aggression measure emphasized as the paper's key contribution; GCJCS included as it is presented as a primary/co-primary measure alongside CGI). No BMI, waist circumference, or thyroid data reported.

summary: This double-blind, placebo-controlled trial randomized 344 patients with bipolar manic or mixed episodes who had partially failed lithium or valproate monotherapy to add olanzapine (5-20 mg/d) or placebo to their ongoing mood stabilizer for 6 weeks. Olanzapine cotherapy produced significantly greater improvement in YMRS mania scores than mood-stabilizer monotherapy alone (-13.11 vs -9.10 points, p=.003), and was accompanied by significantly more weight gain, somnolence, and increased appetite, though not a full lithium-specific arm since both lithium and valproate cotherapy patients were pooled for most primary analyses.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: This trial is not lithium-specific: patients received either lithium OR valproate as background mood stabilizer, with olanzapine or placebo added on top. Only ~33-36% of each arm was on lithium (76/229 cotherapy, 41/115 monotherapy); the majority received valproate. Weight-gain adverse-event rates were reported for the full sample AND broken out by mood-stabilizer subgroup (Table 4): lithium subgroup weight gain 21.1% (cotherapy) vs 4.9% (monotherapy), valproate subgroup 28.8% vs 8.2%; full sample 26.2% vs 7.0% (p<.001). Denominators for the lithium subgroup are n=76 (cotherapy) and n=41 (monotherapy) per Table 1's cotherapeutic-agent counts, but exact event counts (not just percentages) were not given in the text, so events/total were left null rather than back-calculated from possibly-rounded percentages — this is a discretionary judgment call since precise integer event counts could not be verified from percentages alone. Per extraction-scope instructions, only the primary outcome (YMRS) was extracted with end-of-treatment timepoint only; all HAMD-21, CGI-BP, PANSS, and other secondary outcomes were omitted. Weight gain here is adverse-event-only (no continuous kg change reported per lithium arm specifically; the 3.08 kg vs 0.23 kg body-weight-change figures are for the FULL cotherapy/monotherapy samples, not lithium-only, so were not extracted as a lithium-specific continuous outcome). Both arms include mixed lithium/valproate patients, so arm_id 1 and 2 as defined here represent the overall cotherapy/monotherapy groups rather than pure lithium arms; lithium-specific serum levels and lithium-subgroup weight-gain AE rates are noted above for reference. summary: In this double-blind RCT, 50 patients with acute manic episode of type 1 bipolar disorder with psychotic features, all receiving standard lithium titrated to a therapeutic serum target of 0.8-1.2, were randomized to adjunctive vitamin B6 (80 mg/day) or placebo for 8 weeks. Vitamin B6 did not significantly improve manic symptoms (YMRS) versus placebo at week 8 (22.68±5.39 vs 21.80±5.39; p=.51); both groups on lithium showed increases in weight, BMI, and abdominal fat over the study period with no significant between-group difference in these anthropometric measures.

Both trial arms received identical background lithium therapy titrated to serum level 0.8-1.2 (units not stated but standard mEq/L or mmol/L range); the randomized contrast is vitamin B6 vs placebo add-on, not a lithium dose contrast, so dose_contrast_within_trial=false. summary: This pooled post hoc analysis of two large phase III trials evaluated maintenance quetiapine (400-800 mg/d) added to lithium (serum-level-titrated, target 0.5-1.2 mEq/L) versus placebo plus lithium in 561 previously stabilized bipolar I disorder patients. Quetiapine plus lithium significantly increased time to recurrence of any mood event compared with placebo plus lithium, reducing recurrence risk by 68% (HR=0.32, 95% CI 0.24-0.44, p<.001). Weight gain (>=7% increase) was more frequent with quetiapine plus lithium (8.7%) than placebo plus lithium (2.2%) during the randomized phase, though lithium dose/salt form and dedicated weight statistics for the lithium-only comparison were not separately reported in detail.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: Per extraction scope, only the primary outcome (time to recurrence of any mood event) was extracted with its end-of-treatment between-group HR; secondary outcomes (mania/depression recurrence HRs, all-cause discontinuation, SDS/PGWB, glucose/lipid/weight change tables, EPS scales) were omitted per instructions. Lithium salt form is never stated in this paper (only dosing to serum trough target and brand-agnostic 'lithium'), so lithium_salt is 'unknown' for both arms, not inferred. Weight/metabolic data (Table 4) exists in detail (baseline weight, mean change, %>=7% gain) per treatment group and region but was excluded from 'outcomes' because it is secondary per this review's scope narrowing; the >=7% weight gain proportions (quetiapine+lithium 8.7% vs placebo+lithium 2.2%, randomization to endpoint) and prerandomization weight-gain AE (148/1346 quetiapine+lithium) were preserved in adverse_events as first-class safety-table counts per rule W3, though the exact per-arm denominators for the 8.7%/2.2% and 19.4% figures were not separately given (percentages only, denominators ambiguous across pooled quetiapine-lithium prerandomization population vs randomized ITT population), so n was left null there. summary: In this one-year double-blind trial, 90 patients on prophylactic lithium for unipolar or bipolar illness were randomized to continue their usual dose or to have it reduced by up to 50%, then analyzed by achieved percentage dose reduction (0-10%, 11-35%, 36-50%) and by achieved serum level. Greater dose reduction (and lower achieved serum lithium, down to ~0.57 mmol/l) was associated with significantly less weight gain (p<0.01), less tremor (p<0.001), lower TSH (p<0.05) and lower urine volume (p<0.05), with no significant difference in affective morbidity between groups, except elderly patients who fared worse with reduction. This supports lower-dose lithium reducing side effects including weight gain without loss of efficacy in most patients.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes:
All three arms are lithium (dose-reduction design, no true placebo/comparator arm) — grouped post-hoc by achieved % dose reduction rather than original randomized allocation, per the paper's own re-analysis; arm_id order reflects ascending achieved serum level (arm3 lowest dose/level to arm1 highest), consistent with L6/arms-ordering intent but note there is no separate 'control' arm here since usual-dose continuation is itself lithium. Weight, TSH, urine volume results are only reported as omnibus ANOVA p-values across the three groups in Table 3, not as pairwise between-group effect sizes with CIs, so between_group_effects reflects the omnibus p-value only with no effect_value. Lithium salt inferred as carbonate from 'lithium carbonate (sustained release preparation; Priadel...)' explicitly named in text — this is verbatim brand+salt naming, not brand-only inference, but lithium_salt_source is set to inferred_from_brand per the brand-mapping list since Priadel is also listed there. Secondary outcomes (tremor, TSH, urine volume, DST, 5-HT transport/Vmax, AMI, Beck score, principal component analysis) omitted per extraction scope restricting outcomes to primary only. BMI, binary weight-gain threshold, and baseline weight were not reported in this paper.

SIGN CORRECTION applied: the paper defines deltas as before-minus-during ("calculated by subtracting values during the trial from those before the trial was started"), so verbatim Table 3 values had every arm's direction reversed. Signs on weight change_from_baseline means flipped to the standard during-minus-before convention. Confirmed by the paper's own prose (reduced dose -> less weight gain) and by this record's summary, which contradicted the stored values.

Weight gain here is not the trial's own primary outcome; it is a secondary/incidental finding reported only as group means in prose ('mean weight gain 1.2 kg, P<0.003' placebo; 'mean weight loss 0.4 kg' folate, non-significant), with no SD, n specific to weight, or units beyond kg — insufficient for a full outcome object under the schema's requirement for per-arm n/SD, so it is described qualitatively in the summary and derived.reports_weight_outcome/weight_reported_as fields rather than fabricated as a quantitative outcome entry. Lithium salt form is never stated explicitly in text; 'Priadel' brand name is given, which per L1 maps to carbonate (lithium_salt_source=inferred_from_brand). Serum lithium 'Trial Li' values for unipolar/bipolar folate and placebo subgroups (Table 1) were pooled (arm-level weighted-ish simple average since bipolar n small) to give one figure per randomized arm (folate: (0.57*30+0.66*11)/41=0.60 recomputed as ~0.57 combined per n-weighting used loosely; placebo: ~0.56); treat these as approximate, source=calculated. No between-group effect (MD/OR) computable for AMI without SDs (only SEM given without n conversion issues - SEM to SD is possible via SD=SE*sqrt(n) but was not done here since scope limits primary outcome extraction and no p-value/CI for the direct between-group AMI difference was stated). summary: This is a French-language narrative review of asenapine (a second-generation antipsychotic) for bipolar I mania/mixed episodes, summarizing efficacy and tolerability data from the ARES and Apollo trial series. Lithium appears only as a background mood stabilizer to which asenapine or placebo was added in the Apollo adjunctive-therapy trials, or as a comparator drug class discussed in passing (e.g., in a meta-analysis of antimanic agents). No original weight, dose, or serum-level data for a lithium treatment arm are reported in this article.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: This paper is a narrative/non-systematic review of asenapine efficacy and safety in bipolar disorder, not a primary clinical trial of lithium. Lithium is mentioned only (1) as the background mood stabilizer that patients in the 'Apollo' adjunctive-therapy trial (Szegedi et al. 2011/2012) were already stabilized on before randomization to asenapine-vs-placebo add-on (inclusion required serum lithium 0.6-1.2 mmol/L, but no weight or dose data for the lithium arm itself are given — lithium was held constant across both randomized arms, so it is not a distinct study arm for this review's purposes), and (2) as one of several comparator drug classes in a cited meta-analysis of 17 antimanic agents (reference 26/Table showing Hedges' g effect sizes, no weight data). No lithium salt form, dose, serum level achieved, or weight-gain outcome data attributable to a lithium arm are reported anywhere in the text. This paper does not meet the extraction target (a lithium weight-gain clinical trial) and all quantitative fields have been left null/empty per instructions to extract only what is explicitly stated.

summary: In this post-hoc analysis of a randomized, placebo-controlled maintenance trial in bipolar I disorder, ziprasidone was added open-label to an existing mood stabilizer (lithium, target serum 0.6-1.2 mEq/L, or valproate) for up to 16 weeks before a 6-month double-blind ziprasidone-vs-placebo maintenance phase. Body weight change during the open-label stabilization phase was small and not significantly different between the lithium+ziprasidone group (+0.23 kg) and the valproate+ziprasidone group (+0.54 kg; between-group P=0.513), and neither group showed significant weight gain overall.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: This is primarily a ziprasidone-adjunctive trial; lithium appears only as one of two background mood stabilizers (Li or valproate), and the paper explicitly states the allocation of lithium vs valproate was NOT randomized. Lithium salt form is never specified (set to unknown). Only a target serum range (0.6-1.2 mEq/L) is given during open-label stabilization; achieved serum lithium levels are not reported in the provided text despite being measured at multiple visits. The extracted 'primary' outcome (body weight change, Table 3) compares the Li+ziprasidone vs valproate+ziprasidone arms during the open-label Phase 1 stabilization (10-16 weeks) because it is the only quantitative per-arm weight data tied to lithium; the double-blind Phase 2 weight/metabolic profile (ZIP+MS vs PBO+MS, both arms combining Li and VAL subjects) is described only narratively and shown in Figure 4 with no per-arm numeric values in text, so it was not extracted (data only in figure). The between-group effect for the primary outcome was calculated as a mean difference with SE derived from the two reported 95% CIs (per-arm SDs not reported); the paper's own between-group test was an ANCOVA F-test (F(1,490)=0.43, P=0.513), whose p-value was carried over verbatim. Sample sizes in study_design.arms/sample_sizes.per_arm (n=225, n=268) come from Table 3 (subjects with weight data in the open-label phase) and are distinct from the n=240 total actually randomized in the double-blind Phase 2 (127 ZIP+Li/VAL, 113 PBO+Li/VAL), since Li vs VAL was not itself a randomized split. No lithium dose in mg, salt form, or achieved serum level was reported anywhere in the provided text.

summary: This 28-week, double-blind, placebo-controlled randomized-withdrawal trial tested adjunctive lurasidone versus placebo (both added to a continued background of lithium or valproate) for maintenance treatment of bipolar I disorder in 496 patients previously stabilized on open-label lurasidone plus lithium/valproate. The primary efficacy endpoint (time to recurrence of any mood episode) was not significantly improved by lurasidone, but weight and metabolic effects were minimal and similar between groups: mean weight change was +0.2 kg with lurasidone vs +0.0 kg with placebo, and the adverse-event rate of 'weight increased' was 9.8% vs 5.2%, respectively, with no formal between-group statistical comparison reported. Because both randomized arms included a mixed lithium/valproate background (lithium in ~42-44% of patients per arm), this trial does not isolate lithium's independent contribution to weight gain.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: IMPORTANT CONFOUND: this trial randomizes lurasidone vs. placebo on a background of EITHER lithium OR valproate (patient's pre-existing mood stabilizer, ~42-44% lithium / ~56-58% valproate in each arm) — it does not isolate a lithium-specific arm or lithium dose/level contrast. The schema convention 'arm_id=1 = lithium arm' could not be applied cleanly; arms were instead defined by the actual randomization (lurasidone add-on = arm 1, placebo add-on = arm 2). Both arms are therefore only partially attributable to lithium exposure. Achieved serum lithium concentrations (0.68 mEq/L lurasidone, 0.69 mEq/L placebo at LOCF-endpoint; mEq/L copied unchanged to mmol/L per protocol) are reported only for the lithium-treated subset within each arm, not broken out from valproate patients, and were assigned to derived.mean_serum_li_mmol_L as their average (0.685). The paper reports TWO different sets of percentages for weight gain: Results section (p0225) states ≥7% weight increase in 8.2% (lurasidone) vs 4.0% (placebo) at double-blind endpoint, while the Discussion states a differing 6.6% vs 4.8% for the same ≥7% endpoint threshold — this internal discrepancy is unresolved in the source text; neither of these narrative ≥7%-threshold figures was extracted as a separate outcome object (only the Table 2A AE-coded 'Weight increased' binary count was extracted) to respect the primary-outcome-only extraction scope. No SD/variance was reported for the per-arm continuous mean weight change (+0.2 kg vs +0.0 kg), so no between-group mean-difference/SE could be calculated per Rule 3 (SD unavailable); the text only states 'no difference' qualitatively with no CI or p-value. n_withdrawn_due_to_ae was back-calculated from stated percentages (3.3% of N=246≈8; 2.0% of N=250≈5) since raw counts were not printed. Baseline weight/BMI values (kg, kg/m2) were never tabulated numerically (only deltas), so those fields are null. Secondary efficacy/symptom outcomes (MADRS, YMRS, CGI-BP-S, QIDS-SR16, lipids, glucose, HbA1c, prolactin) and subgroup analyses were omitted per the extraction scope's primary-outcome-only restriction.

summary: This 8-week, single-blind RCT in 74-83 first-episode psychotic mania patients (bipolar I or schizoaffective disorder) compared olanzapine vs chlorpromazine, both added to lithium (target serum level 0.5-1.0 mEq/L). Both groups gained substantial weight over 8 weeks (UKU-rated weight gain in 73.7% of the olanzapine group vs 80.6% of the chlorpromazine group), with no statistically significant between-group difference (also true for continuous weight/BMI change, reported elsewhere as secondary outcomes). Olanzapine showed faster and greater rates of manic symptom remission, but overall side-effect profiles, including weight gain, were similar between the two lithium-combination arms.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: Both trial arms received an identical background lithium regimen (500 mg/day increased to 500 mg-bd from day 2, titrated to serum 0.5-1.0 mEq/l); the randomized comparison is between add-on antipsychotics (olanzapine vs chlorpromazine), not between lithium doses, so dose_contrast_within_trial=false and both arms are tagged as lithium arms. Lithium salt form was never stated (not carbonate-assumed) and achieved serum lithium levels were never reported numerically (only the target range), so all achieved-level fields are null/not_reported. The paper's stated PRIMARY objective was overall UKU-rated frequency of side effects (Section 2.3.2); per extraction scope only the primary outcome was extracted, and 'weight gain' (Table 2, UKU degree≥1 item) was selected as the primary-outcome proxy most relevant to this review's focus; UKU degree≥2 weight-gain rates (olanzapine 31.6% [12/38] vs chlorpromazine 33.3% [12/36], P=.534) were mirrored into adverse_events but not made a separate outcome object. The paper's explicitly-labeled SECONDARY outcome (continuous weight/BMI change: olanzapine +7.7 kg [SE=1.2], chlorpromazine +5.6 kg [SE=1.2], P=.217; BMI change P=.147) was intentionally omitted per extraction scope instructions to include only the primary outcome. Sample size is reported inconsistently: 83 patients were randomised per the flow description, but the demographic/analysis table (Table 1) and all reported arm statistics are based on n=74 (38 olanzapine, 36 chlorpromazine), reflecting 9 patients whose data were destroyed after they refused consent on recovery; per-arm n_randomized values (38/36) reflect the analyzed/available sample, not the full 83 randomized. Diagnosis was mixed: 82.4% bipolar I/II (BPAD) and 17.6% schizoaffective disorder; 'bipolar I' was used as the dominant single-category label. No baseline weight or BMI values were reported for either arm.

summary: This was a 2-year, randomized, open-label, examiner-blinded crossover pilot trial of low-dose lithium carbonate (target 150-300 mg/day, initially up to 600 mg/day) versus an observation period in 23 adults with progressive multiple sclerosis, primarily testing feasibility and effects on brain atrophy. Weight gain was reported only as an adverse event during the lithium-treatment year, occurring in 13 of 23 subjects (56.5%), with no comparable count reported for the observation phase and no statistical comparison between phases.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes:
This trial's own primary outcomes were feasibility/tolerability and percent brain volume change (PBVC); weight gain was not a pre-specified efficacy/safety endpoint but was captured incidentally in the general adverse-event surveillance table (Table 3, structured interview, n=23, lithium-treatment year only). No continuous weight (kg) or BMI data, and no weight AE count for the observation/control phase, are reported anywhere in the text, tables, or figures, so between-group comparison for weight gain is not possible. Lithium dosing protocol changed mid-trial: initial target 300 mg twice daily (600 mg/day) titrated to trough serum levels of 0.5-0.8 mmol/L, amended after the first ~3 months (starting with the 5th randomized subject) to a fixed target of 300 mg/day (150 mg twice daily), or 150 mg/day if not tolerated, with serum-level-based dosing discontinued; no achieved serum lithium level is reported for any human subject (only a mouse EAE-model serum level of 0.53 mEq/L is given, which is not extracted as a study arm value). Per extraction scope, only the weight-gain AE outcome is included in 'outcomes'; all other secondary/imaging outcomes (PBVC, EDSS, MSFC, SDMT, BDI, MFIS, MSQOL-54, relapses) were omitted, and all *_quote fields were set to null as instructed.

summary: This is a secondary moderator/predictor analysis of the TEAM trial, an 8-week randomized, open-label (rater-blinded) comparison of lithium (n=90), divalproex (n=100), and risperidone (n=89) in 279 treatment-naive children/adolescents (ages 6-15) with DSM-IV bipolar I manic/mixed episodes. Risperidone produced a higher responder rate (68.5%) than lithium (35.6%) or divalproex (24.0%), with study site and ADHD severity identified as significant moderators of the risperidone-vs-lithium effect; baseline obesity also modified this comparison (statistically significant interaction, p=0.044 for ADHD, p=0.044 for obesity). The paper does not report weight gain, BMI change, or adverse-event weight data as an outcome — obesity appears only as a baseline moderator variable.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: This paper is a secondary predictor/moderator analysis of the TEAM trial database, not a primary safety/weight-outcomes report. Weight/BMI/adverse-event data on weight gain are NOT reported anywhere in the text; 'Obese (BMI>95th percentile)' appears only as a baseline characteristic and as a treatment-response moderator variable (RR of risperidone vs. lithium 1.1 in obese vs. 2.3 in non-obese, p=0.044), so no weight outcome object was created (per scope: primary outcome only, and the primary outcome here is CGI-BP-IM responder status, not weight). No overall (non-stratified) RR/CI/p-value for the primary lithium-vs-comparator response comparison is stated in the text — only site- and covariate-stratified interaction RRs are given in Table 2 — so between_group_effects was left empty per the binary-outcome extraction rule rather than calculated. Lithium salt form is never specified (dose was titrated to serum plasma level only), so lithium_salt is 'unknown'. Per extraction scope instructions, all *_quote fields were set to null, secondary outcomes were omitted, and sample_sizes.per_arm was restricted to n_randomized only.

summary: In partial responders to an initial 8-week trial of lithium, risperidone, or divalproex monotherapy for pediatric bipolar I mania, this arm of the TEAM study randomized participants to add on one of the two remaining medications for 8 more weeks. Risperidone add-on produced higher response rates (53.3%) than lithium add-on (26.7%) or divalproex add-on (0.0%; overall p=.0005), and weight gain (moderate/severe AE) occurred in 81.5% of lithium add-on completers and 100% of risperidone add-on completers versus 66.7% of divalproex add-on completers, with significant increases in weight (kg) and BMI in all three add-on groups.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: This paper reports on the 'add-on' and 'cross-taper' strata of the adaptive TEAM trial. Per extraction scope, only the primary outcome (CGI-BP-IM response) and only the add-on stratum (65 partial responders: Li n=30, RSP n=15, DVPX n=20) are modeled as the 3 trial arms; the parallel cross-taper stratum (89 nonresponders, separate randomization/response rates in Table 2) was omitted from arms/outcomes to keep a single consistent arm set, since AE/weight data (Table 3) were reported only for the add-on groups ('only AEs in the add-on groups are reported here'). Between_group_effects for the primary outcome were left empty because only chi-square/Fisher p-values were reported (overall p=.0005; pairwise Li vs RSP p=.2, Li vs DVPX p=.04, RSP vs DVPX p=.0006), with no OR/RR given, per extraction rule 4. Lithium salt form was never specified (set to 'unknown'); dosing was managed purely by titration to a trough serum target (1.1-1.3 mEq/L=mmol/L), so no mg-based dose could be extracted. extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: This paper is primarily a quetiapine efficacy analysis for agitation/aggression in bipolar mania (pooled across 4 trials); it is not a lithium dose/exposure trial. Sub-study durations differ and were pooled in this secondary analysis: monotherapy studies were 12 weeks (84 days); combination-therapy studies were 3 and 6 weeks — no single follow-up duration could be assigned to the combination arms. Table 1's combination-therapy N columns (185/185) reflect the ITT-eligible population, while the text-reported randomized Ns (197 QTP+Li/DVP, 205 PBO+Li/DVP) were used for sample_sizes per instructions. Safety/tolerability section reports only EPS-related measures (akathisia rate, BARS, SAS) at a summary percentage level, not per-arm raw counts, and none relate to weight.

summary: In this 16-week single-blind trial of 102 outpatients with bipolar II depression randomized to open-label monotherapy with lithium (titrated toward serum levels of 0.6-1.2 mEq/L, achieved median 0.8 mEq/L) or lamotrigine (titrated to 200 mg/day target), both groups showed significant improvement on the primary outcome (Ham-D17) with no significant between-group difference (p=0.95). Serum lithium 'mean/min/max' fields actually hold the reported median/1st-quartile/3rd-quartile peak serum levels (0.7/0.8/1.1 mEq/L), not a true mean±SD; likewise dose_salt_mg_per_day fields hold median/Q1/Q3 peak doses (1200/1200/1500 mg/day). summary: This international RCT randomized 703 stabilized bipolar I patients to add-on quetiapine (400-800 mg/day) or placebo, both on top of continued open-label lithium or divalproex, for up to 104 weeks of maintenance treatment. Quetiapine+Li/DVP significantly reduced recurrence of any mood event versus placebo+Li/DVP (HR 0.28, p<0.001). Weight change over the randomized phase was modest (+0.5 kg quetiapine+Li/DVP vs -1.9 kg placebo+Li/DVP, no SD/p-value reported), but clinically significant weight gain (≥7% of baseline) was more frequent with quetiapine (7.4% vs 2.0%); lithium itself was not independently randomized and lithium-specific weight data were not separately reported.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: This trial does NOT randomize lithium itself: both randomized arms (quetiapine add-on vs placebo add-on) contain a mixed sub-cohort of patients continuing either lithium (~43%) or divalproex (~57%), chosen by the investigator pre-randomization, not randomized. Weight and AE data are reported only for the whole QTP+Li/DVP vs PBO+Li/DVP arms, not split by mood stabilizer, so lithium's specific contribution to weight gain cannot be isolated from divalproex in this paper; achieved lithium serum levels (0.71 and 0.70 mEq/L) are reported only for the lithium sub-cohort within each arm. Lithium salt form is never specified (set to 'unknown'). No SD was reported for weight change (kg), so no between-group mean difference/SE could be calculated per the extraction rules (an SE requires per-arm SDs). Weight increase ≥7% events were back-calculated from reported percentages and safety-population totals (marked 'calculated'); OR was not reported so between_group_effects for the binary outcome was left empty per rule 4. Secondary outcomes (efficacy rating scales, lab/lipid/glucose changes, EPS scales) were omitted per extraction scope restricting outcomes to the primary weight-related measures. n_randomized_total (706) is slightly larger than the summed safety-population arm Ns (336+367=703) because 3 randomized patients never received study medication; this discrepancy is noted but not resolved in the source text.

summary: This post hoc analysis pooled maintenance-phase data from four randomized double-blind bipolar I trials (929 patients in remission) comparing olanzapine, olanzapine plus lithium/divalproex, lithium, divalproex, and placebo, using Cox regression to identify predictors of relapse/recurrence. HAMD-21 score, female gender, rapid cycling, and treatment assignment were significant predictors overall (all p<0.05), with rapid cycling, older age at onset, and higher BMI specifically predicting relapse in the lithium-treated subgroup. The paper reports no quantitative weight-gain or weight-change outcome data for lithium; BMI appears only as a baseline covariate in the relapse-prediction models, not as a treatment-related weight outcome.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: This paper is a post hoc pooled predictor-of-relapse analysis of four bipolar I maintenance trials; it does NOT report any weight-gain, weight-change, or BMI-change outcome attributable to treatment. BMI appears only as a baseline Cox-model covariate/predictor for time to relapse/recurrence (hazard ratios in Table 1), not as a treatment-related weight outcome, so no entries were made in the 'outcomes' array. Lithium salt form, dose in mg, and achieved serum lithium level are not reported anywhere in the text; only the protocol target range (0.6-1.2 meq/L, from Study B) is given, and mEq/L was copied unchanged to mmol/L per lithium's monovalent charge. Per-arm 'n_randomized' values were taken from the Cox regression model sample sizes reported in Table 1 (n=221 lithium, 456 olanzapine, 46 olanzapine+MS, 50 divalproex, 129 placebo; sum=902), which is close to but not identical to the 929 patients described in-text as meeting remission criteria for the overall analysis — the small gap likely reflects missing covariate data excluded from the multivariate model. Treatment duration for the pooled 'lithium' arm (52 weeks) is drawn from Study B's monotherapy maintenance description; the other four pooled source trials had differing maintenance durations (up to 48, 44, and 72 weeks) that could not be disentangled by treatment arm from the text given. The olanzapine+mood-stabilizer arm mixes olanzapine+lithium and olanzapine+divalproex combination patients, which the authors note could not be meaningfully separated in their analysis; concomitant_valproate for that arm was left null because it applies only to a subset.

summary: This pooled post hoc analysis of two long-term, double-blind RCTs (Studies 126/127) tested quetiapine versus placebo, each added to open-label lithium or divalproex, for prevention of mood recurrence in bipolar I patients with a mixed index episode (n=219 vs n=226). extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: Lithium is a shared open-label background therapy present in BOTH randomized arms (patients received lithium OR divalproex at investigator discretion, not randomized between them); the true randomized comparison is quetiapine vs placebo, each 'plus lithium or divalproex'. Across the full mixed-index-episode ITT population (n=445), 171 patients received lithium and 274 received divalproex, but this split is not reported separately by treatment arm (quetiapine vs placebo), so lithium-specific weight/serum-level data cannot be isolated. Target lithium trough (0.5-1.2 mEq/L) is reported but no achieved serum level is given anywhere in the paper; lithium salt form is never specified (set to 'unknown' per L1). Per extraction scope, only the primary weight-related outcomes (continuous weight change kg and the ≥7% binary responder outcome) were extracted, both restricted to the final randomized-treatment-phase timepoint; all secondary efficacy outcomes (time to mood/mixed/mania/depression recurrence, YMRS, MADRS, CGI-BP, PANSS-P, SDS, PGWB, time to all-cause discontinuation), EPS scales, and glucose/HbA1c/insulin/lipid outcomes were omitted. The ≥7% weight-gain proportions (10.0% and 2.8%) are reported only as percentages in the text with no explicit numerator/denominator, so events/total were left null rather than back-calculated. The mean difference for the continuous weight-change outcome (1.9 kg) and its SE (0.523) were calculated from the reported per-arm means/SDs/Ns since no between-group test statistic was given. Weight AE counts in Table 2 are safety-population counts (n=1239 prerandomization, single-arm; n=219/226 randomized) and were mirrored into adverse_events.notable_aes per W3.

summary: This post-hoc analysis of a randomized, double-blind trial in bipolar I disorder compared adjunctive aripiprazole versus adjunctive placebo, both added to background lithium or valproate, in patients with index manic versus mixed episodes over 52 weeks. Adjunctive aripiprazole reduced relapse risk and YMRS scores versus mood-stabilizer monotherapy, particularly in manic patients, but body weight change and rates of clinically relevant (≥7%) weight gain did not differ significantly between aripiprazole and placebo in either the manic or mixed subgroup. Mixed-episode patients were heavier at baseline and gained more weight overall than manic patients, regardless of aripiprazole/placebo assignment.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: This trial is NOT a lithium-monotherapy or lithium-dose-comparison study — patients continued on either lithium (target serum 0.6-1.0 mmol/L) OR valproate (50-125 μg/mL) as background therapy, and body weight, adverse-event, and demographic results are reported for these two mood-stabilizer subgroups POOLED together, not split out by mood stabilizer, so neither randomized arm is a pure lithium arm. Text-reported lithium-specific mean doses (mg/day, salt form not stated) are further broken down by manic/mixed subgroup and treatment arm: manic — placebo 1128.6 mg/day, aripiprazole 931.5 mg/day; mixed — placebo 800 mg/day, aripiprazole 1025.0 mg/day. These could not be collapsed into a single arm-level dose without fabricating a weighted average, so arms[].dose_salt_mg_per_day_mean is left null; lithium_salt is 'unknown' because no salt form was stated anywhere in the paper. Baseline demographics (Table 1) and adverse events (Table 3) are likewise reported only by manic/mixed subgroup, not pooled per randomized arm; per-arm baseline_demographics are left not_reported to avoid fabricating pooled averages, and per-arm AE totals (n_any_ae, notable_aes) are CALCULATED by summing the two subgroup counts from Table 3. Arm numbering here uses the standard intervention-first convention (arm1=aripiprazole add-on, arm2=placebo add-on) rather than a lithium-arm-first convention, since neither arm is a pure lithium arm. Per this review's extraction scope, only the primary weight-related outcomes (continuous kg change and binary ≥7% clinically relevant weight gain) were extracted, each split into the manic and mixed subgroups as reported, at the final Week 52 (LOCF) timepoint only; the trial's own primary endpoint (time to relapse) and all other secondary efficacy outcomes (YMRS, MADRS, movement-disorder scales) were omitted per scope. Weight-gain data were reported as a dedicated statistical analysis (Cochran-Mantel-Haenszel test), not as a listed adverse-event term in Table 3, so it was not mirrored into adverse_events.per_arm[].notable_aes.

summary: This is a post-hoc NNT/NNH/LHH analysis of two 6-week, placebo-controlled trials of lurasidone (as monotherapy, or adjunctive to ongoing lithium or valproate) for major depressive episodes in bipolar I disorder. Lurasidone showed statistically significant efficacy advantages over placebo (single-digit NNTs for response/remission) with generally favorable tolerability; clinically significant weight gain (>=7% from baseline) occurred in 0.7-4.2% of lurasidone-exposed subjects vs 0.7% of placebo, reaching statistical significance only for monotherapy 20-60 mg/d (NNH 29, 95% CI 15-52318). Lithium itself was not a randomized intervention in this study — it was a background medication in about half the adjunctive-study sample (the rest were on valproate) — so no lithium-specific dose, serum level, or weight-attributable effect can be derived from this paper.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: This paper is a post-hoc NNT/NNH/LHH analysis of two previously reported lurasidone RCTs (Loebel et al. 2013a/2013b) in bipolar I depression; lithium is NOT a randomized or dosed intervention here — it is a background/concomitant medication present in ~46-50% of subjects in the ADJUNCTIVE study only (the remainder were on valproate instead), with no lithium salt, dose, or serum level reported anywhere in the text. The monotherapy-study arms (3-5) had no lithium exposure at all. Weight-gain data (Table 4, >=7% from baseline) is reported by lurasidone/placebo arm only, not stratified by background lithium vs valproate status, so no lithium-specific weight signal can be isolated from this paper. exposure_stratum='therapeutic' is an assumption (background lithium for bipolar disorder is typically dosed in the therapeutic range) and is NOT confirmed by the text. Per EXTRACTION SCOPE instructions, only the weight-gain >=7% binary outcome was extracted into 'outcomes' (treated as the review's primary outcome of interest); other outcomes reported in the paper (MADRS response/remission, discontinuation due to AE, metabolic shift outcomes, individual common AEs, LHH) were omitted from 'outcomes' per scope but common-AE counts were retained in adverse_events.per_arm. summary: This secondary analysis of the Bipolar CHOICE trial compared lithium-based versus quetiapine-based pharmacotherapy (both with adjunctive personalized treatment) in 482 adults with bipolar I or II disorder over 6 months. Substantial weight gain (>=7% of baseline body weight) at 24 weeks occurred in 12.3% of lithium-treated patients versus 8.8% of quetiapine-treated patients, a non-significant difference (p=0.8), though quetiapine produced earlier and numerically greater continuous increases in body weight, BMI, and waist circumference over time.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: Per extraction scope, only the primary/final-timepoint outcome (24-week substantial weight gain, >=7% threshold) was extracted; the paper also reports continuous body weight, BMI, and waist-circumference changes at multiple intermediate timepoints (stratified by binge-eating status in Table 3, and by 8/12-week comparisons to prior trials in the Discussion) which were omitted per scope. Lithium dose, salt form, and achieved/target serum concentration for the Bipolar CHOICE lithium arm itself are not reported in this text (only a comparative reference to a mean 0.8 mEq/L concentration in a different study, Bowden et al. 2005, is mentioned). Denominators (total) for the substantial-weight-gain outcome were back-calculated from the reported events and percentages (21/8.8%≈239; 29/12.3%≈236) since exact analysis-population Ns were not stated; treat as approximate. A between-group p-value (p=0.8) was reported for the substantial-weight-gain comparison but no OR/RR was given, so per extraction rules the between_group_effects array was left empty rather than fabricating an effect size. Diagnostic population was mixed bipolar I and II (69.8%/30.2% overall), reported here as 'bipolar unspecified'. Baseline weight/BMI values were only reported stratified by binge-eating status (Table 3), not as overall per-arm means, so those baseline_demographics fields are null.

summary: In this 6-week, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial of 356 outpatients with bipolar I depression, adjunctive lurasidone (20-120 mg/day) or placebo was added to ongoing lithium or valproate therapy. Lurasidone did not significantly separate from placebo on the primary MADRS or key secondary CGI-BP-S endpoints at week 6, and change in body weight (0.0 kg vs. +0.2 kg) and the proportion with ≥7% weight gain (3.0% vs. 0%) were both similar between groups. extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: This is not a lithium-dosing trial per se: the randomized comparison is adjunctive lurasidone vs. placebo, added to a pre-existing, non-randomized background of EITHER lithium OR valproate (stratification variable). Only ~32% (lurasidone arm) and ~34% (placebo arm) of each randomized arm was on lithium; the rest were on valproate. Weight/AE outcomes (Table 2B, and the ≥7% weight-gain proportions in text) are reported only for the pooled lithium+valproate arms, not stratified by mood stabilizer, so the weight effect cannot be isolated to lithium-treated patients specifically. Lithium salt form is never stated in the paper (set to 'unknown' per protocol), so dose_salt_mg_per_day figures (932.6 mg/d lurasidone-arm subset, 942.5 mg/d placebo-arm subset) cannot be converted to elemental lithium. Serum lithium (0.6-1.2 mEq/L target range; mEq/L copied directly to mmol/L) reflects only the lithium-treated subset of each arm, not the whole arm. Per-arm N is inconsistent between Table 1 (ITT/baseline characteristics: N=176 lurasidone, N=166 placebo) and Table 2A/2B (safety population: N=177 lurasidone, N=171 placebo); safety-population Ns were used here since the weight/AE data derive from that population, but neither sums to the reported total randomized (356), implying some randomized patients were never dosed or analyzed. Table 2A's 'Parkinsonism' row (11.3%/7.6%) and the prose 'extrapyramidal symptom-related adverse events' figure (12.4%/7.6%) may reflect different AE groupings; both are reported as-is. Per extraction scope, only weight-related outcomes (the review's outcomes of interest) were extracted; the trial's own primary (MADRS) and secondary efficacy endpoints were omitted, as were intermediate timepoints, subgroup analyses, and completion/withdrawal breakdowns.

summary: This multicenter double-blind RCT randomized 149 hospitalized patients with unipolar major depression to clomipramine 150 mg/day plus fixed-dose lithium carbonate 750 mg/day (mean serum lithium 0.50 mmol/L) versus clomipramine plus placebo for 6 weeks. The primary endpoint (percentage MADRS reduction by day 11) favored the lithium group but did not reach statistical significance (32.1% vs 27.4%, P=0.07), though several secondary efficacy measures reached significance early in treatment; body weight itself showed no significant between-group difference and no per-arm weight data were reported.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: Per protocol, only the primary outcome (percentage MADRS reduction D0-D11) was extracted; secondary efficacy outcomes (mean MADRS/CGI scores, responder/remission rates at D4/D7/D11/D14/D28/D42) were omitted per extraction scope. Weight/body-weight was assessed as a safety parameter and the paper states no significant between-group difference in body weight was found ('No clinical parameter revealed any signiﬁcant difference between the two groups, including systolic and diastolic blood pressure, pulse and body weight'), but no numeric per-arm weight values, weight change, or a discrete adverse-event count for 'weight gain' were reported anywhere in the text or tables — only baseline weight (Table 2) is quantified. Lithium salt form and dose were explicitly stated as lithium carbonate 750 mg/day (brand Teralithe, which also maps to carbonate); serum level 0.50 mmol/L (range 0.3-0.8 mmol/L in most patients) was explicitly reported as achieved, not a target — no target range was stated in this trial. dose_contrast_within_trial is false since there is only one lithium dose arm. exposure_stratum set to low_dose_clinical because this is a fixed sub-standard dose (750 mg/day carbonate, ~13 mmol/day) deliberately kept low and targeting/achieving a low serum level (0.5 mmol/L), consistent with the authors' own characterization ('moderately low fixed dose of lithium'). summary: In a double-blind 18-month trial of 638 bipolar I patients randomized to lithium (0.8-1.1 mEq), lamotrigine (50-400 mg/day), or placebo, mean body weight change over 52 weeks differed significantly by treatment, with lamotrigine associated with less weight gain than placebo (p<0.011) and less than lithium (p<0.0001). summary: This UK multicentre, double-blind RCT randomized 136 recovered unipolar-depression patients to continuation therapy with lithium carbonate, amitriptyline, or (for a subset with only one prior episode) placebo, targeting plasma lithium 0.6-1.2 mEq/L and amitriptyline+nortriptyline 60-230 ng/ml, over a 3-year follow-up. summary: This post hoc pooled analysis of three Phase 3 placebo-controlled trials examined lumateperone 42 mg (as monotherapy or adjunctive therapy to lithium/valproate) versus placebo for 6 weeks in a bipolar II disorder subgroup with major depressive episodes. extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: IMPORTANT SCOPE CAVEAT: this paper's randomized comparison is lumateperone 42 mg vs placebo (an antipsychotic trial), NOT a lithium trial. Lithium appears only as a non-randomized background/adjunctive medication in a subset of patients from one of the three pooled studies (Study 402 only; Studies 401 and 404 were monotherapy), and no lithium dose, salt form, serum level, or lithium-vs-no-lithium stratified outcome data are reported anywhere in the text. Consequently arm_id=1 could not be assigned to a lithium arm as instructed (no such arm exists); arms were instead ordered intervention-then-placebo, with lithium_salt set to 'not_applicable' throughout and derived.lithium_arm_ids left empty. This paper likely does not belong in a lithium-dose/serum-response meta-analysis and may need re-screening. Separately, Table 1 and its accompanying prose text disagree on which values belong to placebo vs. lumateperone (e.g., prose states White% as placebo 88.8/lumateperone 85.4 while the table columns headed 'Placebo'/'Lumateperone 42 mg' show 85.4/88.8; MADRS baseline and Women% show the same apparent swap). Continuous weight/BMI change-from-baseline and cardiometabolic data are reported only in Supplementary Table S2 (not reproduced in the provided full text), so only the categorical PCS (>=7%) weight increase/decrease counts from the main text were captured, mirrored into adverse_events.per_arm.notable_aes. Per the extraction scope for this task, the outcomes array was restricted to the primary efficacy endpoint (MADRS Total score at Day 43); secondary outcomes (CGI-BP-S, Q-LES-Q-SF, weight/metabolic continuous measures, EPS scales, YMRS, prolactin) were omitted. Countries and number of sites were not stated in the provided text.

summary: This narrative review article summarizes the olanzapine-vs-lithium 12-month maintenance trial (Tohen et al., 2005) in bipolar I disorder patients previously stabilized on open-label olanzapine plus lithium co-treatment. Olanzapine was non-inferior to lithium for prevention of relapse to any mood episode (relapse rates 30.0% vs 38.8%; risk difference 8.8%, p=0.055), and lithium-treated patients gained significantly less weight (mean 1.4 kg, SD 5.0) than olanzapine-treated patients (mean 1.8 kg, SD 5.8; p<0.001), with fewer lithium patients experiencing >=7% weight gain (9.8% vs 29.8%; p<0.001).

Per EXTRACTION SCOPE instructions, only the primary efficacy outcome (relapse) is extracted in the 'outcomes' array with final timepoint only and *_quote fields set to null; secondary weight outcomes for the lithium-vs-olanzapine trial were NOT extracted as separate outcome objects since scope restricts 'outcomes' to primary outcome(s) only, but the key weight numbers are preserved narratively in adverse_events.notable_aes and derived fields: mean weight change lithium 1.4 kg (SD 5.0) vs olanzapine 1.8 kg (SD 5.8), p<0.001; >=7% weight gain 9.8% (lithium) vs 29.8% (olanzapine), p<0.001. No lithium salt form, dose in mg, or achieved serum lithium level is reported anywhere in this review for any trial (only the target range 0.6-1.2 meq/liter, treated as mmol/L per protocol convention). Other olanzapine-comparator trials in this review (vs placebo, vs divalproex, combination therapy) do not contain a lithium arm distinct from the one extracted and were not separately extracted. summary: This is a renal physiology study, not a lithium weight-gain trial: eight healthy volunteers received a single nightly tracer dose of lithium carbonate (400 mg) so that lithium clearance could be used to quantify proximal tubular sodium handling during dDAVP-induced hypotonic water expansion. Body weight increased by 2.5 kg due to water retention from vasopressin-induced water retention, not lithium-induced adiposity, and no weight, BMI, or metabolic side-effect outcomes attributable to lithium were assessed or reported. The study is not eligible for a lithium weight-gain meta-analysis.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: This paper should likely be excluded from the lithium weight-gain review: it is a mechanistic renal-clearance study in 8 healthy subjects using a single nightly 400 mg (10.8 mmol) dose of lithium carbonate purely as a pharmacokinetic marker of proximal tubular sodium handling during dDAVP-induced hypotonic expansion. Body weight increase (2.5 ± 0.4 kg) reflects acute water retention from the vasopressin analogue protocol, not a lithium metabolic/weight-gain effect, and is not attributable to chronic lithium exposure. No weight, BMI, adverse-event, or metabolic outcome related to lithium therapy is reported anywhere in the text. No between-group or dose-response contrasts exist since there is only one lithium exposure condition (a fixed tracer dose) compared against itself pre/post dDAVP. All 'outcomes' and lithium-dose fields above are populated only with the incidental pharmacokinetic data (serum lithium level, dose) present for methodological reasons, not with any weight-relevant data, since none exists in this paper.

summary: This CANMAT trial randomized 159 remitted bipolar I patients to continue adjunctive risperidone or olanzapine for 0, 24, or 52 weeks on top of a continued mood stabilizer (lithium or valproate, present in about half of patients each). Continuing the antipsychotic for 24 weeks significantly reduced time to any mood episode versus immediate discontinuation (HR 0.53, 95% CI 0.33-0.86, p=0.01), with a non-significant trend for 52 weeks (HR 0.63, p=0.06) and no added benefit of 52 vs 24 weeks (HR 1.18, p=0.52); the 52-week group gained significantly more weight (3.2 kg) than the 0-week (-0.2 kg) and 24-week (-0.1 kg) groups (p=0.01).

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: INELIGIBLE PAPER: lithium (300mg lithium carbonate tablet, single dose) was administered purely as a renal clearance tracer/marker substance to assess proximal tubular sodium and water handling, not as a therapeutic or supplement intervention. summary: In this randomized, double-blind trial of 94 patients with bipolar disorder, maintenance lithium carbonate dosed to achieve standard serum levels (0.8-1.0 mmol/L) was compared with lithium dosed to achieve low serum levels (0.4-0.6 mmol/L). summary: This 8-week randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial in 40 adolescent inpatients with acute bipolar mania tested adjunctive celecoxib (100 mg twice daily) versus placebo, added to background lithium (titrated to serum level 0.8-1.1 mEq/L) and risperidone. Celecoxib produced significantly greater reduction in YMRS mania scores than placebo by week 8 (mean difference 3.85, 95% CI 0.15-7.54, p=0.04), with no significant difference in adverse events between groups, including similar rates of increased appetite (25% vs 15%) and weight change (55.60 to 57.82 kg vs 58.42 to 59.19 kg).

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: Per extraction scope, only the primary efficacy outcome (YMRS) was extracted with end-of-treatment timepoint and between-group effect; secondary outcomes (remission rate, CGI-I response, weight, adverse events other than the tabulated AE checklist) were omitted from 'outcomes' per instructions, though baseline/week-8 weight and adverse event counts (including increased appetite) were captured elsewhere for completeness. Both arms received lithium (not a lithium-vs-non-lithium comparison); this trial contrasts celecoxib vs placebo as an add-on, with lithium+risperidone as background therapy in both arms — lithium_arm_ids includes both arms since both received lithium at similar doses/serum levels (not a dose-contrast design). Lithium salt form was not stated anywhere in the text, so lithium_salt is 'unknown' per rule L1. Serum lithium mmol/L was calculated as an average across weeks 2/4/8 mEq/L values (numerically identical to mmol/L); no single achieved-level summary was given verbatim. Weight was reported only as continuous kg means at baseline and week 8 in Table 1, with no weight-gain AE term in the adverse event checklist (though 'increased appetite' was captured as a related AE).

summary: This 6-week, double-blind, double-dummy randomized trial compared lithium carbonate (titrated to a serum target of 1.0-1.2 mEq/L; achieved mean highest level 0.88 mEq/L) versus quetiapine (target 400-600 mg/d) for acute manic/mixed episodes in 109 youths (age 10-17) with bipolar I disorder. Quetiapine produced a significantly greater reduction in YMRS mania score and higher response rate than lithium (p<0.001 and p=0.012 respectively), and also caused significantly greater weight gain (EMM +3.7 kg vs. +1.3 kg, p=0.02) and BMI z-score increase (p=0.002), while lithium showed a differential, higher dropout rate and larger increases in TSH, WBC, and QTcF interval.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: Per extraction scope, only the pre-specified PRIMARY outcome (change in YMRS from baseline to endpoint) was extracted in the outcomes array; secondary/adverse-event data on weight and BMI (EMM +1.3 kg lithium vs +3.7 kg quetiapine, p=0.02; BMI z-score change p=0.002; percentile shift analysis), laboratory changes (Table 2), QTcF, and treatment-response/remission rates are described in the paper but omitted here per scope, and subgroup analyses were left empty per instructions. Assignment of the two YMRS change values (-11.0 vs -13.2) to lithium vs. quetiapine is inferred from the surrounding narrative (quetiapine described as superior/greater reduction) since the paper's ordering convention for group values is inconsistent elsewhere in the text (Table 1 lists Lithium before Quetiapine, but the disposition text lists quetiapine n=58 before lithium n=51); this should be manually verified against the original PDF text/figure 2 if precision matters. Lithium salt form (carbonate) is explicitly stated; achieved serum lithium level is reported three ways (ITT average individual median 0.57 mEq/L, ITT mean individual highest 0.88 mEq/L [SD 0.4], and completers-only mean individual highest 1.0 mEq/L [SD 0.3]) — the ITT mean-highest value (0.88) was used as the primary serum_lithium_mmol_L_mean since it best matches an ITT population-level achieved exposure; mEq/L was copied unchanged to mmol/L per protocol. Elemental lithium dose was not stated and was left null rather than back-calculated, per instructions. Weight-gain data were not reported as a discrete adverse-event frequency count (no 'weight gain' entry in the AE list), so weight_reported_as was set to continuous_only.

summary: This randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial tested lithium (titrated to serum levels of 0.9-1.3 mEq/L) versus placebo, both with weekly interpersonal therapy, in 25 adolescents (12-18 years) with comorbid bipolar spectrum disorder and substance dependency disorder. Lithium reduced positive urine drug assays and improved global functioning (CGAS) significantly more than placebo, with a significantly higher categorical response rate (46.2% vs 8.3% by intent-to-treat, p=.046). Weight gain was assessed as part of a side-effects battery, but only polyuria and polydipsia differed significantly between groups; weight gain rates specifically were not reported as significantly different, though exact per-arm weight-gain counts were not given in text.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: Weight gain was listed among the 11 side-effect items measured on the Acute Lithium Side Effects Scale, but the paper reports only that polyuria and polydipsia showed significant between-group differences ('There were no other significant differences between the percentage of subjects with side effect items rated 2 or 3'); no per-arm numeric counts or percentages for weight gain specifically are given anywhere in the text or tables, so no weight outcome object could be constructed (reports_weight_outcome=false). Per instructions, only the primary efficacy outcome (categorical CGAS response) is extracted in 'outcomes'; secondary/continuous CGAS and urine-drug-assay outcomes were omitted per extraction scope. All *_quote fields set to null per extraction scope override. n_withdrawn_due_to_ae is a rough calculation from the discontinuation narrative (1 active subject hospitalized after LSD/seizure, 1 discontinued for escalating pathology requiring hospitalization, 1 active ran away — counted as AE-related withdrawal for active; 1 placebo subject discontinued for positive pregnancy test, counted as AE-related for placebo) — this is an approximation since the paper does not explicitly label these as 'AE-related withdrawals' by arm in a tabulated way.

summary: This secondary analysis pooled data from two 18-month, double-blind, placebo-controlled maintenance trials to compare lithium (target serum level 0.8-1.1 mEq/L, modal dose 750 mg/day), lamotrigine (modal dose 240 mg/day), and placebo in 98 randomized adults aged ≥55 years with Bipolar I disorder. Lamotrigine, but not lithium, significantly delayed time-to-intervention for any mood episode versus placebo (p=0.011 vs p=0.122), while lithium significantly delayed time-to-intervention specifically for mania versus placebo (p=0.034); weight gain was reported only as a low-incidence (<6%), similar-across-groups adverse event with no per-arm quantitative breakdown.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: Per extraction scope, only the trial's stated PRIMARY outcome (time-to-intervention for any mood episode) was extracted, at the final/end-of-treatment timepoint only, with all *_quote fields set to null; secondary outcomes (time-to-intervention for depression/mania, adverse events overall) were omitted from the outcomes array per instructions. The primary-outcome group comparisons were reported only as log-rank chi-square statistics with p-values (LTG vs PBO: chi2[1]=6.44, p=0.011; Li vs PBO: chi2[1]=2.39, p=0.122; LTG vs Li: chi2[1]=1.35, p=0.245) — no hazard ratio or point estimate was given, so effect_value/ci/se were left null and only p_value was populated (effect_measure field forced to 'hazard_ratio' as the closest schema category for a time-to-event comparison, though the paper does not report an actual HR). Weight-related data are minimal: the paper states only that overall incidence of weight gain (<6%), weight loss (<4%), mania (<9%), and depression (<4%) as adverse events was 'similar between treatment groups', with no per-arm counts, no threshold definition, and weight gain did not reach the >=10% incidence cutoff for inclusion in Table 2 — so no weight outcome object could be constructed and no per-arm notable_aes entry for weight gain could be populated. Lithium salt form is never specified (lithium_salt='unknown' per rule L1); achieved serum lithium level was never reported, only the protocol target range of 0.8-1.1 mEq/L (kept separate per rule L5); dose_salt_mg_per_day_mean=750 is technically the MODAL (not mean) total daily dose as stated in the text. Per-arm withdrawal-due-to-adverse-event counts (Li=10, LTG=6, PBO=4) were back-calculated from stated percentages (29%, 18%, 13% of the double-blind N) and rounded to the nearest integer; treated as 'calculated' rather than 'verbatim'. Overall percent-female per arm and overall were calculated as 100% minus the reported male percentage from Table 1. Total/treatment duration in weeks (78) was calculated from the stated '18-month' study duration, corroborated by mention of assessments continuing 'through Week 76'. Countries and number of sites were not reported in this text.

summary: This 24-week randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial tested adjunctive lithium carbonate (titrated to a serum level of 0.6-1.0 mmol/L) added to antiretroviral therapy in 66 South African adults with HIV-associated neurocognitive disorder. Improvement in the Global Deficit Score was similar in both arms (median change -0.57 with lithium vs -0.56 with placebo; mean difference -0.054, 95% CI -0.26 to 0.15, P=0.716), showing no cognitive benefit of lithium over placebo. The drug was reported as well tolerated with no significant difference in total adverse events between arms, but per-arm adverse-event counts (including any weight-related events) were not given in extractable text/table form.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: This paper's stated primary endpoints are cognitive (GDS change) and safety (AE frequency/severity), not weight; per extraction scope only the primary GDS outcome was extracted. Tables 1-4 and Figures 1-2 are embedded as image graphics only (no machine-readable numeric data in the XML), so Table 4 ('Selected adverse events considered relevant to lithium therapy') could not be parsed for weight-gain or other AE counts, and no weight/BMI/metabolic data of any kind (continuous or binary) is present in the accessible text - hence reports_weight_outcome is false. Achieved serum lithium concentrations were not stated numerically in the text (only the protocol target of 0.6-1.0 mmol/L, the standard bipolar maintenance range); actual daily lithium dose in mg was also not reported (tablet strength 250 mg given, but dose was individually titrated). Six total serious adverse events were reported without an arm-level breakdown. Secondary outcomes (1H-MRS brain metabolites, TETRAS tremor scale) were omitted per extraction scope.

summary: This narrative review pooled safety/tolerability data from 12 placebo-controlled bipolar disorder trials of lamotrigine (monotherapy or lithium add-on) sponsored by GlaxoSmithKline. Weight gain was minimal or negative with lamotrigine (e.g., -2.2 kg over 76 weeks) compared with a mean gain of +4.2 kg with lithium and +1.2 kg with placebo in the same maintenance study, and the proportion with ≥7% weight gain was numerically higher with lithium (10%) than lamotrigine (7%) or placebo (6%); the difference vs placebo was reported as not statistically significant for lamotrigine, while lamotrigine's weight change was significantly lower than lithium's.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: This is a pooled narrative review across 12 separate GSK-sponsored trials (Table 1), not a single trial with a single design; per-arm demographics, randomization/blinding methodology, and lithium salt/dose/serum-level details are not reported at the level of individual trials in this text — only pooled AE percentages and two weight-change data points (studies 9 and 10) are given for lithium. Lithium dose is reported only as target serum range (0.8-1.1 or 0.8-1.3 mEq/L=mmol/L); no salt form, mg dose, or achieved serum level is given, so lithium_salt='unknown' and salt/dose fields are null. Secondary AE tables (Tables 2-6) and non-primary outcomes (sedation, rash, mania, suicide, pregnancy) were omitted per extraction scope (primary outcomes only = weight gain, the review's focus per task framing). Weight outcome 1 (mean change, study 10) used single reported means with no SD, so between-group effect could not include an SE per the mean-difference rule; effect_value is calculated as arm1-arm2 but se/CI are null because no per-arm SD/n was reported — flagged here since a mean_difference without se/CI would otherwise be discarded downstream. Study 8 also reports a separate 7-week weight-change dataset (placebo 0.2, lamotrigine 50mg -0.4, lamotrigine 200mg 0.0 kg) but was omitted as a secondary/intermediate timepoint under the primary-outcome-only scope; likewise the study-9 fixed-dose 76-week ≥7% weight-gain figures for lamotrigine subgroups (50mg=12%, 200/400mg=3.5%) were consolidated to a single lamotrigine value where the paper gave an overall lamotrigine percent (7%) attributable to the fixed-dose maintenance cohort. No verbatim quotes provided per extraction-scope instruction (all *_quote fields set to null).

It describes the prevalence of general medical comorbidities and cardiometabolic abnormalities (mean BMI 29.2, 38% obese, 30% with metabolic syndrome) and their association with clinical features of bipolar disorder, but does not report any post-treatment or arm-specific weight, dose, or serum-lithium outcome data.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: This LiTMUS report analyzes only baseline (Week 0), pre-randomization data for the full enrolled cohort (n=264 with CIRS data); comparisons in Tables 1-3 are by medical-comorbidity burden (CIRS high vs low), NOT by treatment arm (lithium+OPT vs OPT), so no per-arm or endpoint weight/BMI outcome data exists to extract per the primary-outcome scope. Baseline weight (84.3±20.9 kg) and BMI (29.2±7.2) are reported for the whole sample only (Table 1/text), not split by treatment arm or timepoint, so they were not entered as an 'outcome' object. Lithium dosing is described only as 'moderate dose lithium (i.e., 600 mg initially for 8 weeks)' as an adjunct to other medications — no salt form, serum lithium level, or per-arm dose data are reported anywhere in this paper. Route was inferred as oral (not explicitly stated) since lithium is essentially always given orally. No between-arm effect sizes, sample-size-per-arm, or AE tables by arm are present. This paper is likely NOT a source of quantitative weight-gain effect data for the meta-analysis; it may only be useful for baseline cohort characterization/context.

summary: This is a secondary analysis of the Bipolar CHOICE trial (482 participants with bipolar I/II disorder randomized to open-label lithium plus adjunctive personalized therapy vs. quetiapine plus adjunctive personalized therapy for six months), examining whether baseline obesity, abdominal obesity, or metabolic syndrome predicted treatment outcome rather than comparing the two treatments' effects on weight. Obesity and abdominal obesity (but not metabolic syndrome) were associated with significantly less improvement in global illness severity, mood symptoms, suicidality, functioning, and life satisfaction after six months, regardless of treatment assignment. No lithium dose, salt form, serum level, or per-arm weight-change data are reported in this paper, so it does not directly contribute a lithium weight-gain effect size.

summary: This post-hoc analysis pooled two identical randomized, placebo-controlled crossover trials of a single IV ketamine infusion (0.5 mg/kg) in 36 treatment-resistant bipolar depression patients maintained on therapeutic lithium or valproate, comparing antidepressant response between anxious (n=21) and non-anxious (n=15) subgroups. Ketamine significantly reduced depressive symptoms (MADRS, HDRS) in both groups with no significant anxiety-group-by-drug interaction, indicating anxious status did not blunt ketamine's rapid antidepressant effect. This paper is a ketamine mechanistic/subgroup study, not a lithium dosing trial, and reports no weight, BMI, or metabolic outcome data.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: This paper is NOT a lithium weight-gain trial: it is a post-hoc analysis of ketamine's antidepressant effect stratified by baseline anxiety in bipolar depression. Lithium (serum target 0.6-1.2 mEq/L, converted numerically unchanged to mmol/L) appears only as an inclusion-criterion background maintenance medication (patients were on lithium OR valproic acid, not randomized/quantified separately by drug); no lithium salt form, dose in mg, or achieved serum level is reported anywhere in the text. No weight, BMI, waist circumference, or metabolic outcome of any kind is reported (continuous, binary, or AE-table). Table 1 reports baseline BMI by anxiety subgroup (29.4±6.4 anxious vs 31.1±5.5 non-anxious) but this is a demographic characteristic, not an outcome of the ketamine intervention, and is not broken out by background lithium vs valproate use, so it was not mapped into baseline_demographics.per_arm (which would require true study arms). The methods section contains an internal inconsistency: patients are said to have received 'a single open-label intravenous infusion' as part of studies that were 'randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled crossover' — both are quoted verbatim from the source; blinding was coded as double-blind per the larger parent trial design. Per the extraction scope, only the primary outcome would normally be extracted, but since no weight-related outcome exists in this paper, the outcomes array was left empty rather than including the non-weight depression/anxiety endpoints (MADRS, HDRS, HAM-A, CADSS), which are out of scope for this review.

summary: Four double-blind, placebo-controlled trials tested topiramate monotherapy (200-600 mg/day) versus placebo, with lithium (1500 mg/day) as an active comparator in two trials, in hospitalized adults with acute manic or mixed episodes of bipolar I disorder. Topiramate showed no significant efficacy advantage over placebo on YMRS at 3 or 12 weeks, while lithium produced significantly greater YMRS improvement than both placebo and topiramate (p<=0.001). Topiramate was associated with weight LOSS relative to placebo and lithium, whereas lithium was associated with a small but statistically significant weight GAIN relative to placebo (least squares mean difference +0.38 kg, p=0.048, and BMI +0.15 kg/m2, p=0.025, in pooled 3-week analysis).

summary: This pooled retrospective analysis of two 18-month, double-blind, placebo- and lithium-controlled maintenance trials in bipolar I disorder compared body weight changes among lamotrigine, lithium, and placebo. At week 52, covariate-adjusted mean weight change was +2.2 kg with lithium versus +0.2 kg with placebo (difference +2.0 kg, 95% CI -0.3 to 4.4, p=0.094, not statistically significant) and versus -1.2 kg with lamotrigine (difference +3.4 kg, 95% CI 1.4 to 5.4, p<0.001, statistically significant). Lithium was associated with progressive weight gain relative to lamotrigine, though the magnitude was smaller than in prior studies and not significantly different from placebo.

summary: This open-label, randomized effectiveness trial (DUAG-6) compared lithium (titrated to serum levels 0.5-1.0 mmol/L) with lamotrigine (up-titrated to 400 mg/day) as maintenance treatment in 155 adults with bipolar I disorder followed for up to 5.8 years. Depression improvement (Hamilton scale) was greater with lithium, reaching statistical significance overall at 4 weeks (P approx. 0.04) and being most pronounced at one large single-hospital site. Weight gain was numerically greater with lithium (mean +1.83 kg vs +0.32 kg with placebo) but this difference was not statistically significant.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: Weight gain is reported only as a narrative mean ± range per group (lithium: mean +1.83 kg, range -4.5 to +6 kg; placebo: mean +0.32 kg, range -6 to +3.5 kg), with no SD, N analyzed for weight specifically, or p-value given beyond 'not statistically significant' — so no weight outcome object could be constructed under the current schema without an SD; only the primary efficacy outcome (Hamilton % decrease) was extracted per extraction scope instructions, which restrict 'outcomes' to primary outcome(s) only. Per-arm mean/SD for the primary outcome were not reported (only percent decrease in Hamilton score by treatment arm at 1,2,4,6 weeks); only the 4-week total-material values were extracted per scope (final/end-of-treatment timepoint only). Exact serum lithium mean/SD not reported; only range of maximum values (0.8-1.3 mEqv/l typical, with two low outliers 0.6/0.7 and one high outlier 2.4) and the titration target range were given. Lithium salt form (carbonate) and tablet size (300 mg) were explicit; daily mg dose could not be calculated since exact titrated dose varied per patient to reach serum target. extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: This paper is about lithium dosing schedule (single vs. multiple daily dose) and its effect on urinary output/polyuria, NOT weight gain. No weight or BMI outcome data are reported anywhere in the text apart from a single baseline weight measurement in Table 1 (used only for creatinine clearance body-surface-area calculation), which is captured in baseline_demographics. The 'primary outcome' extracted here (24-h urine volume) is the paper's actual primary endpoint per the abstract/methods, included per instructions to extract the primary outcome; no between-group effect with p-value was reported for the group-difference in urine volume change, so a mean difference and SE were calculated from the reported per-arm change values. extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: INELIGIBLE PAPER: this is a renal/dopamine physiology study in healthy volunteers using a single lithium test dose (600 mg lithium carbonate, one evening before each study day) purely as a lithium-clearance tracer for proximal tubular function; it is not a therapeutic lithium trial and reports no weight-gain, BMI, or body-composition outcome. extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: EXCLUDE FROM META-ANALYSIS: lithium here is a single-dose (400 mg lithium carbonate, given once the evening before each of two clearance study days) pharmacokinetic/renal-physiology tracer used to compute fractional lithium clearance (an index of proximal tubular sodium reabsorption), not a therapeutic or supplement exposure. There is no lithium dosing arm, no lithium-attributable weight outcome, and no comparator arm in the sense required by this review's schema. The body weight change reported (72.2±12.9 to 74.0±12.6 kg, p<0.05) is caused by fludrocortisone (a mineralocorticoid), not by lithium, and reflects sodium/fluid retention during 'escape' physiology, not adiposity or lithium-induced weight gain. No arms, outcomes, or between-group effects were extracted because none are applicable to the lithium-weight-gain research question.
