summary: This post hoc analysis pooled two 18-month randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled maintenance trials of lamotrigine, lithium, and placebo in 556 adults with bipolar I disorder, stratified by baseline obesity. At week 52, obese patients (n=155) gained a mean of 6.1 kg on lithium versus -0.6 kg on placebo (a statistically significant difference) and versus -4.2 kg on lamotrigine, while nonobese patients (n=399) showed no significant weight differences among groups (lithium +1.1 kg, lamotrigine -0.5 kg, placebo +0.7 kg).

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: Weight data are reported stratified by baseline obesity status (obese N=155, lithium/lamotrigine/placebo n's per subgroup not individually reported; nonobese N=399), not by overall pooled arm — both obese and nonobese continuous outcomes extracted as separate primary outcome objects since the paper's whole point is this subgroup split; no single overall pooled weight-change outcome across all 556 patients is reported. Per-arm SDs/SEs and per-arm/subgroup Ns were not reported (only overall obese N=155 and nonobese N=399), so between-group effects could not be assigned an SE/CI and are reported as calculated point differences only per the paper's stated significance (p<0.05 threshold, not exact) for the obese subgroup; nonobese subgroup differences were not significant and no effect size was stated, so between_group_effects is empty for that outcome. Lithium salt form not stated anywhere in text (set to unknown per L1). Dose and serum-level values were given separately for obese and nonobese subgroups; means combined here via simple averaging across the two reported subgroup means (marked calculated) since no single overall value was given. Secondary/safety outcomes (thyroid, polydipsia, other AEs) were not reported in this paper and thus omitted per extraction scope (primary outcome only).

summary: This RCT evaluated adjunctive aripiprazole (15-30 mg/day) versus adjunctive placebo added to open-label lithium or valproate monotherapy in 384 bipolar I patients with mania partially nonresponsive to lithium/valproate alone. Aripiprazole produced significantly greater improvement in mania symptoms (YMRS) than placebo at week 6, but the lithium and valproate arms themselves were not randomized against each other and lithium was given per usual therapeutic dosing (target serum 0.6-1.0 mmol/L) with no lithium-specific weight-gain contrast reported beyond a non-significant subgroup finding. Weight change (a secondary/safety outcome) did not differ significantly between aripiprazole and placebo overall or within the lithium or valproate subgroups.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: This is primarily an aripiprazole-adjunctive-therapy trial; lithium is one of two background mood stabilizers (the other being valproate), not the intervention of primary interest for this weight-gain review. Lithium salt form was never specified anywhere in the text, so lithium_salt is 'unknown' for both lithium arms per rule L1. No separate per-arm weight data for the lithium-only subgroup were given numerically (only 'no significant treatment differences in the lithium or valproate subgroups' stated qualitatively) — the only quantitative weight change numbers reported are pooled across lithium+valproate subgroups by treatment arm (aripiprazole +0.55 kg [SD 2.66] vs placebo +0.23 kg [SD 3.51], LOCF), so weight/binary-weight-gain outcomes were extracted at the overall-population level, not lithium-arm-specific, and per instructions the outcomes section only includes the PRIMARY (YMRS efficacy) outcome — weight change is a secondary outcome per this paper's stated hierarchy and was therefore omitted from 'outcomes' per the EXTRACTION SCOPE override (primary outcome only). Per-arm demographics (age, sex, weight, BMI) were reported only for the overall placebo vs aripiprazole groups (Table 1), not broken out by lithium/valproate subgroup, so per-arm demographic fields for arms 1-4 are null; overall-population age/sex were calculated by pooling Table 1's placebo (N=131) and aripiprazole (N=253) rows. Sample size per-arm for lithium/valproate subgroups is by MOOD STABILIZER (Table 1: lithium N=51 placebo/106 aripiprazole; valproate N=80 placebo/147 aripiprazole), not literal randomization arms of a 2-arm trial, but structured this way per instruction to make arm_id=1 the lithium arm. Between-group effect for primary outcome (mean difference -2.6, derived from -13.3 minus -10.7) is an ANCOVA-adjusted estimate as reported by the study (F=9.54, p<0.01), not a simple recalculation from unadjusted per-arm SDs, so no SE could be derived from the two SDs; effect_source set to 'calculated' since the paper did not print a formatted mean-difference value directly. All *_quote fields set to null per EXTRACTION SCOPE override.

summary: In this North American maintenance trial (Trial 127), 623 patients with bipolar I disorder stabilized on quetiapine plus lithium or divalproex were randomized to continue quetiapine or switch to placebo, while remaining on lithium or divalproex. Continued quetiapine combination therapy significantly reduced the risk of mood-event recurrence versus placebo combination therapy (20.3% vs 52.1%; hazard ratio 0.32, 95% CI 0.24-0.42, p<0.0001). Weight increase, sedation, and hypothyroidism were significantly more common with quetiapine; this extraction focuses on the lithium-cotreatment subset for exposure characterization, as lithium dose/salt/serum-level data specific to the lithium-only subgroup were not separately reported beyond median serum concentration.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: This trial's two randomized arms are 'quetiapine + lithium or divalproex' vs 'placebo + lithium or divalproex' — lithium was only one of two permitted co-treatments (divalproex being the other), and the paper does not separately report arm-level lithium salt, dose in mg, or serum levels restricted to the lithium-only subgroup; only overall median lithium serum concentrations (0.74 quetiapine group, 0.71 placebo group) are given across the combined lithium+divalproex randomized population, mixed with divalproex-treated patients. Per EXTRACTION SCOPE instructions, only the primary time-to-event outcome (time to recurrence of any mood event) was extracted; weight-gain and other secondary/AE-table outcomes (weight increase AE counts by arm, mean weight change +0.46 kg quetiapine vs -1.95 kg placebo, BMI change, glucose/lipid changes, hypothyroidism) were omitted from 'outcomes' per scope but weight AE counts were still mirrored into adverse_events.per_arm.notable_aes as instructed by rule W3. Lithium salt form and per-arm mg dose were never stated in the paper (only serum target 0.5-1.2 meq/L), so lithium_salt is 'unknown' for both arms per rule L1. Because this trial does not isolate a pure lithium arm (both randomized groups contain a lithium-or-divalproex mix), dose_contrast_within_trial is false and this paper primarily contributes indirect/mixed lithium exposure data rather than a clean lithium-vs-placebo weight-gain contrast.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: This paper is a lurasidone-adjunctive-therapy RCT where lithium (and valproate) are the pre-existing background mood stabilizer, not the randomized intervention itself; lithium/valproate arms were pooled as a stratification variable, not separately randomized doses, so weight/metabolic outcomes (Table 3) are reported for the pooled lurasidone vs placebo groups (across both lithium and valproate strata) and cannot be cleanly attributed to lithium alone. Per scope instructions, only the primary outcome (MADRS change at week 6, pooled across lithium/valproate strata) was extracted in 'outcomes'; secondary outcomes (CGI-BP, HAM-A, QIDS, QOL, Sheehan) and weight/lipid/glycemic continuous data (Table 3: weight, cholesterol, LDL, triglycerides, glucose, HbA1c, insulin, prolactin) were omitted per the narrowed extraction scope, though Table 3 does contain per-arm (pooled lurasidone vs placebo, not lithium-only) mean/SD/median weight change data if a fuller extraction is later needed. No lithium salt form, elemental dose, or lithium-specific weight-gain binary/AE data (e.g. 'weight gain' as a named adverse event) were reported separately for the lithium subgroup in this paper — Table 2's adverse event list also pools lithium+valproate patients and does not include 'weight gain' as a listed AE term. summary: This nine-week, double-blind, concentration-controlled RCT randomized 224 older adults (mean age 68) with bipolar I mania to lithium (target 0.80-0.99 mEq/L, mean achieved 0.76 mEq/L) or divalproex. Lithium produced significantly greater reduction in mania severity (YMRS) by week 9 than divalproex (difference 3.90 points, 95% CI 1.71-6.09, p<0.0001), while sedation and the proportion reaching target drug concentration did not differ significantly between groups. A continuous Weight Gain item (UKU35) showed a significant treatment-by-time interaction but no significant between-group difference at week 3 or week 9.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: Per extraction scope, 'outcomes' includes only the trial's three explicitly-designated PRIMARY measures (YMRS efficacy, proportion achieving target serum concentration, and UKU Sleepiness/Sedation); the Weight Gain item (UKU35) is explicitly labeled a 'planned secondary measure' in the text and its Table 2 statistics (significant treatment x time interaction, F1,1372=8.08, p=0.0045 unadjusted/0.027 adjusted, but no significant between-group difference at week 3 [0.09, CI -0.10-0.29] or week 9 [-0.16, CI -0.42-0.11]) were therefore omitted from 'outcomes' per instructions, though flagged here and in derived.reports_weight_outcome. Tremor and Nausea/Vomiting UKU items were likewise omitted as secondary. Lithium salt form is never specified in the text (dose reported only in mg/day of study medication), so lithium_salt is 'unknown' rather than assumed carbonate. For the 'Target Blood Level' outcome, Table 2's model-based D-L estimates (e.g., -0.07 at week 9) appear to be on an unspecified/transformed scale inconsistent with the plain-language percentages reported in text (57.1% vs 56.3% at week 9), so that ambiguous effect estimate was omitted from between_group_effects; only the verbatim percentages were kept as arm_results. Country of conduct (United States) is inferred from 'six academic centers,' Weill Cornell data management, and NIMH DSMB oversight, not stated explicitly. Baseline weight/BMI were not reported anywhere in the text or tables.

summary: This 6-week randomized double-blind placebo-controlled trial tested adjunctive midday bright light therapy (7,000-lux white light) versus dim red placebo light in 46 adults with bipolar I/II depression on stable antimanic medication. The active light therapy group had significantly higher remission rates (68.2% vs 22.2%; adjusted OR=12.64) and lower depression scores (SIGH-ADS 9.18 vs 14.94; adjusted mean difference=-5.91) than placebo, both statistically significant. This paper does not involve lithium as an intervention and reports no weight-gain outcome data relevant to this review; roughly 22% of participants were incidentally taking lithium as part of their stable background medication regimen, with no dosing or serum-level detail provided.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: MD was garbled, used PDF text. This trial is NOT a lithium intervention study — the intervention is bright light therapy vs. dim red placebo light for bipolar depression. Lithium appears only as a background/concomitant medication in a minority of participants (6/23 active, 4/23 placebo per Table 1), with no dose, salt form, or serum level reported. No lithium arms were created (arms array reflects the actual light-therapy arms, not lithium exposure, per the arm_id=1-is-lithium convention which does not apply here). No weight, BMI, or metabolic outcome data of any kind appear in this paper — omitted from outcomes entirely per this review's scope, which is restricted to primary outcomes and this study's primary outcomes (remission rate and continuous SIGH-ADS score) are unrelated to weight gain. This paper likely does not meet the eligibility criteria for a lithium weight-gain review and should be flagged for exclusion/re-screening.

summary: This post hoc analysis of the CANMAT randomized double-blind trial compared lithium (n=85) and valproate (n=74), each used as monotherapy or with adjunctive olanzapine/risperidone continued for 0, 24, or 52 weeks, in bipolar I disorder maintenance treatment. Weight gain was reported as an adverse event with similar rates in both groups (11% lithium vs 11% valproate), and there were no significant differences between lithium and valproate on the primary efficacy outcome of time to any mood episode (HR 0.99, 95% CI 0.66-1.48, p=0.95).

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: This is a post hoc, non-randomized (for mood-stabilizer assignment) analysis of the CANMAT trial; lithium and valproate assignment was clinician-chosen, not randomized, though AA discontinuation timing (0/24/52 weeks) was randomized. Lithium salt form is not reported anywhere in the text (set to 'unknown' per L1). Mean serum lithium level 0.80 (0.20) mmol/L is reported as an overall mean across all lithium sub-arms in Table 1 ('Mood stabilizer levels'), not broken out per treatment-duration sub-arm, so a single pooled lithium arm is used here rather than 3 dose-contrast arms since sub-arms differ by AA-continuation duration, not lithium dose/serum-level target. Weight gain is reported ONLY as an adverse-event count in the safety table (Table 2: 9/85 lithium vs 8/74 valproate), with no threshold specified, no continuous kg data, and no BMI data — per W3 this was extracted as a binary clinically_significant_weight_gain outcome and mirrored into adverse_events.notable_aes. Only the primary outcome (time to any mood episode) was included in 'outcomes' per extraction scope, but since its result is a between-group HR without per-arm continuous data, and the weight AE is the primary weight-related quantitative data in this paper, the weight-gain AE was extracted as the outcome object of interest for this weight-focused review; the formal 'primary outcome' (mood episode relapse) is efficacy, not weight, and is not separately extracted since this review's scope is weight/metabolic outcomes. Secondary efficacy outcomes (manic/depressive episode HRs) omitted per extraction scope. All *_quote fields set to null per extraction scope override.

summary: This narrative review summarizes the Tohen et al. 2005 double-blind RCT comparing lithium monotherapy versus olanzapine monotherapy for relapse prevention in bipolar I disorder over 52 weeks, following open-label co-treatment stabilization. Overall mood episode recurrence did not differ significantly between groups (38.8% lithium vs 30.0% olanzapine, p=0.055), though olanzapine was significantly better at preventing manic and mixed relapses. During the double-blind period, mean weight change was significantly greater with olanzapine than lithium (+1.8kg vs -1.4kg, p<0.001), and significantly more olanzapine patients gained >=7% of baseline weight (29.8% vs 9.8%, p<0.001).

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: This source is a narrative/review article (Dando & Tohen 2006) summarizing the Tohen et al. 2005 lithium-vs-olanzapine RCT, not the primary trial publication; per-arm continuous weight change (1.8kg vs -1.4kg) and the binary >=7% weight gain proportions (29.8% vs 9.8%) are reported only as aggregate double-blind-phase results without per-arm SDs or exact n at that timepoint, so no separate weight outcome objects were built per the extraction scope (primary outcome only was requested in 'outcomes'; weight data is captured in adverse_events.notable_aes and the summary). Lithium salt form, dose in mg, and achieved/target serum levels beyond the stated 0.6-1.2 mmol/L acute-phase target were not reported in this text. Cholesterol change data (5.4±29.8 mg/dl vs -12.4±29.4 mg/dl) also appears but is a metabolic secondary outcome, out of scope per extraction instructions. Three additional trials (olanzapine vs placebo, olanzapine vs divalproex, olanzapine+mood stabilizer vs mood stabilizer alone) are also described in this paper but contain no lithium arm meeting inclusion criteria as a standalone therapeutic lithium comparison beyond the one extracted (the fourth study's 'mood stabilizer' arm was investigator's choice of lithium OR valproate, not separable into a pure lithium arm), so they were not extracted as separate arms/outcomes.

summary: This 4-week, multicenter, double-blind RCT in 154 Chinese inpatients with acute bipolar mania compared quetiapine (100-800 mg/day) with lithium (titrated to serum level 0.6-1.2 mmol/L, achieved mean 0.85 mmol/L at Day 28). YMRS response rate at Day 28 was significantly higher with quetiapine than lithium (77.9% vs 59.7%, p=0.0132). Weight gain was a secondary/safety outcome: quetiapine-treated patients gained more weight on average (1.45 kg) than lithium-treated patients (0.25 kg), and a higher proportion had >=7% weight gain with quetiapine (9.9%) than lithium (6.5%).

summary: This 46-week open-label extension study evaluated adjunctive aripiprazole added to lithium or valproate in bipolar I patients who were partial responders to mood-stabiliser monotherapy. Mean weight gain from double-blind endpoint to Week 46 (LOCF) was 2.3 kg (SE 0.6) with aripiprazole+lithium and 2.0 kg (SE 0.4) with aripiprazole+valproate, a small, non-significant difference not formally tested since the study was not powered to compare subgroups. Weight increase was also reported as an adverse event in 11.3% of the lithium group vs. 8.6% of the valproate group.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: Lithium salt form not stated anywhere in the paper (only '250 mg tablets' and dose range in mg/day); left as unknown per L1 rather than assuming carbonate. Serum lithium achieved levels not numerically reported — only percentages of patients within the 0.6-1.0 mmol/L therapeutic range at each visit (67.0%, 81.6%, 69.8%, 73.5%), which do not map to a mean/SD and were left null per L5. Weight change SE values used directly (se field) rather than SD since paper reports mean (SE). Between-group mean difference for weight change (0.3 kg) was calculated from the two arm SEs (sqrt(0.6^2+0.4^2)=0.7211) since no direct between-group comparison/p-value was reported for this outcome (aripiprazole was adjunctive in both arms so this is an ARI+LI vs ARI+VAL comparison, not a lithium vs placebo comparison). Binary 'clinically significant weight gain' outcome (>=7% gain from baseline) omitted per extraction scope narrowing to primary outcome only — the paper reports 23.7% (ARI+LI) vs 28.8% (ARI+VAL) with >=7% gain, and this would normally be a first-class binary outcome per W3, but scope restricts 'outcomes' to primary outcome/timepoint only. Secondary outcomes (YMRS, MADRS, LIFE-RIFT, SF-36, metabolic parameters, EPS scales) omitted per extraction scope. Sample sizes per arm restricted to n_randomized only per scope; n_completed/withdrawals omitted from sample_sizes.per_arm (though present in adverse_events for AE-related counts, which were retained as those are a separate schema section not restricted by scope). No true 'lithium arm vs comparator arm' contrast exists here in the classic sense — both arms received adjunctive aripiprazole; arm 1 is lithium-based combination therapy and arm 2 is the valproate-based combination therapy used as an active comparator per study design, not a placebo/monotherapy lithium contrast.

summary: This 6-week randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial in Iranian psychiatric patients (schizophrenia, bipolar I, or schizoaffective disorder) on background olanzapine plus lithium or olanzapine plus valproate tested whether add-on low-dose omega-3 fish oil (vs placebo) could prevent metabolic side effects. Body weight increased significantly in both groups (omega-3: 70.68→75.03 kg, +4.35 kg; placebo: 74.27→78.35 kg, +4.07 kg), with no significant between-group difference (group-effect p=0.875), indicating omega-3 did not prevent weight gain. Lithium dosing (~1060-1150 mg/day, salt form unspecified) and serum levels were only partially reported and applied to a lithium-treated subset mixed with valproate-treated patients within each randomized arm, limiting attribution of weight gain specifically to lithium.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: This trial's actual randomized factor is omega-3 fish oil vs placebo, added to background olanzapine+lithium OR olanzapine+valproate combination therapy (stratified by combination-therapy type but pooled within each randomized arm). Lithium exposure is therefore a background co-intervention present in only a subset of patients in EACH randomized arm (exact per-arm split between Li and VPA patients not reported), not a distinct trial arm — so the Table 3 weight/BMI results reflect a mixed lithium+valproate population and cannot be cleanly attributed to lithium alone. Given this, lithium_arm_ids is left empty and arms are structured as the actual randomized comparison (omega-3 vs placebo) rather than a lithium-vs-comparator design; per L1, lithium_salt is 'unknown' since only 'Li' dose in mg is given with no salt form stated. The reported Li mean doses (1057.50±288.20 mg/day in the omega-3 group; 1150.00±300.00 mg/day in the placebo group) were placed in dose_salt_mg_per_day for the corresponding randomized arm as the best available proxy, but these are means over the lithium-subgroup of each arm only, not the whole arm N — treat with caution for pooling. No serum lithium levels are reported anywhere in the paper. Body weight (kg) was selected as the primary outcome for this extraction per the review's focus, since the paper itself designates no single primary endpoint among its several cardiovascular risk factor outcomes (BMI, WC, BP, TC, LDL, HDL, non-HDL-C, TG, Lp(a), fibrinogen, CRP-hs were all reported but omitted here per extraction scope). The between-group mean difference for weight was calculated from reported endpoint means/SDs/Ns (SE via sqrt(sd1^2/n1+sd2^2/n2)); the attached p-value (0.875) is the paper's own repeated-measures ANOVA group-effect p-value, which tests a related but not identical quantity (group×time interaction on change scores) — reported alongside as the paper's stated between-group result. Design is described by the authors as a 'within-subject trial' despite reporting two independent-N parallel arms (N=20 vs N=21) with no crossover mentioned; treated here as parallel-group RCT. No formal binary 'clinically significant weight gain' threshold outcome was reported in this paper.

summary: This pooled post-hoc analysis combined five 8-week randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trials of quetiapine for acute bipolar I/II depression; only one trial (EMBOLDEN I) included an active lithium comparator (600-1800 mg/day, n=136), alongside pooled quetiapine (n=1760), paroxetine (n=118), and placebo (n=717) arms. Mean weight change was small and similar between lithium (+0.17 kg) and placebo (+0.03 kg), versus a larger gain with quetiapine (+1.17 kg); no formal statistical comparison of weight change between groups was reported and lithium serum levels were not measured or reported.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: Lithium salt form is never specified in this paper, so lithium_salt=unknown; the 600-1800 mg/day range is assumed (per standard convention) to represent mg of salt, but this is not explicitly confirmed. No serum lithium levels (achieved or target) are reported anywhere in the text. Only EMBOLDEN I contributed a lithium arm among the five pooled trials, while the placebo and quetiapine comparator data reported in Tables 5-7 are pooled across all five trials — a heterogeneity caveat for any lithium-vs-placebo comparison. Weight outcomes (Table 7) are reported separately for bipolar I and bipolar II subgroups only, with no combined value given; per-arm combined means/SDs (continuous outcome) and combined events/totals (binary ≥7% outcome) were calculated by pooling the two subgroups using standard formulas (weighted mean and pooled-variance SD for the continuous outcome; simple summation for the binary outcome) — marked result_source='calculated'. No between-group statistical test for weight change was reported by the authors; mean differences and their SEs vs placebo were calculated per protocol. No OR/RR was reported for the ≥7% weight-gain threshold, so between_group_effects for that outcome was left empty per instructions. Baseline demographics (age, weight) are reported only by bipolar subtype (I vs II), not by treatment arm, so per-arm baseline_demographics fields are null; overall pooled baseline weight was 82.1 kg (SD 20.9) across bipolar I (83.4, SD 21.4) and II (79.7, SD 19.7) but is not attributable to a specific treatment arm. Sample-size figures differ by population: 'randomized' n's used here (summing to 2731, matching the stated ITT total) come from the explicit sentence naming patients 'randomized to 8-week treatment'; these differ from both the overall 2873 randomized total and the larger safety-population n's used for the AE/weight tables (2848 total) — the latter were used for the weight/AE outcome arm_results per the tables' own headers. Secondary metabolic outcomes reported in Table 7 (glucose, insulin, total/LDL/HDL cholesterol, triglycerides) were omitted per the extraction-scope narrowing to primary weight outcomes only. Thyroid and polydipsia/polyuria outcomes were not reported in this paper. All quote fields were set to null per the extraction-scope override.

summary: This open-label randomized trial in young adults (18-35) with bipolar I disorder compared lithium plus valproic acid versus lithium plus carbamazepine over up to 24 months of treatment. Both combinations produced similar improvements in mood symptoms with no significant between-group differences in response, remission, or symptom scale reductions, but the lithium+valproate group showed more frequent weight gain (100% vs 79.2% by UKU rating; mean +2.1 kg vs -0.2 kg, between-group p=0.047) and higher rates of fatigue and decreased sexual desire, while lithium+carbamazepine had more diarrhea.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: Both arms are lithium-COMBINATION therapy (Li/VPA vs Li/CBZ); there is no lithium-monotherapy or placebo arm. Arms ordered by ascending mean lithium salt dose per convention (arm1=Li/CBZ 989.6 mg, arm2=Li/VPA 1024 mg); this ordering is incidental (the intended contrast is the combination partner, not lithium dose), so dose_contrast_within_trial=false. Lithium salt form is never stated in the text; do not assume carbonate. Weight gain is a SECONDARY/adverse-event outcome in this paper and per extraction scope was captured only in adverse_events (Table 3, UKU Side Effect Rating Scale: 30/~30 Li/VPA vs 19/24 Li/CBZ, denominators back-calculated from percentages since raw N per UKU assessment wasn't stated directly), not in the 'outcomes' array. Paper also reports weight change from baseline to week 8 as continuous kg (Li/VPA: +2.1 kg, within-group p=0.03; Li/CBZ: -0.2 kg, within-group p=0.001; between-group p=0.047) — flagged here but not extracted into 'outcomes' per scope restricting that section to primary outcomes only. Table 1's Li/CBZ baseline weight cell appears blank/missing in the source markup (likely a typesetting drop), so it is null rather than genuinely not measured. VPA serum level '70.35 mg' and CBZ dose/serum level in 'μg/dL' are copied verbatim as printed, though these units look atypical (VPA is usually reported in μg/mL and CBZ dose in mg/day) — likely source typos, not corrected per instructions. Primary outcome is ambiguous in the paper: Methods define it as response (acute phase)/remission (maintenance phase) rates, while the Results narrative separately calls the CGI-BP score reduction 'our primary outcome'; both are extracted as primary outcomes. illness_phase set to 'mixed' as the closest available enum value since the trial enrolled patients in any current mood state (depression, mania/hypomania, or mixed) rather than a single defined phase — 27 depressed, 17 manic/hypomanic, 16 mixed at baseline. Sample sizes: 64 were randomized/included after screening (36 Li/VPA, 28 Li/CBZ) but 4 withdrew consent before any treatment (3 Li/VPA, 1 Li/CBZ), leaving the analyzed baseline sample of 60 (33 Li/VPA, 27 Li/CBZ) shown in Table 1; n_randomized per arm uses the pre-withdrawal figures per instructions.

summary: This 6-week, double-blind, placebo-controlled RCT in 356 adults with acute bipolar I mania tested flexible-dose lithium (immediate-release, target serum 0.8-1.2 mEq/L, achieved mean 0.72 mEq/L) versus placebo, both added to open-label quetiapine XR. Add-on lithium produced significantly greater reduction in YMRS total score than add-on placebo (LS mean difference -2.69, 95% CI -4.09 to -1.29, p<0.001). Lithium was associated with more tremor, somnolence, GI adverse events, and a numerically higher rate of clinically significant (≥7%) weight gain (8.0% vs 4.7%) than placebo.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: Lithium salt form is never specified in the text (only 'lithium (immediate release)'); set to unknown per L1 rather than assuming carbonate. Randomized n for the placebo arm shows a discrepancy between prose ('n = 182') and Table 1/safety-set header ('n = 183'); the table value (183, which reconciles with the stated total of 356) was used per the rule that table numbers are authoritative. Per EXTRACTION SCOPE instructions, only the trial's primary efficacy outcome (YMRS) is included in the 'outcomes' array at the final (day 43) timepoint only, with per-arm arm_results omitted since a between-group effect with p-value is reported; all secondary efficacy outcomes (CGI-BP-S, CGI-BP-C, PANSS, MADRS, response/remission) and weight-specific outcome objects were omitted from 'outcomes' per scope, but weight-related adverse-event counts (weight increased AE term; weight gain ≥7% proportions) are preserved in the adverse_events section. Denominators for the weight gain ≥7% proportions (8.0% lithium, 4.7% placebo) are not explicitly stated in the text, so events/n were left null rather than assumed equal to the safety-set N. No subgroup analyses extracted per scope.

summary: This one-year double-blind trial compared prophylactic lithium carbonate against maprotiline (a tetracyclic antidepressant) in 39 patients with recurrent affective disorders. The mean Affective Morbidity Index was numerically lower with lithium but not statistically significantly so, though a dichotomized analysis (no morbidity vs some morbidity) found lithium significantly superior to maprotiline overall (p<0.02) and in unipolar patients specifically (p<0.05). Weight-related findings were incidental: a highly significant negative correlation (r=-0.97, p<0.001) was found between plasma maprotiline concentration and body weight, with no quantitative weight-gain data reported for the lithium arm.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: This paper does not report quantitative weight data for the lithium arm at all — weight was recorded on the affective disorders chart per methods, but no lithium-arm weight/BMI values or weight-gain adverse-event counts appear in text or tables. The only quantitative weight-related finding concerns maprotiline plasma level correlating with body weight (r=-0.97), which is not a lithium exposure and thus not extractable as a lithium outcome. Per extraction scope, only the primary outcome (Affective Morbidity Index) was extracted at the single reported endpoint (patients completing the one-year trial); the mean difference and SE were calculated from the per-arm mean±SE values in Table II (lithium 'All patients' 0.10±0.05, maprotiline 'All patients' 0.24±0.08). A separate dichotomized (Fisher's exact, p<0.02) result from Table IV is also reported verbatim as a second between-group effect for the same outcome/timepoint since no OR was computed in the source. OCR/text garbling (e.g. '&#128;o... 97' for r=-0.97, degree symbols, stray characters) affected some numeric parsing; values were cross-checked against surrounding context. Age/sex baseline figures were taken from Table I ('All patients' rows); percent female calculated from N/F counts. Sample sizes per arm (25 lithium, 14 maprotiline) taken from Table I total row counts.

summary: This is a post-hoc analysis of clinical and endocrine predictors of response to lithium versus T3 antidepressant augmentation in tricyclic-resistant depression, pooling 51 subjects from two double-blind trials (one comparing T3, lithium, and placebo). No continuous body weight (kg) outcome was reported; the paper instead reports a Hamilton Depression Scale 'weight loss' factor score, finding lithium non-responders had significantly higher (worse) baseline weight-loss and sleep-disturbance scores than responders, and that T3 responders had higher weight-loss factor scores than lithium responders (p<0.05). No true body-weight-gain data suitable for this meta-analysis were reported.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: MD was garbled, used PDF text. This paper does not report actual body weight, BMI, or weight-gain adverse-event data for lithium; it only reports a Hamilton Depression Scale 'weight loss' factor subscore (an item cluster measuring appetite/weight loss as a depressive symptom, NOT weight gain as a lithium side effect), used here as a predictor of antidepressant-augmentation response. Given this, the outcome extracted is not usable for the weight-gain meta-analysis and reports_weight_outcome is set to false. Lithium dose is a fixed range (900-1200 mg/day) with no salt form stated (set to unknown per rules) and no per-arm breakdown by exact dose. Achieved serum lithium level (mean 0.68 mmol/L, range 0.56-0.93) was reported for the lithium group as a whole with no difference between responders/non-responders, but no SD was given. OCR artifacts in the source text (e.g. 'HRSD', garbled table formatting) made some table values unparseable/ambiguous; Tables 2-4 report F/p values for response and treatment effects on Hamilton factor scores rather than per-arm weight data usable for pooling. Secondary outcomes and full HRSD/thyroid tables omitted per extraction scope (primary-outcome-only instructions), and no genuine 'primary outcome' for weight gain exists in this paper.

summary: This 3-week, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial randomised 151 patients with acute manic/mixed bipolar episodes (already on lithium, divalproex, or carbamazepine) to add-on risperidone (median modal dose 4 mg/day) or placebo. Risperidone add-on produced a numerically larger reduction in YMRS score than placebo add-on (-14.5 vs -10.3 points) but the primary end-point comparison was only marginally significant (mean difference -4.2, 95% CI -7.60 to 0.54, p=0.089); adverse events were similar between groups except more extrapyramidal symptoms with risperidone, and mean weight gain was greater with risperidone (1.7 kg) than placebo (0.5 kg, p=0.012).

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: This is NOT a lithium-arm-vs-comparator trial: the randomised comparison is risperidone-add-on vs placebo-add-on, with lithium/divalproex/carbamazepine used as investigator-selected background mood stabilisers (lithium in ~56-59% of patients in each arm), so lithium salt form, dose, and serum level specific to lithium are never reported and lithium_arm_ids is left empty. summary: In patients with bipolar I disorder who had achieved remission on olanzapine plus lithium or valproate, this 18-month double-masked trial randomised them to continue olanzapine (combination therapy) or switch to placebo (mood-stabiliser monotherapy). Combination therapy patients gained a mean 2.0 kg while monotherapy patients lost 1.8 kg (between-group difference 3.8 kg, 95% CI 1.8-5.9), and clinically significant weight gain (≥7%) was far more common with combination therapy (27% vs 6%, risk difference 21.2%, 95% CI 7.2-35.2). Lithium itself was not randomised or dose-contrasted (background mood stabiliser choice was left to clinicians, and roughly two-thirds of patients received valproate rather than lithium), so weight findings mainly reflect the added antipsychotic rather than a lithium dose-response.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: This trial randomises olanzapine vs placebo ADDED TO a background mood stabiliser (lithium or valproate), with the choice of lithium vs valproate made by the site investigator, not randomised — it is not a lithium dosing trial. Only 36/99 (36%) of the relapse-prevention-phase sample received lithium as their mood stabiliser (63/99 received valproate), so arm-level weight and relapse results reflect a MIXED lithium+valproate population, not lithium alone. Table 2 lithium dose/serum-level figures (daily dose ~1024-1065 mg/day; blood level 0.74-0.76 mmol/l) are means with 95% CI (not SD, not min/max) and apply only to the lithium subgroup within each randomised group — the lithium-only subgroup Ns are not reported, so per-arm N used in sample_sizes/baseline_demographics/outcomes reflects the whole randomised arm (lithium+valproate combined), not the lithium subgroup alone. Lithium salt form is never stated in the paper, so lithium_salt is 'unknown'. Because the schema requires arm_id=1 to be the 'lithium arm', arm 1 was set to the monotherapy (mood-stabiliser-alone) group and arm 2 to the olanzapine-combination group; neither arm is a pure lithium arm, and derived.monotherapy/dose_contrast_within_trial were left null/false accordingly. Three weight outcomes were extracted per the review's weight-outcome rules: (1) continuous mean change in kg (Table 5, ANOVA-adjusted CI including terms for treatment/investigator/interaction), (2) 'weight gain' as an investigator-reported treatment-emergent adverse event with exact n/N (Table 4), and (3) proportion with a clinically relevant (≥7%) increase in weight (text only, percentages given with no exact n/N, so events/total were left null rather than back-calculated from an ambiguous denominator). The trial's own stated primary outcome (time to syndromic/symptomatic relapse, an efficacy endpoint) was omitted entirely per this review's weight/metabolic-outcome scope. All *_quote fields were set to null per the extraction-scope instructions for this paper.

summary: This 6-month randomised trial in 208 out-patients with mild-to-moderate DSM-IV major depression compared Short Psychodynamic Supportive Psychotherapy alone with the same psychotherapy combined with a 4-step pharmacotherapy protocol (venlafaxine, then SSRI, then nortriptyline, then lithium augmentation). The trial's main finding was that HRSD-rated efficacy did not differ significantly between groups, though patient-rated (SCL-D) outcomes favored combined therapy; no quantitative weight-gain data were reported for either arm.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: This paper is not a lithium trial in any meaningful sense for this review: lithium is only step 4 of a stepped antidepressant protocol used within the 'combined therapy' arm, reached by only ~1% of that arm's patients by week 20 (Table 3: Venlafaxine/SSRI/Nortriptyline/Lithium addition columns), with no lithium dose, salt form, or serum level ever stated. Weight gain was one of 17 items on a somatic-complaints checklist (rated 1-5, dichotomised to present/absent) but the paper reports only a composite mean complaint score per group and lists which of the 17 individual items differed significantly between arms (dry mouth, excessive sweating, headache, nausea, trembling/shaking, 'other complaints') — weight gain/weight loss are not among those, and no numeric per-item data (means, percentages, or counts) are given anywhere in the text or tables for weight gain specifically. Outcomes array is therefore empty; this study contributes essentially no usable quantitative data to the lithium weight-gain meta-analysis.

summary: This is a double-blind, randomized crossover trial testing metformin (850 mg twice daily) versus placebo for 4 weeks each in lean, insulin-resistant, essential hypertensive patients with normal glucose tolerance, assessing insulin sensitivity, blood pressure, and cation handling. Lithium was administered only as a single 16.2 mmol oral dose the evening before each metabolic study day, solely as a renal clearance tracer to assess proximal tubular sodium handling — it was not a therapeutic intervention, was given identically in both treatment periods, and no lithium-related weight or metabolic outcome data are reported.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: SCOPE MISMATCH: this paper is not a lithium therapeutic/weight-gain trial. It is a metformin-vs-placebo crossover study in hypertensive patients. Lithium carbonate (16.2 mmol single oral dose) is used only as a renal clearance tracer administered identically at the end of each treatment period (both metformin and placebo arms), to compute Li clearance/reabsorption as a marker of proximal tubular Na+ handling (Tables 4). There is no lithium treatment arm, no lithium dosing regimen, no serum lithium level relevant to therapeutic exposure, and no lithium-attributable weight/BMI/metabolic outcome anywhere in the paper. The only weight data point (BMI 24.5±2.2 kg/m2, unchanged with metformin or placebo) is unrelated to lithium and is not extracted as an outcome per the primary-outcome-only scope restriction, since it is not this paper's primary endpoint (insulin sensitivity is) and has no lithium linkage. Recommend excluding this paper from the lithium weight-gain meta-analysis at the eligibility-screening stage rather than extracting it as a lithium arm.

summary: This double-blind, placebo-controlled trial randomized 81 children and adolescents (ages 7-17) with bipolar I disorder in a manic or mixed episode to lithium carbonate (n=53, titrated to a mean end-of-study dose of ~1483 mg/d, mean serum level 0.98 mEq/L) or placebo (n=28) for up to 8 weeks. Lithium produced a significantly greater reduction in YMRS manic symptom scores than placebo (adjusted treatment effect 5.51, 95% CI 0.51-10.50, P=.03). Weight gain was numerically similar in both groups (lithium 0.9±1.6 kg vs placebo 1.2±1.7 kg) and not significantly different, while TSH rose significantly more with lithium.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: MD was garbled, used PDF text. Per scope instructions, only the primary outcome (YMRS change at week 8/ET) is extracted in the outcomes array; secondary outcomes (CDRS-R, CGAS, CGI-S/CGI-I, response/remission, weight gain 0.9±1.6 kg vs 1.2±1.7 kg, TSH change 3.0±3.1 vs -0.1±0.9 mIU/L) are described narratively in the summary but omitted as structured outcome objects per scope. Weight gain (kg change) figures also appear only in Figure 3 (z-score change) beyond the text-reported means. Lithium salt form (carbonate) is stated explicitly as '300-mg, regular-release capsules' of lithium carbonate per the CoLT program methodology; dose range min/max taken from Table 2 (300-3600 mg/d total range). Elemental lithium dose and mmol/day were not directly stated and were left null per instructions (not calculated). All *_quote fields set to null per extraction scope override.

summary: In this 6-month, double-blind, placebo-controlled randomized-withdrawal trial in adults with bipolar I disorder stabilized on open-label ziprasidone plus lithium or valproate, continuing adjunctive ziprasidone significantly delayed time to a mood episode requiring intervention compared with switching to adjunctive placebo (19.7% vs 32.4% required intervention, p=0.0104, NNT 8). Lithium itself was used as a background mood stabilizer (target serum level 0.6-1.2 mEq/L, achieved mean 0.7-0.9 mEq/L) in both arms rather than as the randomized intervention; ziprasidone had no remarkable effect on weight or blood glucose, and 7%+ weight gain incidence was similar between double-blind ziprasidone and placebo groups (5.6% each).

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: This paper is a review/drug-profile article summarizing the Bowden et al. 2010 registration trial (ref 10), not the primary report itself; lithium was not the randomized intervention but a background mood stabilizer shared by both arms (subset also included valproate-treated patients, whose data are not separable from lithium-treated patients in most reported statistics). summary: This RCT randomized 30 hospitalized adolescents with bipolar-I disorder (manic or mixed episode) to lithium plus quetiapine or lithium plus risperidone, with lithium in both arms titrated to a serum level of 0.8-1.2 mEq/L (achieved ~0.92-0.96 mmol/L). Both combinations significantly reduced YMRS scores from baseline, with no significant between-group difference in endpoint YMRS (7.46±4.32 vs 10.2±4.64, p=0.1). Weight did not change significantly within or between groups over the 6-week trial, though no per-arm endpoint weight means were reported numerically.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: Per extraction scope, only the paper's stated primary outcome (YMRS reduction) was extracted into 'outcomes'; weight was a secondary/safety outcome in this paper (baseline weight in Table 1; endpoint comparison reported only as t(28)=-0.23, p=0.8 with no per-arm endpoint means/SDs given, so no weight outcome object was created). Table 1 age values for both arms and the screening count ('Frothy one potential study candidates') appear OCR-garbled ('2/7' read as 2.7 SD, '5/87±2/1' read as age 15.87±2.1, 'Frothy one' read as 41); these are best-effort reconstructions. Lithium salt form is never stated in the text, so lithium_salt is 'unknown' per protocol rather than assumed carbonate. The between-group mean difference for YMRS was back-calculated from the reported per-arm means/SDs (arm1 7.46±4.32, n=15; arm2 10.2±4.64, n=15); the resulting t-value (-1.674) closely matches the paper's reported t(28)=-1.66, p=0.1, confirming consistency.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: This paper is a narrative/pooled-safety review of eight bipolar-disorder RCTs (studies 1-8), not a single trial; lithium here serves as an active comparator to lamotrigine, not the primary intervention under study. Lithium salt form was never specified in the text (only mean daily dose in mg and target serum mEq/L range), so lithium_salt is 'unknown' per rule L1. Weight-gain adverse-event counts (events) were back-calculated from the stated percentages (1% of 280, 2% of 827, 2% of 685) since the source text gave only percentages, not raw numerators — result_source and n_source set to 'calculated' accordingly. Serious AE and AE-related withdrawal counts were similarly back-calculated from stated percentages (8% lithium/lamotrigine, 7% placebo for SAEs; 18% lithium, 12% lamotrigine, 10% placebo for withdrawals). No per-arm dose/serum-level breakdown by individual study was given, so the lithium arm reflects a pooled figure across studies 1,2,7,8. Only the two 18-month monotherapy trials (studies 1 and 2) reported continuous weight-change data (lamotrigine -2.2kg vs placebo +1.2kg), but no lithium-arm continuous weight data or per-arm SD/n were given for this comparison, so no continuous weight outcome object could be extracted with usable per-arm statistics; per instructions only the primary/binary AE-based weight outcome is included. No treatment-arm comparison of weight or body-mass change was reported.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: This paper is not a lithium-as-drug/supplement trial: it is an exploratory secondary analysis of the BEAST exercise trial, which randomized healthy young males to Greek yogurt (GY) vs. an isoenergetic carbohydrate pudding, and separately examined trace dietary lithium naturally present in yogurt (~0.02 mg/kg, 0.0025 mM). Arm 1 (GY) was coded as the 'lithium' arm only because it is the higher-dietary-lithium-exposure arm; lithium_salt/dose fields are not_applicable/null because no lithium salt or supplement was administered. Serum lithium concentrations are shown only in Figure 1 with no numeric values in text or tables (post-GY serum Li is only described qualitatively as 'closely matched' to the yogurt's 0.0025 mM content) — treated as not_reported. Weight/body-mass data are limited to baseline values in Table 1 (reported as mean ± SEM, not SD, for the analyzed subsample of GY n=12/CHO n=13, not the originally randomized n=15/15) and a pooled (both arms combined) Pearson correlation between change in serum Li and change in body mass (r=0.11, p=0.59, n=25, Table 2) — no per-arm post-intervention body mass, no between-group weight comparison, and no BMI or binary weight-gain threshold data are reported in this paper. exposure_stratum was set to 'drinking_water' by analogy given the trace magnitude of dietary lithium exposure from yogurt, though it is food-sourced rather than water-sourced. Secondary outcomes (total strength, P1NP, CTX, P1NP:CTX) were omitted per extraction scope (primary outcome only).

summary: In this 4-year randomized, double-blind (2 years) placebo-controlled trial followed by single-blind extension, 61 elderly patients with mild cognitive impairment received low-dose lithium carbonate (titrated to serum levels 0.25-0.5 mmol/L) or placebo. Lithium did not significantly affect renal function (aMDRD or CKD-EPI) after 4 years, but was associated with significant weight gain (25% of lithium patients gained 2-14 kg, median 5.5 kg, P=.015), increased neutrophil count, elevated TSH, and higher incidence of diabetes mellitus and arrhythmia.

No lithium dose (mg) achieved or serum lithium mean/SD values were reported in the text — only the target range (0.25-0.5 mmol/L) and titration tablet strengths (150/300/450/600 mg lithium carbonate) were given. summary: This is a systematic review and meta-analysis (not a primary trial) pooling two double-blind RCTs (Amsterdam 2016 and Altshuler 2017) that compared second-generation antidepressant monotherapy (venlafaxine or sertraline) against lithium monotherapy in adults with acute bipolar II depression (N=223 in the primary pooled analysis). Response rates for antidepressant monotherapy versus lithium were not significantly different (RR=1.44, 95% CI 0.78-2.66, p=0.24), treatment-emergent affective switch rates were similar between groups, and discontinuation due to side effects was significantly lower with antidepressant monotherapy than lithium (RR=0.32, 95% CI 0.11-0.96, p=0.04). Weight data are minimal: a small but statistically significant weight decrease favored venlafaxine over lithium in the Amsterdam 2016 trial (p=0.004, no kg values given), and 'weight gain' was listed as one of several reasons for early treatment discontinuation in that trial's lithium arm, but no quantitative weight values, per-arm means, or event counts specific to weight gain are reported anywhere in this paper.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: CRITICAL: This paper is a SYSTEMATIC REVIEW AND META-ANALYSIS of second-generation antidepressant monotherapy vs lithium in BD-II depression, NOT a primary trial with its own patients. It synthesizes 5 RCTs (Parker 2006, Amsterdam 2008 open-label, McElroy 2010, Amsterdam 2016, Altshuler 2017), of which only Amsterdam 2016 and Altshuler 2017 have lithium arms and were quantitatively meta-analyzed by this review (its own primary outcome is RESPONSE RATE, not weight). The 'arms'/'outcomes'/'adverse_events' above are reconstructed at the arm level from Table 1 and the narrative text of the two lithium-containing double-blind RCTs; arms 1,4,5 are from Altshuler 2017 (16 weeks) and arms 2,3 are from Amsterdam 2016 (12 weeks) — these must NEVER be cross-compared as if from one trial. Lithium salt form is never stated in this paper for either trial (set 'unknown' throughout, per L1). Only two weight-related mentions exist in the entire text, both narrative with no extractable numeric kg/BMI values: (1) 'a small but statistically significant weight change in the venlafaxine group (decrease) compared to the lithium group (p = 0.004)' — from Amsterdam 2016, direction/significance only, no per-arm means/SDs; (2) 'weight gain' is listed as one of four reasons (jitteriness, headache, weight gain, tremor) for early discontinuation among 3 lithium-arm participants in Amsterdam 2016 — no per-symptom count given (note: this conflicts with Figure 2C, which shows 5 total discontinuation-due-to-side-effects events for the Amsterdam 2016 lithium arm, vs the text's '3 participants'; both are reported verbatim in adverse_events with the discrepancy flagged). Per EXTRACTION SCOPE, 'outcomes' was restricted to the paper's actual primary outcome (response rate) only; secondary outcomes (TEAS rate, all-cause discontinuation) were populated only where they overlap adverse_events reporting requirements. Text (256.55 mg/d) and Table 1 (256.66 mg/d) disagree slightly on Amsterdam 2016's venlafaxine mean dose; Table 1 value used. Text describes Amsterdam 2016 serum lithium units as 'mEq/L' while Table 1 uses 'mmol/L' for the same 0.94 value — treated as numerically identical per L3. Detailed per-domain Cochrane RoB ratings for Amsterdam 2016 and Altshuler 2017 came from the paper's own Supplement Table 1 (pages 60), not the main text. Baseline age/female% are TRIAL-level (both arms of a trial combined), not split by arm, since the paper does not report them per arm — the same trial-level values were duplicated across each trial's arms. No baseline weight, BMI, or thyroid/polydipsia data reported anywhere in this paper.

Per extraction scope instructions, only the primary/final timepoint's between-group effect would normally be extracted, but this is a single-arm pre/during/post design with no between-group comparison, so within_group_change was used instead per rule 2; all three timepoints were kept because none is a true 'intermediate' timepoint being skipped — each is a distinct clinically meaningful state (before/during/after) rather than serial follow-ups within one treatment period. No dose (mg/day) or achieved serum lithium level was reported for the sample as a whole; only a target range of 0.4-0.8 mEq/L (=mmol/L) was stated as the treatment aim, and Table 4 gives mean lithium levels split by 'good outcome' (0.67 mmol/L) vs 'bad outcome' (0.65 mmol/L) subgroups rather than for the whole cohort, so serum_lithium_mmol_L_mean was left null at the arm level per rule L5 (achieved level must not be imputed and subgroup-only values were not assigned to the single overall arm). Weight gain (15%, N=9/60) was reported only as a safety/tolerability frequency with no threshold or measurement method specified; treated as the primary/only outcome per extraction scope. treatment_duration_weeks calculated from stated mean duration of follow-up from lithium initiation of 9.67 years (9.67*52=502.8, rounded 503).

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: This paper's exposure of interest for a lithium weight-gain review is diluted: the 'adjunctive therapy' arm reported in Table 2 (weight, BMI, waist circumference, labs) pools lithium-treated (39.4%) and valproate-treated (60.6%; percentages sum >100%, implying some overlap/combination) patients, so weight/metabolic outcomes cannot be attributed to lithium alone. No SD was reported for the mean weight-change values, so no between-group effect (mean difference) could be calculated per the SE requirement; between_group_effects was left empty rather than emitting an unsupported estimate. Adverse-event 'at least one TEAE' percentages in Table 2A are reported only split by original double-blind assignment (LUR-to-LUR vs PBO-to-LUR) rather than as single per-arm (monotherapy/adjunctive) values, so n_any_ae was left not_reported rather than computed as an approximate weighted average.

BMI is reported as a baseline demographic/covariate for the whole BD-vs-control and primary-vs-replication samples (Table 1), and is used as a dependent/independent variable in fit-comparison models (Tables 3-4), but there is no BMI or body-weight outcome reported specifically by lithium-exposure status, so no weight/BMI outcome object could be extracted per the review's primary-outcome scope. extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: This paper reports NO weight, BMI, or metabolic outcome data of any kind — its focus is depressive symptom response (Hamilton/NOSIE ratings) and neuromuscular toxicity. Weight loss is mentioned only as a pre-treatment depressive SYMPTOM in case vignettes (e.g. '45-lb weight loss' prior to admission), not as a treatment-related outcome, so 'outcomes' is left empty per extraction scope (primary-outcome-only) since no weight-gain outcome exists to extract. summary: This study tested sildenafil (a PDE5 inhibitor) and riociguat (a soluble guanylate cyclase stimulator) in 2 adult male subjects with congenital nephrogenic diabetes insipidus caused by an AVPR2 receptor mutation, to see if stimulating the cGMP pathway could reduce urinary output and improve urinary concentrating ability. Neither drug had a consistent beneficial effect on urine output, urine osmolality, or plasma sodium/osmolality despite increasing urinary cGMP and lowering blood pressure. This paper is NOT a lithium exposure or lithium weight-gain study — lithium is mentioned only once, in background text, as an unrelated citation to a rat model of lithium-induced acquired NDI — so it contains no lithium dosing, serum lithium, or lithium-related weight data relevant to this review.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: This paper is NOT a lithium treatment/exposure study. It is a clinical trial of sildenafil and riociguat for congenital nephrogenic diabetes insipidus (AVPR2 mutation) in 2 obese adult male subjects. Lithium appears only in a single background sentence citing an unrelated rat model of lithium-induced acquired NDI (ref. 8) — no human lithium dosing, serum levels, or lithium-attributable weight outcomes are reported anywhere in the text. Body weight loss reported during water-deprivation testing (2-4 kg over 4 hours) reflects dehydration from the underlying diabetes insipidus, not lithium exposure, and is out of scope for this review. No lithium arms, no weight-gain outcome, and no risk-of-bias assessment relevant to this meta-analysis could be extracted. Recommend excluding this paper from the lithium weight-gain corpus at the screening stage.

summary: This is a prospective mother-infant cohort study in the Argentinean Andes examining pre- and postnatal environmental BORON exposure (via drinking water, blood, urine, breast milk) and infant growth (weight, length, head circumference) over the first 6 months of life; lithium (drinking water range 8-1000 µg/L) was measured only as a co-exposure and entered as a covariate in the boron regression models. Higher infant urinary boron was significantly associated with lower infant weight and head circumference at 0-3 and 3-6 months, but lithium itself was not significant in any model and no quantitative lithium-weight effect estimate is reported, so this paper contributes no extractable lithium-specific weight-gain data.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: This paper's primary exposure of interest and all reported quantitative growth associations concern BORON, not lithium; lithium (and arsenic) were measured only as co-exposures/confounders adjusted for in the boron-anthropometry regression models ('Neither arsenic, nor lithium, in infant urine was significant in the models'), with no lithium-specific beta, CI, or p-value ever reported. No individual-level lithium dose, serum lithium, or per-person lithium exposure summary statistics appear anywhere in the text (only the background drinking-water range of 8-1000 µg/L, cited from Concha et al. 2010). Per rule O1 this is treated as a drinking-water/ecological-type lithium exposure with dose recorded verbatim as the water concentration range and all individual dose/serum fields left null. Weight data given for the single cohort (median, no SD, from Table 1) at the final 3-6 month timepoint; no arm-level breakdown by lithium exposure exists. No between-group or within-group lithium-attributable effect size could be extracted.

summary: This retrospective, two-site Australian study audited hospital records of 535 pregnant women with severe mental illness to describe psychotropic prescribing practices, co-morbidities and pregnancy outcomes, rather than to test lithium's effect on weight. Among women with bipolar disorder, lithium was used by 28.2% at Mercy Hospital versus 17.9% at King Edward Memorial Hospital (OR 0.55, 95% CI 0.25–1.23), a non-significant difference; no lithium dose, salt form, serum level, or weight/BMI/metabolic outcome data were reported anywhere in the paper.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: This paper is a retrospective audit of psychotropic prescribing practices, co-morbidities and pregnancy/neonatal outcomes across two Australian antenatal SMI clinics — it is NOT a study of lithium's effect on weight gain. Lithium appears only as one mood stabilizer whose USE RATE (not dose, salt, or serum level) is reported by primary diagnosis and hospital in Table 3 (e.g., bipolar disorder: 11/39 (28.2%) at Mercy vs 32/179 (17.9%) at KEMH, OR 0.55 [0.25, 1.23]; psychosis: 2/29 (6.9%) vs 1/125 (0.8%), OR unstable/not reported; non-psychotic SMI: 2/54 (3.7%) vs 2/109 (1.8%), OR unstable/not reported). No lithium dose, salt form, serum lithium level, target range, or any weight/BMI/waist-circumference/metabolic outcome is reported anywhere in the text or tables, so the 'outcomes' array is empty and all lithium dosing/serum fields are null. Table 1 gives whole-sample (not lithium-specific) maternal BMI, weight-related covariates unrelated to lithium exposure. This paper contributes essentially no quantitative data to the lithium-weight-gain meta-analysis beyond a usage-rate comparison.

summary: In a prospective, multicenter, single-arm German cohort of 185 patients with major depressive disorder receiving lithium augmentation (lithium carbonate plus antidepressants), BMI rose significantly over follow-up (mean 25.71 kg/m2 at baseline to 27.21 kg/m2 at 7 months, p<0.05 for each comparison to baseline). The study's primary aim was to identify LEP polymorphisms (rs2278815, rs10487506) modulating this lithium-associated BMI increase, finding that AA-genotype carriers gained significantly less weight than G-allele carriers; no fixed dose was reported, but mean achieved serum lithium after 4 weeks was 0.705 mmol/L (SD 0.167).

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: Per extraction scope, only the primary BMI outcome was extracted, restricted to baseline and the final available timepoint (second follow-up, 7 months); the intermediate 4-week and 4-month BMI timepoints (n=185 mean 26.16 SD 5.42; n=61 mean 25.89 SD 4.22) were omitted per instructions. This is a single-arm naturalistic cohort (all patients received lithium carbonate augmentation); genotype groups (rs2278815, rs10487506) are effect-modifier subgroups, not treatment arms, so no between-group treatment effect exists and between_group_effects is empty; within-group change (baseline to 7 months) was calculated from the two reported means. The table 1 footnote indicates the same P<0.05 (paired t-test vs baseline) applies to the 4-week, 4-month, and 7-month BMI comparisons collectively; no separate exact p-value for the 7-month comparison alone is given. No numeric lithium dose (mg/day) was reported anywhere in the text — only 'individual doses of lithium carbonate' and achieved serum levels. Concomitant valproate use could not be confirmed (only 'antiepileptic drugs' 14/185 (7.6%) reported without specifying agent), so concomitant_valproate was left null. percent_on_antipsychotics combines atypical antipsychotics (51/185) and low-potency antipsychotics (9/185) = 60/185 = 32.4% (calculated). All *_quote fields set to null per extraction scope instructions.

summary: This prospective cohort study followed 180 treatment-resistant MDD patients receiving lithium augmentation, examining whether the LEP SNP rs6979832 (a proxy for rs10487505) modifies BMI change over up to 7 months of treatment. BMI increased significantly over the observation period overall, and GG-genotype carriers showed a significantly smaller BMI increase than A-allele carriers (genotype*time interaction p=0.001), but the paper does not report simple unadjusted whole-cohort BMI means, and lithium salt form, dose, and serum levels were not reported (detailed in companion papers Bopp et al. 2019 and Ricken et al. 2016).

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: This is a genotype-association substudy, not a dedicated weight-gain outcomes paper; lithium salt form, dose, and serum level are not reported here (see companion papers Bopp et al. 2019 and Ricken et al. 2016 for those details). No raw unadjusted whole-cohort BMI means are given; the extracted baseline mean (24.34) and change-from-baseline at 7 months (0.21, 95%CI -0.74 to 1.16, p=0.668) are mixed-model estimates for the GG reference genotype (additive genetic model, Table 1), adjusted for time, sex, age, obesity-before-LA, HDRS-17, and MRWG co-medication. The 7-month endpoint mean (24.55) was CALCULATED by summing the baseline estimate and the time-4 change estimate; no CI is available for this derived sum. Sample size for BMI shrank from 180 (baseline/4 weeks) to 66 (7 months), a large attrition not otherwise explained. No formal adverse-event or binary weight-gain-threshold data are reported.

summary: This retrospective, single-arm chart review of 23 adolescents with severe, treatment-refractory conduct disorder examined naturalistic add-on olanzapine (mean 8 mg/day) after failure of non-pharmacological treatment and adequate-dose mood stabilizers (lithium and/or valproate); roughly 56% of patients remained on concomitant lithium and/or anticonvulsants during olanzapine treatment. extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: This is fundamentally an olanzapine add-on treatment study, not a lithium dosing study. Lithium appears only as (a) a prior mood stabilizer that patients had 'failed' at adequate dosage (threshold >0.8 mEq/l, recorded as serum_lithium_target_low) before olanzapine was started, and (b) a concomitant medication continued during olanzapine treatment in a subset of patients (Table 2: lithium in 9/14 responders and 4/9 non-responders, i.e. ~13/23 = 56.5% of the whole cohort at some point, though exact concurrent-use timing/dose is not given). No lithium salt, dose, or achieved serum level is reported for any patient, and the single reported weight-gain figure (4.6 ± 3 kg mean, whole cohort n=23) cannot be disaggregated by lithium-exposure status. Set lithium_arm_ids to empty and arm 1 intervention_category to 'antipsychotic' (olanzapine) rather than lithium, since no distinct lithium arm with quantifiable dose/serum/weight data exists in this paper. Weight data are only reported as narrative mean ± SD change with a range (2-12 kg); no per-timepoint table, no baseline absolute weight, and no binary 'clinically significant weight gain' threshold count were given. Secondary outcomes (MOAS, CGI-I, CGAS, responder predictors) were omitted per extraction scope (primary outcome only).

summary: This retrospective Swiss chart review examined adjunctive topiramate (flexibly titrated, mean final dose ~187 mg/day) given to 100 psychiatric patients for weight gain attributed to antipsychotics, lithium, or valproate. Mean BMI fell significantly from 29.7±3.6 to 28±3.3 kg/m2 over a mean 41-week treatment period (P<.0005), with fewer responders among patients on lithium/valproate alone versus antipsychotics (Fisher's exact P=.009, proportions not given numerically). The study reports no lithium dose, salt form, or serum level, and lithium-exposed patients (6.1% of the cohort) cannot be disaggregated from those on valproate in any reported result.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: This paper's studied intervention is topiramate (for treating weight gain), not lithium itself, so it is a marginal fit for lithium dose-response extraction. No lithium salt form, dose, or serum level is ever reported. Only 6.1% of the 100-patient cohort was on lithium (vs. 38.8% valproate; 90% of lithium/valproate patients also had a concomitant antipsychotic) and lithium patients are never analytically separated from valproate patients in any reported result (Table 1 'Mood-stabilizing agent' row and the Fisher's exact subgroup test both pool 'lithium or valproate'). The subgroup comparison of BMI-response rates between the antipsychotic group (71% lost weight, 18.5% no change, 10.5% gained) and the 'lithium or valproate alone' group (only described qualitatively as having 'almost double' the proportion of non-responders, no numeric percentages given; Fisher's exact P=.009) was therefore omitted from structured outcome/subgroup extraction per the extraction scope (subgroup_analyses must be left empty) and because exact per-subgroup N/percent for the lithium/valproate-alone group are not stated. The paper also reports mean weight loss as 4.4±0.9 kg (a secondary restatement of the same BMI-driven finding); this was not extracted as a separate outcome per the primary-outcome-only scope. baseline_bmi_category, exposure_stratum ('therapeutic', inferred — no dose data exists to verify), monotherapy, and several concomitant-medication arm fields are inferred/null due to the mixed, non-lithium-specific population and are not verbatim-sourced.

summary: This 6-month, single-site, open-label study sequentially assigned 40 children/adolescents with bipolar I disorder (mixed or manic episode) to combination therapy with either lithium carbonate+risperidone or divalproex sodium+risperidone. Both regimens produced similar, statistically significant improvement in manic symptoms, and weight gain was substantial but not significantly different between groups (mean increase 6±3.8 kg with lithium+risperidone vs. 6.8±4.2 kg with divalproex+risperidone; weight gain reported as an adverse event in 35.3% vs. 40% of subjects, respectively).

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: Lithium was given in combination with risperidone (not monotherapy); comparator arm (divalproex+risperidone) contains no lithium. Salt form 'carbonate' is explicitly stated verbatim ('lithium carbonate mean dose was 750±400 mg (0.9 mEq/l)'); elemental dose (141 mg) was calculated as 750 mg carbonate × 0.188. No between-group p-value or CI was reported for the continuous weight-gain comparison, so the mean difference (-0.8 kg, Li+Risp minus DVPX+Risp) and its SE were calculated from the reported per-arm means/SDs/Ns. Per extraction scope, only weight-related outcomes were extracted as 'primary' for this review and all *_quote fields were set to null; efficacy (YMRS), demographic detail tables, and other secondary safety outcomes (thyroid, prolactin, ECG, liver enzymes) were omitted.

summary: This cross-sectional study of 136 bipolar I outpatients in Turkey compared metabolic syndrome (MetS, NCEP ATP-III criteria) prevalence across drug-treatment subgroups, including patients on lithium, sodium valproate, or lithium+valproate as mood stabilizers, alongside atypical antipsychotic users. Overall MetS prevalence was 32%; patients on atypical antipsychotics alone had significantly higher MetS rates than mood-stabilizer-only or combination users, but there was no significant difference in MetS prevalence among the specific mood stabilizers (lithium 22.2%, sodium valproate 27.3%, lithium+valproate 20.8%; χ²=0.18, df=2, p=0.91). No lithium dose, salt form, serum level, or weight/BMI values specific to the lithium subgroup were reported.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: This paper is a cross-sectional prevalence study of metabolic syndrome (MetS) in bipolar I patients, not a dedicated lithium weight-gain treatment study. No lithium dose, salt form, target range, or achieved serum lithium level is reported anywhere in the text. No weight (kg) or BMI values are reported broken down by drug/lithium exposure group; the only BMI data (Table 2, lower panel: 31.6±4.6 vs 25.2±3.8 kg/m2) is split by MetS status, not by drug, so it could not be assigned to a lithium arm and was omitted. The only quantitative outcome linked to lithium exposure is the binary MetS prevalence by mood-stabilizer subgroup (Table 2, 'Mood stabilizers' rows: Lithium 12/54, Na Valproat 3/11, Lithium+Valproat 5/24; χ2=0.18, df=2, p=0.91), extracted here as the primary outcome (composite/metabolic, not a pure weight measure). It is unclear whether the 'Lithium' row (n=54) includes patients also receiving atypical antipsychotics concomitantly, since the paper's 'Drug type' (AA/AA+MS/MS) and 'Mood stabilizers' (Lithium/Na Valproat/Lithium+Valproat) breakdowns use overlapping but not perfectly reconciling denominators (e.g., text states 79 patients (63.2%) were treated with lithium overall, vs 54 in the 'Lithium' row + 24 in 'Lithium+Valproat' row = 78, and various table subtotals sum to 125 vs the stated total N=136); these are apparent rounding/reporting inconsistencies in the source and are reproduced as printed rather than reconciled. No adverse-event table, thyroid, or polydipsia data are reported.

summary: This naturalistic study followed patients hospitalized for acute major depression or manic/hypomanic bipolar episodes, treated with SSRIs (depression) or mood stabilizers including lithium, valproic acid, and risperidone (bipolar), measuring total serum cholesterol before and after 4 weeks of treatment. Total cholesterol significantly increased in depressed patients (p<0.016) but significantly decreased in bipolar patients (p<0.001); only 3 of the 22 bipolar patients received lithium alone (750-1000 mg/day, salt form unstated), and no lithium-specific or weight-change data were reported — weight/BMI were measured only once at enrolment.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: This paper's primary outcome is total serum cholesterol (TC) change with treatment of acute mood episodes, not weight. Weight/height/BMI were measured only once at enrolment ('body mass index was measured once at the time of enrolment'), so no pre/post weight-change data exists anywhere in the paper; outcomes array left empty and derived.reports_weight_outcome=false. The lithium-treated bipolar subgroup (n=3, dose 750-1000 mg/day per Table 1) is not broken out separately for weight, BMI, or cholesterol in Tables 2/3 — those tables report only pooled bipolar-group (n=22, mixed lithium/valproate/valproate+risperidone) values, so no lithium-arm-specific numeric outcome could be extracted. Lithium salt form is not stated anywhere (lithium_salt=unknown). Table 1's medication breakdown (8 valproic acid + 3 lithium + 11 valproic acid+risperidone = 22) conflicts with the Method section's prose ('4 of the bipolar patients were treated with valproic acid, and 18 were treated with a combination of both risperidone and valproic acid'); per instructions, the table figures were treated as authoritative. Sample-size figures elsewhere in the paper (recruited vs. completed vs. withdrawn, e.g. '22 bipolar patients... recruited' vs '22... completed the study' vs '7... withdrew') are internally inconsistent, likely a source-text artifact; only the Table-1-reported lithium arm n=3 is extracted with confidence. No quotes were populated per the extraction-scope instructions for this task.

summary: In a naturalistic, non-randomized cohort of 179 acutely manic bipolar I inpatients in a Korean closed-ward hospital, mean weight gain after 4 weeks was 2.7±3.0 kg overall, with lithium monotherapy patients (n=13) gaining 2.2±2.9 kg — less than combination regimens like olanzapine+valproate (3.8±2.9 kg) but similar to other lithium-combination arms (2.0-3.3 kg). Differences among the four lithium-containing regimens were not statistically significant (F=0.823, P=0.486), and lithium salt, dose, and serum levels were not reported.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: Lithium salt form, dose (mg/day), dose strategy details, and serum lithium levels were not reported anywhere in the text for any arm. Treatment regimens (Table 3/5) are used as separate arms since this is a naturalistic multi-regimen cohort rather than a two-arm comparison; 'Others' (n=52, 29.1%) and combined typical/atypical antipsychotic and mono/combo summary groups (Table 4) were not extracted as separate arms per the primary-outcome scope restriction. All reported between-group statistics (Table 3 vs. 'all others combined'; Table 5 omnibus ANCOVA F-tests across 3-4 regimen groups) are omnibus/ANCOVA comparisons that do not reduce to a single arm-vs-arm mean difference with CI, so only one illustrative pairwise mean difference (lithium monotherapy vs. valproate monotherapy) was calculated from reported per-arm means/SDs, with SE derived via the pooled-SE formula. Per-arm demographic breakdowns (age, sex, baseline weight/BMI) by treatment regimen were not reported — only whole-sample values (Table 1) are available. Per extraction scope, only the primary weight-change outcome at the 4-week endpoint was extracted; secondary outcomes (obesity/overweight prevalence, SWG proportions, demographic correlates) were omitted.
