summary: This was a single-arm, open-label, prospective trial of combination lithium plus valproate in 98 outpatients with rapid-cycling bipolar I or II disorder and co-occurring substance use disorders, primarily examining medical comorbidity burden (CIRS) as a predictor of bimodal treatment response. Mean baseline BMI was 28.1 (SD 6.08), with 38% overweight and 29% obese, but no post-treatment or follow-up BMI/weight value was reported, and BMI did not significantly differ between high vs. low medical-comorbidity burden groups or between treatment responders and non-responders. The study is not informative about lithium-induced weight change since only a single baseline BMI measurement was captured.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: This paper (Kemp et al. 2009, J Affect Disord 116:64-69) is centrally about medical comorbidity burden (Cumulative Illness Rating Scale) and treatment response in rapid-cycling bipolar I/II with co-occurring substance use disorders treated open-label with combination lithium+valproate for up to 24 weeks (companion trial report: Kemp et al., J Clin Psych 2009). It is not a dedicated weight-gain study. Only ONE BMI value is reported for the whole cohort (mean 28.1, SD=6.08, N=98) as a static baseline/demographic characteristic; no follow-up or endpoint weight/BMI is reported anywhere in the text, tables, or figure, so no within-group change or between-arm weight comparison could be extracted. Table 3 compares baseline BMI between high-CIRS (n=68) and low-CIRS (n=30) medical-comorbidity subgroups (mean 28.8 vs 27.0, p=0.172) and text states no BMI difference between responders/non-responders to lithium+valproate — these are baseline-characteristic comparisons unrelated to lithium exposure/dose, so they were not extracted as treatment effects. Lithium dosing in mg/day and the mean achieved serum level for the cohort are not reported in this paper; the only quantitative lithium value given is the ≥0.8 mEq/L threshold required (sustained ≥4 consecutive weeks) as one of five criteria defining 'bimodal response,' which is a response-criterion target, not an achieved cohort mean, so serum_lithium_mmol_L_mean was left null and 0.8 was placed only in serum_lithium_target_low. Lithium salt form is not stated anywhere in the paper (kept 'unknown' per L1). concomitant_antipsychotic/antidepressant were set to false as a default since neither is reported as part of the open-label protocol, but their use was not explicitly excluded or confirmed either. Per the review's extraction-scope override, all *_quote fields were set to null.

summary: This cross-sectional study compared metabolic abnormalities in 117 Taiwanese bipolar outpatients grouped by naturalistic mood-stabilizer regimen (lithium alone, lithium+SGA, lithium-valproate+SGA, valproate alone, valproate+SGA). Body weight and BMI, stratified by sex, did not differ significantly across the five medication groups (all p>0.05), though SGA co-treatment overall was associated with higher rates of metabolic syndrome, hyperglycemia, and hypertriglyceridemia. The very small lithium-only arm (n=4) and lack of adjustment for confounders limit causal inference about lithium's independent effect on weight.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: Naturalistic cross-sectional study, not a treatment trial: weight/BMI reflect a single assessment during ongoing treatment of variable duration, not pre/post change, so within_group_change and change_kg outcomes are not applicable. Lithium salt form is never specified anywhere in the text; set to 'unknown' per L1. Table 1 'BW (Males)' value for the Li-VPA plus SGAs group (9.6 ± 6.5 kg) and the corresponding 'Hip (Males)' value for the same group (9.7 ± 5.5 cm) both appear to be typesetting/data errors (implausible for adult body weight/hip circumference) — extracted verbatim as printed per instructions, not corrected. The female W/H ratio value for the VPA column ('0.870.03') appears to be missing a '±' separator and could not be reliably parsed; not extracted. Per-arm male/female subgroup N's were back-calculated from the percentages in Table 1 (e.g. Li+SGAs 45.5% of 11 ≈ 5 males); the summed subgroup male count (50) differs slightly from the paper's reported total of 49 males, likely due to rounding of percentages in the source table. Between-group effects (mean differences) were calculated only for the cleanest lithium-monotherapy vs valproate-monotherapy contrast (arm1 vs arm4); the paper's own p-values (BW males p=0.564, BW females p=0.078, BMI males p=0.415, BMI females p=0.153) are omnibus one-way ANOVA p-values across all 5 groups, not pairwise, and were not mapped to a single comparison. Per extraction scope, only weight and BMI (the review's primary outcomes) were extracted; secondary outcomes (lipids, glucose, blood pressure, waist circumference, metabolic syndrome prevalence, hip circumference, W/H ratio) were omitted. All *_quote fields set to null per extraction scope override.

summary: In this prospective, naturalistic, open-label study of patients recovering from a first manic episode (STOP-EM program), patients treated with lithium over 12 months of maintenance treatment gained more weight on average than those treated with divalproex (6.57 kg vs 2.60 kg), though this difference was not statistically significant after adjustment for baseline BMI and SGA use. However, significantly more lithium-treated patients experienced clinically significant weight gain (≥7% of baseline weight) than divalproex-treated patients (63.2% vs 26.3%, p=0.022).

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: This paper's primary focus is weight gain in bipolar I disorder patients vs healthy subjects after a first manic episode; lithium data come from a naturalistic, non-randomized subgroup analysis (lithium vs divalproex, patients on >1 mood stabilizer excluded). No lithium salt form, dose (mg/day), or serum level data were reported anywhere in the text. The mean weight-gain comparison (6.57 vs 2.60 kg, F=0.821, df=1, p=NS) had no per-arm SDs reported, so no mean_difference/SE could be calculated per the no-SE-no-CI rule; it was left as an empty between_group_effects array. The binary clinically-significant-weight-gain comparison (63.2% vs 26.3%, χ2=5.216, df=1, p=0.022) was tested via chi-square with no OR/RR reported, so between_group_effects was left empty per instructions (events/total were back-calculated from stated percentages and N=19 per arm). Per extraction-scope instructions, all secondary outcomes (BMI, overweight/obesity rates, metabolic indices, thyroid, olanzapine/risperidone/quetiapine subgroups, sex subgroups) were omitted, only the final 12-month timepoint was extracted, and all *_quote fields were set to null.

summary: In this 2-year naturalistic observational study (EMBLEM) of 1076 bipolar patients treated with olanzapine either as monotherapy (n=313) or in combination with other antipsychotics, anticonvulsants, and/or lithium (n=763, of whom only 20.3% also took lithium), the olanzapine monotherapy group gained significantly more weight during the maintenance phase (mean +1.4 kg, SD 5.5) than the combination group (mean +0.4 kg, SD 7.4; p=0.024), and significantly more monotherapy patients had ≥7% weight gain (54.8% vs. 19.4%; p<0.001). Because lithium was only one of several concurrent combination partners and no lithium-specific dose or serum-level data were reported, this study cannot isolate lithium's individual contribution to weight gain.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: This paper is NOT a lithium-isolated study: it compares olanzapine monotherapy vs. olanzapine combination therapy, and lithium was only one of several combination partners (20.3% of the combination group, alongside valproate 27.8%, other anticonvulsants 19.7%, and antipsychotics ~6.6%). No lithium salt form, dose, or serum level was reported for any patient. Weight-gain event counts (events, total) for the binary ≥7% weight-gain outcome and the tolerability table AEs were CALCULATED (rounded) by multiplying reported percentages by the overall arm N (313 monotherapy, 763 combination), since raw counts and the exact denominator for these specific measures were not given in the text — treat as approximate. The between-group mean-difference SE for weight change (kg) and the risk-difference/SE for the ≥7% weight-gain outcome were also calculated by the extractor from reported per-arm SDs/percentages and overall arm N, since the paper reported only a p-value without an explicit effect estimate or CI. No secondary outcomes (efficacy, relapse/remission/recovery, other tolerability items, BMI, thyroid, polydipsia) were extracted per the review's PRIMARY-outcome-only scope.

summary: This cross-sectional study compared 159 bipolar disorder outpatients (55% on current lithium medication) and 258 population controls in Umeå, Sweden, examining associations between age, lithium treatment history, and HPA-axis activity (post-dexamethasone-suppression-test cortisol). extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: This paper's outcome is HPA-axis activity (dexamethasone suppression test cortisol), not weight gain; it reports no weight, BMI-change, or weight-gain-adverse-event data — BMI (Table 1) appears only as a baseline/adjustment covariate (patients 26.3±4.2 vs controls 25.5±3.4 kg/m2, p=0.050), so no outcome objects were extracted per the weight-outcome rules. Lithium salt form, dose (mg/day), and serum lithium level are never reported anywhere in the text; lithium exposure is captured only categorically (current medication yes/no, and lifetime years of lithium prophylaxis) and used as a predictor of cortisol status, not as a graded dose exposure. 'Currently on lithium medication for on average ten years' (Discussion) was the only quantifiable lithium-duration figure and was applied to arm 1's duration_value/duration_unit. Concomitant antipsychotic/valproate/antidepressant use is reported only for the whole bipolar sample (Table 1) and by hypo/eu/hypercortisolism subgroup (Table 3), not split by current-lithium-medication arm, so those fields were left null for both arms. extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: Per review scope, only the weight-relevant outcome (Obesity, BMI>30) was extracted; the paper's own primary outcomes were psychiatric (CES-D, CGI-S, psychiatric admissions) and were omitted. All *_quote fields set to null per instructions. Obesity table denominators (n=278 total vs. n=281 enrolled) imply ~1-2 missing values per arm; per-arm totals (43 and 235) were back-calculated from the stated percentages (9/43≈20.9%, 44/235≈18.7%) since exact per-arm denominators were not printed — marked result_source 'calculated'. extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: Single-arm retrospective/naturalistic cohort (N=323); no comparator group, so between_group_effects is empty and the BMI change was captured as a within_group_change (calculated as 26.7-24.9=1.8 kg/m2; no SD/CI/p-value for the BMI change itself was reported, so uncertainty fields are null). Per review scope, only the primary weight-related outcome (BMI) was extracted in 'outcomes'; secondary metabolic/lab parameters (glucose, cholesterol, BUN, creatinine, TSH, WBC) and the clinical-response/episode-frequency outcomes (Tables 1, 2, 4, 5) were omitted from 'outcomes' but their symptomatic-value proportions were mirrored into adverse_events.notable_aes (n's back-calculated from percentages of N=323, source='calculated'). summary: This retrospective TriNetX cohort study of 1.23 million adults with bipolar disorder examined whether SGLT2 inhibitor use (vs. non-use) was associated with lower risk of suicidality, all-cause mortality, and hospitalization, finding significant protective adjusted hazard ratios for all three outcomes (suicidality aHR 0.75, mortality aHR 0.55, hospitalization aHR 0.71; all p<0.001). Lithium use appears only as one of several psychopharmacologic subgroups examined in sensitivity analyses (e.g., SGLT2i benefit for suicidality was aHR 0.69 and for mortality aHR 0.60 among the lithium-treated subgroup) — this paper does not study lithium as an intervention, does not report any lithium dosing, salt form, or serum level data, and does not report any weight or metabolic outcomes, so it contains no data relevant to a lithium weight-gain meta-analysis.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: This paper is OFF-TOPIC for the lithium weight-gain review: it is a TriNetX retrospective cohort study of SGLT2 inhibitor exposure and psychiatric/mortality/hospitalization outcomes in bipolar disorder. Lithium is mentioned only as (1) one of several psychotropic covariates adjusted for in the Cox models, and (2) one of several subgroup strata in sensitivity analyses (aHR for SGLT2i benefit on suicidality = 0.69, p=0.001; on mortality = 0.60, p<0.001, among patients concurrently on lithium). No lithium dose, salt form, serum level, or weight/BMI/metabolic outcome data are reported anywhere in the paper. summary: In this 12-week, open-label, single-arm trial, adjunctive ziprasidone (mean final dose 190.4 mg/day) was added to existing weight gain-implicated psychotropic regimens (including lithium in 7/25 patients at baseline) in 25 obese/overweight bipolar disorder outpatients. Mean weight decreased significantly by 4.5 ± 3.4 kg (9.8 ± 7.5 lbs) from baseline to endpoint (p < 0.00001), but because the design was uncontrolled and multiple concomitant medications (including lithium) were tapered in some patients, no lithium-specific weight effect could be isolated.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: This paper's tested intervention is adjunctive ziprasidone for weight loss, not lithium; lithium is only a concomitant background medication present in 7/25 patients at baseline (664 ± 298 mg/day, salt form unstated) and 4/25 at endpoint (544 ± 488 mg/day) (Table 3). No lithium-specific weight outcome, serum level, or salt form is reported, and lithium was sometimes discontinued (3 patients) as part of the protocol's medication-tapering strategy, confounding any inference about lithium's own effect. Only the paper's explicitly stated PRIMARY outcome (total-sample weight change, baseline to endpoint) was extracted per the extraction scope; secondary outcomes (BMI, waist circumference, lipids, mood/anxiety scales, weight-loss responder thresholds of 5%/7%, and medication-subgroup comparisons) were omitted per instructions. Endpoint weight in kg (88.6 ± 14.4) was calculated by converting Table 1's pound values (195.4 ± 31.7 lbs) using 1 lb = 0.4536 kg.

summary: This cross-sectional naturalistic study assessed weight gain and metabolic complications in 196 Swiss psychiatric out-patients treated with second-generation antipsychotics and/or mood stabilizers (including 35 lithium-treated patients, median dose 24 mmol/day, salt form and achieved serum level not reported). Half of the lithium-treated patients (16/32 with available data, ~50%) experienced an important weight gain (≥10% of baseline weight), and in adjusted analyses lithium/valproate combined was associated with significantly less weight gain and lower predicted BMI than clozapine/olanzapine, but no lithium-specific comparative statistic (independent of valproate) was reported.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: This is a naturalistic cross-sectional study covering 6 drugs (clozapine, olanzapine, quetiapine, risperidone, lithium, valproate); only the lithium-specific data (Table 1, n=35) were extracted. Lithium dose is reported as median (IQR) 24 (22–30) expressed in mmol/day (per table footnote a), NOT mg/day despite the column header; dose_elemental_mg_per_day was calculated as 24 mmol x 6.94 mg/mmol = 166.56 mg elemental Li/day. Lithium salt form and achieved serum lithium level are never stated (serum lithium was measured only to confirm compliance against a 0.05 mmol/L threshold = 10% of the assumed minimal therapeutic level, not reported as a per-patient/group achieved value). For the primary binary outcome (weight gain >10%), Table 1 reports 16 patients (50%) for lithium, but 16/35 = 45.7%, not 50%, indicating the denominator for this row differs from the header n=35 (likely a smaller subset with weight-gain data available); total was back-calculated as 16/0.50=32 and result_source set to 'calculated'. The paper also reports a between-group effect (OR=0.17, CI 0.04–0.63, p=0.008 for important weight gain; predicted 24-month BMI 24.45 [23.01–25.89] vs 26.30 [25.07–27.53] for clozapine/olanzapine, p=0.005) but these combine lithium WITH valproate as a single category and were therefore excluded from between_group_effects to avoid misattributing valproate's contribution to lithium. No omitted secondary outcomes beyond scope instructions (BMI continuous outcome and appetite/other covariates were not extracted per the narrowed extraction scope).

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: This paper is a forensic medico-legal case report of a fatal carbamazepine overdose with incidental co-ingestion of lithium (among ~13 psychiatric drugs); it is not a treatment study of lithium and weight gain. Lithium's specific dose/regimen was never stated (only an empty package was found at the scene); the only lithium-related quantitative datum is a single postmortem blood concentration of 2.9 μg/ml, converted here to 0.418 mmol/L (2.9 mg/L ÷ 6.94), compared against a cited toxic reference level of 140.4 μg/ml (Moffat) — this is a postmortem redistribution-affected value, not a therapeutic monitoring level, and should not be pooled with clinical serum-lithium data. summary: This single case report describes a 67-year-old man with severe major depressive disorder and an atypical persistent sweet-taste dysgeusia who was treated with clomipramine, lithium 200 mg/day, mirtazapine, modafinil, and olanzapine in combination. The paper's focus is the mechanism of dysgeusia, not lithium's metabolic effects, and no post-treatment weight, BMI, or serum lithium data are reported. The patient's depressive symptoms and dysgeusia improved over about two weeks, attributed to overall antidepressant response rather than to lithium specifically.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: This paper is a case report about dysgeusia in depression, not a lithium weight-gain study. Lithium 200 mg/day (salt form not specified) was one of five concurrent psychotropic medications (clomipramine, mirtazapine, modafinil, olanzapine). No post-treatment weight, BMI, or serum lithium level is reported anywhere in the text, so no weight or serum-level data could be extracted; the only weight figure in the paper (10 kg involuntary weight loss) is a pre-admission depressive symptom, not a treatment outcome, so it was not extracted as an outcome. Exposure stratum defaulted to 'therapeutic' as the closest fit (routine clinical psychiatric use, not a supplement or drinking-water exposure), though the 200 mg/day dose falls below the >=300 mg carbonate-equivalent threshold given in the rules.

summary: Twenty-five lithium-naive bipolar depression patients were started on lithium 450 mg/day (flexibly titrated to clinical response and serum levels, reaching a mean endpoint level of 0.49 ± 0.16 mEq/L) and followed for 6 weeks; using the UKU side-effects scale, 28% (7/25) of patients reported weight gain during treatment. The study's primary focus was plasma adipokines (a significant fall in adiponectin was found), and no continuous weight or BMI change data were reported.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: Paper's primary aim is adipokine levels (adiponectin, leptin, resistin), not weight; weight is reported only as a binary side-effect frequency (7/25 = 28% reported weight gain via UKU scale) with no threshold, no kg/BMI change data, and no endpoint BMI (authors note this as a limitation). Lithium salt form is never stated in the text, so lithium_salt is coded 'unknown' rather than assumed carbonate. Starting dose was 450 mg/day with subsequent flexible titration to clinical response/serum levels; no mean/final daily dose in mg was reported, so dose_salt_mg_per_day fields are left null and serum level (0.49 ± 0.16 mEq/L at endpoint) is used as the exposure metric per protocol. Sample includes both BD-I (40%) and BD-II (60%) patients, coded as 'bipolar unspecified'. Healthy controls (arm 2) had only a single baseline visit and were not assessed for weight gain, so no arm_results exist for that arm. All *_quote fields set to null per extraction scope instructions.

summary: This retrospective, uncontrolled observational study at a single US addiction treatment center examined whether adding low-dose lithium carbonate (150 mg/day, 4.1 mmol) to a multidisciplinary 'Triad Approach' improved addiction-treatment outcomes (medication reduction, program completion, retention, employment) compared to a historical pre-program cohort and to program participants who declined lithium. Lithium recipients showed the highest program completion rate (59% vs 45% in non-recipients vs 36% historically), and serum lithium remained undetectable (<0.1 mmol/L) with no reported dose-limiting toxicity, but the study reports no group-level weight or metabolic outcome data (only an anecdotal single-patient weight loss) and had no formal statistical significance testing or randomization, limiting causal inference.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: This paper's primary outcomes are addiction-treatment metrics (program completion, retention, employment, medication reduction), not weight; per extraction scope only primary outcomes are captured, so 'outcomes' is empty. No group-level weight data are reported anywhere in the paper — the only weight-related datum is an anecdotal case report of one 47 y/o patient losing 10 kg after olanzapine was substituted with low-dose lithium (single-patient narrative, not a systematic measurement, so not extracted as a quantitative outcome). Table 2 lab data (BUN, creatinine, TSH, Free T4, WBC) are secondary/safety labs and were omitted per the narrowed extraction scope (primary outcome only). Elemental lithium dose (28.2 mg/day) was calculated from the stated 150 mg/day lithium carbonate salt dose using the standard 18.8% elemental fraction for carbonate, since the paper states both the salt form and salt mass but not elemental content directly. Serum lithium was reported as 'undetectable (<0.1)' in the text with unit 'mg/dl' but as '<0.1' under a table column header of 'mmol/L' (Table 2); treated as mmol/L per the table header, consistent with the paper's own framing relative to the standard 0.6-1.2 mmol/L therapeutic range. Duration of lithium treatment per patient is not stated; the only duration figure ('average duration of 7 month stay') applies to overall program completion, not specifically to the lithium arm, so arm-level duration fields were left null and a general treatment_duration_weeks (~30 weeks) was derived cautiously at the follow_up level only.

summary: This is a single case report of a 17-year-old girl with bipolar I disorder, acute mania, treated with lithium (dose titrated between 900-1500 mg/day, salt form unspecified) with quetiapine added as an adjunct and later discontinued. The patient gained substantial weight (66 kg to 77 kg, a 16.6% increase) while on combined lithium plus quetiapine, which the authors attribute primarily to quetiapine; weight partially reversed (down to 72 kg) after quetiapine was tapered off and she remained on lithium 1500 mg/day monotherapy. No formal statistical testing was performed given the single-patient design.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: Single-patient case report (n=1); lithium dose changed multiple times over the course (900→1200→1500→1200→900→1500 mg/day) and quetiapine was co-administered for a large portion of follow-up, confounding attribution of weight change to lithium alone. No numeric serum lithium level was ever reported (blood level draws failed repeatedly after day 5). Lithium salt form is never specified in the text (only 'Lithium (Li)'), so lithium_salt is set to 'unknown' per extraction rules rather than assumed carbonate. Per extraction scope, only the primary outcome (body weight) is extracted at its final timepoint (week 29 outpatient, on lithium monotherapy 1500 mg/day, weight 72 kg); intermediate weight measurements (68 kg at discharge, 69 kg at first outpatient visit, 74 kg at week 16, 77 kg at week 20) are described in the narrative but omitted here per scope restriction to final timepoint only. Total duration (34 weeks) is calculated by summing the 38-day inpatient/early-outpatient period plus the subsequent 29 weeks of outpatient follow-up referenced from the outpatient transfer date; this is an approximation since the paper does not give a single continuous week count. Country of study not stated in the provided text.

summary: This retrospective chart-review study of 2,529 psychiatric inpatients in Israel examined lower limb edema (LLE) as related to acute episode type (manic, non-affective psychotic, or depressive), finding manic episode significantly increased LLE risk versus depressive (OR 8.72) and non-affective psychotic (OR 3.96) episodes. Lithium treatment on admission is reported only as a background covariate (percent of each diagnostic group prescribed lithium) and did not differ between manic patients with vs. without LLE; the study reports no lithium dose, salt form, serum level, or weight-gain outcome, so it contributes no usable data to a lithium weight-gain meta-analysis.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: This paper is about lower limb edema (LLE), not lithium weight gain, and is essentially out of scope for this review. Lithium appears only as one of several psychotropic drugs 'prescribed on admission' (a categorical covariate): Table 1 reports % on lithium by diagnostic group (NAP 3.5%, manic 35.5%, depressive 8.3%) and Table 3 reports % on lithium by LLE status within manic patients (13/38=34.2% with LLE vs 117/328=35.7% without LLE, NS) — no dose, salt form, formulation, or serum lithium level is given anywhere in the text. Weight on admission (Table 3) is compared between manic patients with vs. without LLE (89.66±23.77 kg vs 75.56±19.02 kg, p<0.001), not between lithium-treated and non-lithium-treated patients, so it cannot be used to construct a lithium exposure vs weight-gain comparison. No arms, sample sizes per arm, or outcomes tied to lithium exposure could be extracted; all lithium-dose and weight-outcome fields are left null/empty per the extraction rules (never infer salt form or impute values).

summary: This cross-sectional case-control study (n=1450: 66 lithium users, 1384 non-users, from the Oslo TOP cohort of bipolar/schizophrenia-spectrum patients and healthy controls) examined associations between lithium serum levels and whole-blood gene expression, and between expression of the resulting lithium-associated genes and self-reported adverse effects (including a UKU-scale 'weight gain' severity item). Fifty-two genes were significantly associated with lithium serum levels (FDR<0.01), and weight gain severity was significantly associated with expression of a single gene (reported as LAMTOR4 in the discussion text, though Table 2 lists LAMTOR1 with a significant weight-gain coefficient of -0.04, p≤0.01). No quantitative weight, BMI, or weight-gain-incidence data comparing lithium users and non-users were reported, so no meta-analyzable weight outcome could be extracted from this paper.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: This is fundamentally a blood transcriptomics association study (lithium serum level vs gene expression), not a weight-outcome treatment study. Weight gain appears only as one of six self-reported UKU adverse-effect severity items (scored 0-3) used as a continuous explanatory variable regressed against gene expression across the sample — no per-arm (lithium vs non-user) mean weight, BMI, or weight-gain incidence/percentage is reported anywhere in the text or tables, so no outcome arm_results or between-group effects could be populated; per the review's primary-outcome-only scope, and because this exploratory adverse-effect/gene-expression correlation is not a primary weight outcome, the outcomes array was left empty. Note a discrepancy: the Discussion text states weight gain was associated with 'LAMTOR4', but Table 2 (the actual data table) lists the associated gene as 'LAMTOR1' with a weight-gain regression coefficient of -0.04 (p≤0.01) — likely a naming inconsistency between prose and table, flagged here rather than resolved. Lithium salt form and daily dose (mg) were never reported (only serum concentration used as a continuous covariate, with no summary mean/SD/range given in the provided text/tables), so all dose fields are null/unknown. Sample-level psychiatric diagnosis mix (bipolar spectrum, schizophrenia spectrum, healthy controls) does not map cleanly onto the single-diagnosis enum; 'other' was used for participants.psychiatric_diagnosis as an approximation.

summary: This is a post-hoc analysis of 98 outpatients with rapid-cycling bipolar I/II disorder and comorbid substance use disorder treated openly with lithium plus valproate for up to 24 weeks, examining the relationship between medical comorbidity burden (CIRS) and treatment response. extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: This paper is a medical-comorbidity/CIRS analysis, not a weight-gain treatment outcome study. Baseline BMI (28.1, SD 6.08) and overweight/obesity rates (38%/29%) are reported only as cross-sectional sample descriptives (also broken down by sex and by CIRS burden group in Table 3), not as pre/post or between-group treatment outcomes — no outcome object was created per the extraction scope (primary-outcome-only) since no weight/BMI change or binary weight-gain outcome tied to lithium exposure duration is reported. Lithium salt form, dose in mg, and achieved serum lithium level are not reported anywhere in the text; only the protocol response-criterion threshold (serum lithium >=0.8 mEq/L, numerically equal to mmol/L) is given as a target, not an achieved level. No comparison group exists (single-arm combination therapy); all outcomes in this paper concern CIRS medical-comorbidity burden and bimodal psychiatric treatment response, not weight/metabolic endpoints, so this paper contributes no extractable data to the weight-gain meta-analysis.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: This paper's primary focus is plasma homocysteine prevalence/correlates in bipolar disorder, not weight or lithium dosing. Lithium appears only as one of several mood-stabilizer categories (Table 1: 31/198 patients overall; Table 2: 17/69 in the HHcy group vs 14/129 in the non-HHcy group). No lithium dose, salt form, duration on lithium, or serum lithium level is reported anywhere in the text or tables. Body mass index (Table 1, Table 2) is reported only by BD-vs-control status and by hyperhomocysteinemia status, never broken down by mood-stabilizer/lithium exposure, so no weight or BMI outcome could be extracted for the lithium-exposed group. Category counts for mood stabilizers (valproate 125 + lithium 31 + others 12 = 168) and antipsychotics (34+85+42+20=181) do not sum to the total N=198, suggesting non-mutually-exclusive or partially missing categorization; percent_on_antipsychotics was calculated from these totals and should be treated as approximate. No outcomes relevant to this review's weight-gain focus were extracted.

summary: This prospective, single-arm cohort study followed 89 patients with major depressive disorder who received open-label lithium carbonate augmentation (dose individually titrated to serum levels, mean achieved serum lithium 0.715±0.15 mmol/L) added to ongoing antidepressant treatment for 4 weeks. BMI increased significantly from baseline to endpoint in a linear mixed model (adjusted estimate +0.24 kg/m2, 95% CI 0.05–0.43, p=0.016), and higher leptin levels were independently and significantly associated with higher BMI.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: Single-arm, pre-post design (no comparator arm); lithium salt explicitly stated as carbonate but no numeric mg/day dose is reported (dose was individually titrated to serum level). BMI within-group change was taken from the paper's headline linear-mixed-model estimate (0.24 kg/m2, 95% CI 0.05-0.43, p=0.016); Table 1 also reports a simpler crude paired difference (25.55->25.91 kg/m2, paired t-test p<0.05, non-exact) which was not separately extracted to avoid duplicating the same underlying comparison. Serum lithium level (0.715±0.15 mmol/L) was available for only 80/89 patients and is labeled 'at last visit', close to but not perfectly aligned with the 4-week BMI endpoint. Secondary outcomes (leptin levels, HDRS-17) omitted per extraction scope (primary outcome only = BMI).

summary: This retrospective chart-review study compared body weight and BMI changes among 214 psychiatric inpatients (mostly schizophrenia, schizoaffective disorder, or bipolar I) treated with lithium, valproate, or topiramate monotherapy over a mean of ~90-131 days at a state psychiatric hospital. Patients receiving lithium or valproate gained a mean of 6.3 kg and 6.4 kg respectively, while topiramate-treated patients lost a mean of 1.2 kg, a statistically significant difference (p<0.001). The study was open-label, nonrandomized, and subject to assignment bias, but shows a clear and statistically significant weight-gain signal for lithium relative to topiramate.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: Lithium salt form was not stated verbatim; carbonate inferred as the overwhelmingly standard clinical formulation in the US (this is a weaker inference than a brand-name mapping, flagged accordingly). Per-arm change-in-weight n's (70/94/36) differ from baseline enrollment n's (74/104/36) due to 14 patients with missing height/weight data. A mean_difference (lithium vs topiramate) and its SE were calculated from Table II per-arm means/SDs/Ns since no direct pairwise between-group effect was reported (only the 3-way ANOVA F-test). Per scope restrictions, only the primary continuous weight-change outcome at the final timepoint was extracted; BMI change, percent-weight-change, and the binary any-gain/no-change/any-loss outcome in Table II were omitted as secondary outcomes. All monotherapy arms had high concomitant antipsychotic/antidepressant/other-mood-stabilizer use (Table I), so derived.monotherapy is false despite drug-class exclusivity for lithium/valproate/topiramate combinations specifically.

summary: This was a naturalistic 6-year follow-up study of 76 patients with bipolar, unipolar depressive, or schizoaffective disorder who started lithium prophylaxis at specialized outpatient clinics in Vienna and Berlin, examining medication adherence, attitudes, and side effects. Weight gain was reported as a side effect by 18.4% (14/76) of patients over the 6-year follow-up, among the most common side effects alongside increased thirst, tremor, polyuria, and GI complaints, but showed no significant correlation with adherence status (r=0.11, not significant) and was not otherwise quantified (no dose, serum level, or measured kg/BMI data reported).

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: This paper's primary focus is lithium adherence/attitudes, not weight gain; no lithium salt form, dose (mg/day), or serum lithium level is reported anywhere in the text despite routine serum monitoring being described qualitatively. Weight gain appears only as a cumulative side-effect frequency (14/76, 18.4%) pooled across the whole 6-year cohort with no breakdown by adherence group, no baseline or follow-up body weight/BMI values, and no threshold definition for 'weight gain' - treated here as symptom_domain clinically_significant_weight_gain / weight_metric 'other' per rule W3. All per_arm dose/serum/concomitant-medication fields are null because they are genuinely not reported. extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: This paper's actual focus and primary outcome is efficacy of adjunctive quetiapine (CGI-BP severity change) in bipolar I patients already stabilized on lithium or valproate — NOT a lithium dosing or weight-gain study. Weight gain appears only once, as one of several quetiapine-related side effects ('weight gain' n=1) listed for the 14 subjects who continued quetiapine treatment; this count is POOLED across the lithium- and valproate-stabilized subgroups (n=9 and n=8, overlapping by 1 combination-therapy subject) with no arm-level split, no threshold definition, and no baseline/endpoint weight values in kg or BMI anywhere in the text. Lithium salt form is never stated (set to 'unknown' per L1); only serum level (meq/l, copied unchanged to mmol/L per L3) and a serum-level inclusion threshold (≥0.8 meq/l) are reported — no lithium dose in mg/day is given anywhere (only quetiapine dose in mg is reported). One subject was on low-dose combination lithium (0.62 meq/l) + valproate (60.6 μg/ml) and is counted within both the n=9 lithium and n=8 valproate groups. Given the near-total absence of arm-attributable, quantitative weight data, this paper contributes minimal evidentiary value to a lithium weight-gain meta-analysis and the single weight-gain AE count should likely be treated with high caution or excluded from pooling.

summary: This retrospective population-pharmacokinetic and genome-wide association study analysed 2357 lithium-treated patients with bipolar disorder from two Swedish clinical cohorts to identify clinical and genetic predictors of lithium clearance. Age, sex, kidney function (eGFR), serum lithium concentration, and comedication with diuretics or RAAS-acting drugs were significantly associated with lithium clearance, and one genetic locus (rs583503, chromosome 11) reached genome-wide significance. The paper reports lithium dosing (mean 24.3 and 21.6 mmol/day in cohorts 1 and 2) and achieved serum levels (mean 0.7 and 0.6 mmol/L) but does not report any weight, BMI, or other metabolic outcome data.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: This paper is a population-pharmacokinetics/GWAS study of lithium clearance, not a weight-gain or metabolic-outcome study — no weight, BMI, or metabolic data are reported anywhere in the text or tables, so the outcomes array is empty. Two arms were modeled as the two study cohorts (no untreated comparator exists); lithium_salt was set to 'unknown' per arm because each cohort is a heterogeneous mix of lithium sulphate/carbonate/citrate preparations (verbatim percentages given in the dose field) and no per-salt dosing/serum data were reported. dose_elemental_mg_per_day and the combined derived dose/serum values were calculated (mmol × 6.94 for elemental mg; enrollment-weighted average across cohorts for the combined derived fields) since the paper reports lithium intake in mmol, not mg. BMI per arm was calculated from reported mean weight and height (not from an authors' reported BMI value). All *_quote fields were left null per this extraction's scope instructions.

summary: This prospective observational study followed 166 unipolar and bipolar out-patients (aged 21-78) on long-term lithium carbonate treatment over 2 years to examine whether age affects lithium efficacy and side-effects (tremor, polydipsia/polyuria) after adjusting for plasma lithium level and other confounders. Older patients required significantly lower weight-related lithium doses to achieve the same plasma level, and hand tremor prevalence/severity increased significantly with age, but polydipsia/polyuria and overall psychiatric efficacy did not show a significant age-related decline. Body weight itself was not reported as an outcome in this paper — it was only used as a covariate to calculate weight-related dosing.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: This paper reports NO weight/BMI outcome data — body weight was measured at ~90% of visits solely to compute a hypothetical weight-related dose (mg/kg) needed to achieve a plasma lithium level of 1 mM, used as a dose-normalization covariate in the age analysis, not as an outcome. No mean weight, BMI, or weight-gain incidence is given anywhere in text or tables. Outcomes array left empty per this review's scope (weight/metabolic outcomes only) since none are reported. Serum lithium levels are reported only as regression coefficients vs. age within Table 2 (garbled OCR table), not as arm-level means; the actual plasma lithium mean/SD values could not be reliably extracted from the corrupted table text. Percent female (71.7%) and n=166 patients calculated from 119/166 female stated in text. Sex/diagnosis breakdown by decade is in Table 1 (visits/patients by age band) but not weight-relevant. No lithium dose in mg/day, mg/kg/day, or mmol/day is stated anywhere as an absolute value — only the dose-per-plasma-level parameter and its age coefficient.

summary: This cross-sectional, multicenter ENIGMA-BD mega-analysis pooled MRI, medication, and BMI data from 1231 people with bipolar disorder (48.5% on lithium at the time of scanning) and 1601 healthy controls to study associations between BMI, bipolar diagnosis, and cortical brain structure. It did not test lithium's effect on weight gain longitudinally; the only lithium-BMI comparison reported was a non-significant cross-sectional association between current lithium treatment and BMI (t(736) = -0.42, p = 0.676), with no dose, salt form, or serum lithium level reported.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: This is a cross-sectional multicenter neuroimaging (cortical thickness/surface area) study, not a lithium weight-gain treatment trial. Lithium is captured only as a binary 'currently treated with Li at time of scanning' covariate (556/1231 = 48.5%, of whom 182/556 = 46.7% monotherapy); no dose, salt form, formulation, or serum lithium level is reported anywhere in the text. BMI is used throughout as a continuous predictor/covariate of brain structure, not as a treatment outcome, and per-arm (Li vs non-Li) BMI means/SDs are never reported — Table 1 gives BMI only by diagnosis (case vs control), not by lithium status. The single quantitative BMI-lithium result extracted is the non-significant test of association between BMI and Li treatment status reported in the Results (t(736) = -0.42, p = 0.676); no effect size/mean difference magnitude was given, only the t-statistic and p-value. No adverse event, weight-gain-specific, thyroid, or polydipsia data are reported. All *_quote fields set to null per extraction scope instructions.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: Single-arm retrospective case-series audit (n=44) of combined clozapine-lithium therapy; no comparator arm, so between_group_effects is empty. Weight gain extracted as a first-class binary AE outcome per W3 (3/44, 7%, Table 1) since this is a safety-table-only report of weight gain with no threshold specified (weight_metric set to 'other'). A separate prospective re-assessment subsample (n=23) also reports weight gain severity counts (DOTES/TWIS) in Figure 1, but the OCR'd figure values are a jumbled, unattributable list of numbers with no reliable category-to-value mapping and are not extracted (data only in figure/ungrabbable). Individual-patient lithium plasma levels (e.g. 1.08 mEq/L, 0.9 mEq/L, 0.79 mEq/L) are reported only for isolated case examples, not as an aggregate cohort statistic, so serum_lithium_mmol_L_mean is left null/not_reported.

summary: This 8-week single-blind trial randomized 36 bipolar I/II depressed outpatients on background mood stabilizer therapy (lithium or divalproex) to adjunctive topiramate (50-300 mg/day) or bupropion SR (100-400 mg/day). Both arms showed significant and comparable improvement in depressive symptoms (56% vs 59% response, not significantly different, p=0.097), and both groups lost weight (mean 5.8 kg with topiramate, 1.2 kg with bupropion SR) rather than gaining it. This paper is included in the lithium weight-gain review only incidentally, as roughly a third of participants were on background lithium (Table 2: n=13, mean dose 980 mg/day, mean plasma level 1.16 mEq/L), but no lithium-specific weight data are reported.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: This trial is NOT a lithium intervention study — lithium is a background mood stabilizer in a subset of patients (13 of 36) receiving adjunctive topiramate or bupropion SR for bipolar depression; no arm in the schema's sense represents a lithium exposure group, so lithium_arm_ids is empty and no lithium arm object was created despite Table 2 reporting lithium dose (980.0 ± 388.3 mg/day) and plasma level (1.16 mEq/L, treated as mmol/L per L3) for the pooled lithium sub-cohort (salt form not stated, so lithium_salt would be 'unknown' if an arm were created). No weight data are reported specific to lithium-treated vs non-lithium-treated patients; the only weight data in the paper are for topiramate vs bupropion SR arms and reflect weight LOSS, not lithium-attributable weight gain, so reports_weight_outcome is false and no weight outcome object was created per this review's scope (lithium weight gain). Per EXTRACTION SCOPE instructions, only the primary efficacy outcome (HDRS-17 response) was extracted; all quote fields set to null as instructed; sample_sizes.per_arm limited to n_enrolled only.

summary: This single-center, open-label, cross-sectional pilot study compared 20 lithium-treated and 18 valproate-treated women with bipolar I/II disorder for reproductive endocrine and metabolic parameters, including weight and BMI, after at least 2 months of treatment. Mean weight (71.0 kg vs 72.4 kg) and BMI (29.21 vs 31.14 kg/m2) did not differ significantly between lithium and valproate groups (p=0.82), though valproate was associated with more menstrual irregularities, hyperandrogenism, adverse metabolic markers, and higher leptin levels. No baseline (pre-treatment) weight data were available for either group.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: Cross-sectional design with no baseline/pre-treatment weight data; only single-timepoint absolute weight/BMI values available, so within_group_change could not be computed. Lithium salt form was never specified in the text (dose reported only as mean mg/day and plasma level in meq/L), so lithium_salt set to 'unknown' per L1. Serum lithium level (0.92 meq/L) copied unchanged to mmol/L per L3 (meq/L numerically equals mmol/L for lithium); marked 'calculated' only because the raw value required unit-equivalence reasoning, not arithmetic. Weight/BMI SD values in Table 3 as extracted from the paper (e.g. BMI SD=53.13 and 60.89, weight SD=56.44 and 62.58) appear implausibly large relative to their means (likely a transcription/formatting error in the source PDF table, possibly conflating SD with another statistic), but are reported here verbatim as printed since no correction can be verified from the text. Mean differences for weight and BMI were calculated from per-arm means/SDs since no direct between-group effect size was reported beyond p=0.82; SE calculated per rule 4 as sqrt(sd1^2/n1+sd2^2/n2), but given the anomalous SDs this SE is likely also inflated/unreliable. Extensive endocrine/metabolic outcomes in Table 3 and Table 4 (cholesterol, HDL, LDL, glucose, triglycerides, testosterone, SHBG, androstenedione, estradiol, progesterone, DHEAS, LH, FSH, prolactin, TSH, C-peptide, IGF-1, IGFBP-1, leptin, menstrual irregularities, hyperandrogenism) were omitted per extraction scope instructions limiting outcomes to primary weight/BMI only. No binary 'clinically significant weight gain' outcome was reported in this paper (no AE table, no 7% threshold reported).

It found that lithium treatment was associated with higher FA in several tracts and a weaker (less negative) BMI-FA association than in non-lithium-treated patients, but it reports no lithium dose, salt form, serum level, or weight/BMI-change outcome data, so it contributes no extractable weight-gain effect data for this review.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: This paper is a neuroimaging (DTI/FA) study, not a lithium weight-gain treatment study. BMI is used solely as a covariate/predictor variable for white matter microstructure, not as an outcome measured before/after or during lithium treatment; there is no weight-gain, BMI-change, or weight-related adverse-event data of any kind. Lithium exposure is captured only as a binary current-treatment status (43.7% of BD group, n=389/899); dose, salt form, formulation, treatment duration, and serum lithium levels are explicitly stated as unavailable ('we are also missing key parts of medication information including dose, history of medications as well as other treatments, and exposure length'). Non-lithium BD arm n=510 was calculated as 899-389. summary: This is a mechanistic study, not a lithium weight-gain treatment trial: it examines how lithium (Li) exposure causes trophoblast ferroptosis via a suppressed ER/METTL1/MBOAT1 axis to induce unexplained miscarriage, using a human UM-vs-HC serum Li case-control comparison, a dose-response pregnant-mouse LiCl model, and human trophoblast (Swan 71) cell experiments. The only weight-related finding is that oral LiCl doses ≥20 mg/kg/d (≥5.6-fold the estimated real environmental exposure dose) reduced gestational weight gain in pregnant mice, but this is attributed to embryo resorption/miscarriage rather than a metabolic weight-gain effect, and no numeric means/SDs are given in text (data only in Fig. 1g, h). No human weight-gain outcome is reported anywhere in the paper.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: This paper (Nature Communications, DOI 10.1038/s41467-025-67026-7) is fundamentally about Li exposure causing trophoblast ferroptosis and unexplained miscarriage (UM), NOT a lithium weight-gain treatment study — it appeared in this queue but has essentially no usable weight-gain data for the review. Two lithium-exposure components exist: (1) a human case-control comparison of serum Li (μg/L, ICP-MS) between UM patients (13.04 ± 4.61 μg/L) and healthy controls (4.70 ± 2.68 μg/L), n=80/group, which has NO weight outcome at all; (2) a randomized pregnant-mouse oral-gavage LiCl dose-response model (0, 3.6, 20, 100, 200 mg/kg/d for 13 days, n=6/group, corresponding to 0, 1-, 5.6-, 28-, 56-fold 'real environmental exposure dose' [REED]), which measured gestational body-weight gain (Fig. 1g, h) — the paper states only qualitatively that '≥20 mg/kg/d LiCl ... reduced the increase in body weight,' with no exact means/SDs/p-values given in text or tables (figure-only data, per rule 10, hence all arm_results are result_source='not_reported'). Notably this is a DECREASE, not increase, in weight gain, and is attributed to embryo resorption/miscarriage rather than a metabolic weight-gain mechanism, so it is not analogous to the clinical lithium weight-gain outcome this review targets. Mouse blood Li levels (Fig. 1f) were reported only as an aggregate range ('increased from 6 to 177 μg/L with increasing Li exposure doses') with no per-arm breakdown in text, so serum_lithium fields were left null/not_reported for all arms. Per-mouse dose was given in mg/kg/day (not absolute mg/day), so dose_salt_mg_per_day_mean was left null (verbatim mg/kg/d values are preserved in each arm's 'dose' field). No baseline demographics, adverse-event tables, or between-group statistical effects for the weight outcome were reported. Given the near-total absence of relevant weight data, this record likely contributes nothing quantitatively to the pooled meta-analysis beyond confirming a qualitative dose-response direction.

summary: This is a case series of two patients (a 35-year-old man and a 55-year-old woman) treated with lithium sulfate for affective psychoses, both of whom developed acute nephrotic syndrome while on therapeutic (or near-therapeutic) serum lithium levels. Case 1 showed rapid weight gain (80kg to 88kg) and massive proteinuria (up to 11.74 g/24h) with serum lithium only mildly elevated (1.08-1.43 mmol/L); renal biopsy was normal and the syndrome fully resolved after lithium discontinuation. Case 2 developed milder proteinuria in the context of lithium intoxication (serum level up to 2.0 mmol/L) during a dehydration episode; both cases were fully reversible, and no statistical inference is applicable given the case-series design.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: German-language case report (with English abstract) of two nephrotic syndrome cases under therapeutic lithium. Only Case 1 reports quantitative body weight data (80kg -> 88kg over ~1 week before nephrotic syndrome onset); Case 2 reports no weight values. Dose given only in mval/die (mEq/day, numerically equal to mmol/day for lithium); no mg salt dose stated for either case, so dose_salt_mg_per_day left null per rules (elemental/mmol only reported). Per scope instructions, only primary/final timepoint extracted, quotes set to null, and secondary outcomes (renal function labs, EKG, thyroid, etc.) omitted from 'outcomes' though noted here as AEs/context. Case 1 also had elevated cholesterol (745 mg/dl) and hypoalbuminemia at nephrotic syndrome presentation, consistent with nephrotic syndrome physiology rather than direct lithium weight-gain mechanism — flagged as a confound for the weight-gain finding.

summary: This naturalistic, non-randomized cross-sectional study of 114 psychiatric inpatients in Germany examined psychoactive-drug-induced changes in plasma lipid/lipoprotein levels (not body weight) from hospital admission to discharge, subdividing patients into 8 treatment groups including four lithium-containing combination groups (with butyrophenones and/or tricyclics and/or SSRIs). The paper found that co-administration of lithium inhibited the increase in total cholesterol and LDL otherwise induced by butyrophenones/tricyclics, but did not report body weight or BMI outcomes by treatment/lithium group (only overall/by-diagnosis body weight and BMI in Table 1, not broken out by drug regimen). No lithium dose in mg or serum lithium level was reported — only relative 'units of standard daily therapeutic dose.'

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: This paper's primary focus is plasma lipid/lipoprotein changes, not weight — no weight or BMI outcome is reported by treatment/lithium group; Table 1 shows body weight and BMI only by DIAGNOSTIC group (D2/S3/SA,Mi4/SA,Ds), not by the 8 treatment groups, so no per-lithium-arm weight data exists to extract. No 'outcomes' array entries were created because there is no primary weight/BMI outcome by lithium exposure group. Lithium dose is reported only as a relative 'unit of standard daily therapeutic dose' (TD/SD/D formula relative to lithium carbonate 800mg/day standard dose per Table 2) with no absolute mg or serum level; salt form is inferred as carbonate from Table 2's 'Lithiumcarbonate 800 mg' standard-dose definition (this is the standard-dose reference, not necessarily every patient's actual salt, but no other salt is mentioned). Per-arm relative lithium dose units and their SDs are reported in Table 2 and included in the arms' 'dose' field verbatim; these are NOT absolute mg/day and were left as dose_salt_mg_per_day = not_reported per instructions not to infer. All *_quote fields set to null per extraction scope override.

summary: This is a single case report of a 56-year-old woman with bipolar disorder on lithium carbonate (1125 mg/day, serum level ~1.0 mmol/L) who developed severe thyrotoxicosis secondary to Hashimoto thyroiditis after iodine contrast medium administration, with a rapid mood swing to mania and subsequent psychotic depression. The patient experienced marked weight loss and cachexia (BMI falling from 18.5 to a nadir of 12.2 kg/m2) during the thyrotoxic/manic-depressive episode, with partial weight regain (BMI to 13.3 kg/m2) after lithium was discontinued and thyrostatic/immunosuppressive therapy begun; no statistical testing was performed as this is a single-patient case report.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: Single case report, not a trial or cohort — extracted as a case series with n=1. Weight changes (via BMI) in this patient are confounded heavily by concurrent Hashimoto thyroiditis/thyrotoxicosis, iodine contrast exposure, severe illness/cachexia, and eventual lithium discontinuation, so attributing weight loss/regain to lithium itself is not appropriate; included per instructions to extract all lithium-exposed group data. No formal baseline weight in kg was reported, only BMI values at three timepoints (18.5 at first admission, 12.2 at University Medical Center admission, 13.3 after three weeks of thyrostatic/immunosuppressive therapy and lithium discontinuation); only baseline (18.5) and final reported (13.3) values were extracted as per primary-outcome/final-timepoint-only scope. Dose given only in mg of lithium carbonate salt with no elemental conversion or mmol/day stated. No formal statistics, p-values, or between-group comparisons possible in a single-subject case report.

summary: This cross-sectional clinical audit assessed obesity and metabolic syndrome (IDF criteria) in 221 patients with chronic psychotic disorders (predominantly schizophrenia/schizoaffective disorder) attending a psychiatric rehabilitation service in Australia, all on antipsychotic medication. Obesity prevalence was 59% and metabolic syndrome prevalence was 68% overall; among the 70 patients also receiving a mood stabilizer (lithium and/or sodium valproate, not reported separately), metabolic syndrome prevalence was 77.1% (54/70), the highest of any drug-category subgroup though the paper does not report whether this difference was statistically significant. No lithium-specific dose, salt form, serum level, or weight data are reported, as lithium is not distinguished from valproate anywhere in the paper.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: This paper is a cross-sectional prevalence audit, not a lithium dose/weight-gain study. Lithium is never reported separately from sodium valproate — both are pooled as 'mood stabilizers' prescribed to 70/221 patients (32%), always alongside antipsychotics — so no lithium-specific salt, dose, serum level, or weight/BMI data exist anywhere in the text. Overall cohort BMI (mean 32.2, SD 6.6) and obesity/overweight rates (59%/29%) are reported for the whole 221-patient population, not stratified by mood-stabilizer exposure, so they cannot be attributed to the lithium-exposed arm and were not extracted as an outcome. The only lithium-related quantitative datum usable for this review is the metabolic-syndrome prevalence in the mood-stabilizer subgroup (Table 2: 54/70, 77.1%), extracted as a single binary composite outcome with no comparator arm. Diagnosis mix was predominantly schizophrenia/schizoaffective disorder (93%), not bipolar disorder (4%), which is atypical for a lithium review and is flagged via psychiatric_diagnosis='other'.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: This paper is a case series about lithium-associated transient thyrotoxicosis, not a weight-gain study; no primary weight outcome exists to extract, so outcomes[] is empty and derived.reports_weight_outcome is false. Two patients (1 and 4) had incidental weight LOSS of 4 kg and 3 kg respectively as symptoms during acute thyrotoxic episodes (opposite direction, non-systematic, single timepoint, no comparator) — these are not usable as a lithium weight-gain effect estimate and were not extracted as an outcome. Each of the 4 patients is modeled as a separate n=1 arm (dose_contrast_within_trial=true per protocol) because doses (750-1,250 mg/day lithium carbonate) and achieved serum levels (0.45-0.7 mmol/L) differed and changed over each patient's course; dose/serum values given reflect the most recent/maintenance values stated in the text (with min/max noted for patients 1 and 2 whose dose changed). extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: This is a psychometric validation/reliability study of the UKU-SERS-Pat side-effects scale in a mixed bipolar cohort, not a lithium dose-response or weight-gain outcome study. No lithium dose, salt form, or serum level is reported anywhere in the text (only that 55/93 patients, 59.1%, were 'treated with lithium' as part of polypharmacy). No arms are defined by exposure since this is not a comparative treatment study — all 93 patients form one cross-sectional cohort with heterogeneous, unspecified medication regimens. 'Weight gain' appears only as one item on the side-effects checklist, reported as a prevalence percentage (patient-rated 43.0% vs clinician-rated 35.5%) with a Spearman correlation (r=0.79) and a mean severity-difference score (0.10, SD 0.47) between patient and clinician ratings — these are item-level severity/frequency scores on the UKU scale, not kg, %, or BMI weight-change data, and are not per-lithium-arm. 'Weight loss' is reported similarly (19.4% vs 11.8%). Because there is no lithium-specific arm, no dose/serum data, and no quantitative weight metric usable for meta-analysis, no outcomes array entries were extracted; this paper should likely be excluded from the quantitative synthesis at the screening stage.

summary: This is a single case report of an 11-year-old prepubertal boy treated with lithium carbonate (900 mg/day, achieved serum level 0.9 mmol/L) alongside multiple other psychotropics, who developed nephrotic syndrome (minimal change disease) with a 20-pound weight gain from edema/fluid retention. extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: Case report, not a treatment-efficacy trial for weight gain per se; the 20-lb weight gain described is edema/fluid-retention related to lithium-induced nephrotic syndrome (minimal change disease), not typical adiposity-related lithium weight gain, and should be interpreted cautiously in a weight-gain meta-analysis. Patient was on five concurrent psychotropic medications including olanzapine (itself strongly associated with weight gain), which severely confounds attribution of weight gain to lithium. The only extractable quantitative weight/BMI comparison is the 'Weight gain' section: 42 lithium clinic patients matched to 42 general-practice controls. Per scope instructions only this primary weight/BMI outcome was extracted; the renal (n=101), thyroid (350 patient-years), and suicide (11,030 patient-years) findings were omitted as secondary/non-weight outcomes. Lithium salt form is not stated for this 42-patient weight cohort (elsewhere 'lithium carbonate' is mentioned only for the separate 101-patient renal cohort), so lithium_salt was set to 'unknown' per rule L1 rather than inferred. The clinic's general serum-lithium target range (0.5-0.9 mmol/L, mentioned in the Renal Problems section) was not explicitly stated as applying to this weight-comparison cohort, so it was left not_reported per rule L5 rather than imputed. No SD was reported for BMI in either group, so no between-group mean difference/SE could be calculated (rule 4); the paper only states 'in paired t-tests weight gain was not significant' with no exact statistic, so between_group_effects was left empty rather than emit an unusable value. Duration of lithium exposure per patient is not individually reported, only a group total (400.5 patient-years / 42 patients ≈ 9.5 years average), so arm duration fields were left null rather than force an approximate/averaged value into ill-fitting units.

summary: This retrospective chart review examined 14 adolescents with TCA-resistant nonbipolar major depression who had lithium added to their ongoing tricyclic antidepressant treatment. Six of 14 (43%) were classified as responders, with group mean CGI severity improving significantly from baseline through 6 weeks of lithium augmentation; only 1 of 14 patients was reported to have weight gain as a side effect, and no side effects necessitated lithium discontinuation. As an open-label, uncontrolled case series, no comparison group or formal statistical test of weight change was reported.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: Single-arm retrospective case series; no comparator group, so no per-arm continuous weight data or between-group effects exist. Weight gain reported only as 1/14 patients experiencing it as a side effect during TCA+lithium combination treatment (Table 2 side-effects table); denominator of 14 assumed from total sample since Table 2 does not restate N. Individual per-patient lithium salt mg doses and serum levels are given in Table 1 (patient-level, e.g. 600-1500 mg/day, levels 0.16-1.32 mEq/L) but were not extracted as separate arms per scope rules limiting to primary outcome/final timepoint; overall dose range (600-1,500 mg/day) and overall serum level range (0.16-1.32 mEq/L) taken from Table 2 caption. Lithium salt form not stated anywhere in text (no brand name given), so lithium_salt set to unknown per rule L1. OMI in tables likely OCR artifact for DMI (desipramine); NT = nortriptyline, AMI = amitriptyline — these are TCA doses, not lithium, and were excluded from the lithium dose fields. All *_quote fields set to null per extraction scope instructions.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: This is fundamentally a risperidone add-on trial, not a lithium-specific study; only 34/102 patients (33.3%) were on lithium monotherapy plus 13 on lithium/valproate and 3 on lithium/carbamazepine (44/102 total lithium-exposed), and weight/BMI outcomes are reported only for the whole cohort (all mood stabilizers combined), not broken out by lithium vs valproate vs carbamazepine subgroup, so a lithium-specific weight-gain arm cannot be extracted separately. Baseline mean serum lithium (0.72 ± 0.28 mmol/l) and target range (0.6-1.2 mmol/l) apply to the lithium-exposed subgroup only, not the whole arm. BMI change reported as 0.8 ± 1.5 at week 12 and 0.8 ± 1.4 at last observation but omitted from outcomes per extraction scope (primary outcome only; BMI treated as secondary here since body weight change is the more directly stated primary safety/weight metric and only one primary outcome was requested). extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: This paper is a case-report series about misdiagnosis of delirium, not a dedicated lithium weight-gain study. Only Case 2 involves lithium; weight gain is mentioned only narratively ('had recently gained weight and could not close her skirt') with no numeric value, so no continuous, BMI, or binary weight outcome could be extracted — weight_reported_as set to 'none' despite a qualitative mention. Serum lithium level of 0.91 mg/dl was reported as 'mg/dl' in the source text but this is almost certainly the conventional mEq/L (=mmol/L for lithium) unit as typically reported in clinical practice; copied across unchanged per L3 given the numeric plausibility (0.91 mmol/L is within/near therapeutic range) versus an implausible mg/dl-to-mmol/L conversion. Lithium salt form (carbonate) taken verbatim from text ('lithium carbonate'). No dose in mg/day was reported. Other three cases (phenobarbital toxicity, hypoglycemia, lupus cerebritis) do not involve lithium and were excluded from arms.

summary: In this 6-week open-label, single-arm trial, 28 adolescents (mean age 15.6, 82% female) with bipolar I disorder currently experiencing a depressive episode received lithium carbonate monotherapy titrated to a target serum level of 1.0-1.2 mEq/L (mean endpoint dose 1355.8 mg/day, mean endpoint serum level 0.9 mEq/L). summary: This retrospective study reviewed case records and questionnaire responses from 70 manic-melancholic (bipolar) patients maintained on lithium for 2 to 10 years. 45 of the 70 patients (about 64%) gained weight, with those who gained weight already overweight at baseline and gaining roughly 10 kg on average; increased thirst, not appetite, was strongly correlated with the weight gain. No control group or formal statistical comparison was reported.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: Provided text appears to be an abstract/introduction-level excerpt with no methods, tables, dose, or serum-level data — lithium salt form, dose, and serum lithium were not reported anywhere in the given text. Treatment duration was stated only as a range ('2 to 10 years'), so it could not be encoded as a single duration_value/duration_unit or follow-up week value. The 'mean weight gain of about 10 kg' applies only to the subgroup of 45/70 patients who gained weight, not to the whole cohort's mean change, so it was not extracted as a full-arm continuous within_group_change value (would misrepresent the whole arm); the 45/70 count was extracted instead as the primary binary outcome. Percent (64.3%) was calculated from 45/70. No comparison group exists, so between_group_effects is empty. Baseline demographics (age, sex, weight, BMI) were not numerically reported for the full cohort, only qualitatively for the subgroup who gained weight ('overweight already before the start', 'about 20% higher than their ideal weight').

summary: This cross-sectional study measured 24-hour plasma lithium peak levels in 35 chronically lithium-treated bipolar outpatients (single bedtime dosing) and correlated the peak level and dose with several lithium-associated changes, including weight gain above ideal body weight. Lithium-treated patients had significantly greater weight increase above ideal body weight than controls (14.4 vs 4.7 kg, p<0.001), but weight gain was not significantly correlated with either plasma lithium peak level or lithium dose, suggesting weight gain is not directly concentration-dependent.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: Lithium salt form and numeric daily dose (mg) are never stated in this paper — only serum/plasma peak lithium level (1.64 ± 0.35 mmol/L) and correlation coefficients with an unspecified 'dose' variable are given, so dose fields are left null/unknown. Weight outcome is a single cross-sectional 'weight increase above ideal body weight' value (kg above ideal, per Metropolitan Life Insurance Co. tables), not a pre-post change or standard kg/BMI measure; treated as the primary (and only) outcome per scope. Between-group mean_difference and its SE were calculated from Table 1 means/SEs (labeled 'standard error' in the table, entered here as sd per schema absence of a distinct field) treating n=35 lithium and n=57 controls. summary: This Danish single-center follow-up study reexamined 184 of 237 patients originally surveyed for lithium's effects on kidney function two years earlier, comparing those who continued lithium (n=147), those who discontinued (n=37), and a lithium-naive pre-lithium comparison group (n=68). Kidney glomerular filtration was unaffected by lithium, but renal water-handling impairment (increased urine volume, decreased maximum urine osmolality) persisted and was related to serum lithium level and treatment duration in continuers, while it partially reversed after discontinuation; weight gain was reported qualitatively as similarly frequent in continuers versus their own prior exam, with only a quantified mean weight loss of 2.5 kg reported in those who discontinued lithium, and no formal between-group statistical test of weight was presented.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: Weight data in this paper are almost entirely narrative: for the lithium (continued) group only 'a slight increase was observed in average body weight' with no numeric value; for the post-lithium (discontinued) group 'an average weight loss of 2.5 kg had taken place' (extracted as within-group change, no SD/p reported); for the pre-lithium group only the absolute mean baseline weight (69.7 kg) is given, stated as significantly lower than both lithium groups but no p-value given. No per-arm event counts for 'weight gain' as a discrete AE are given (only qualitative frequency comparisons to Examination I), so the outcome could not be populated as a true binary count; events/total left null. Body weight and age at Examination I/II are given in Table 1 mixing several exam timepoints for age/weight/dosage/serum-lithium — I extracted the Examination II values (most complete, matching current lithium status) for arms 1 and 2, and the single reported pre-lithium values for arm 3. Lithium salt form is never stated in this paper (only 'sustained-release' vs 'conventional lithium carbonate tablets' split 9:1, but not tied to specific arms), so lithium_salt is 'unknown' rather than assuming carbonate, per L1. Per EXTRACTION SCOPE instructions, only primary-outcome final timepoint extracted and all *_quote fields set to null; secondary renal/urine-volume/osmolality outcomes were omitted despite being the paper's actual primary focus, since weight is this review's outcome of interest.

summary: This longitudinal cohort study followed 13 previously lithium-naive psychiatric patients before and after a mean of 16.5 months (range 12-25) of twice-daily sustained-release lithium, kept within a serum range of 0.6-1.2 mmol/L, to assess renal glomerular filtration rate (GFR). Absolute GFR fell slightly (101.9 to 98.3 ml/min, not significant), but standard-GFR (corrected for body surface area) fell significantly (96.5 to 90.9 ml/min/1.73m², p<0.05), driven mainly by a significant rise in body weight from 71.7 to 74.9 kg (p<0.05). The authors concluded lithium therapy for this duration did not truly impair GFR, and that the apparent standard-GFR decline was an artifact of weight-driven surface-area changes.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: This paper's primary focus is renal function (GFR), not weight gain; weight is reported only as a secondary/mechanistic variable explaining the standard-GFR change, so the weight outcome above is not the paper's stated primary outcome (is_primary=false) but is the only outcome relevant to this review's weight-gain focus and is extracted per the weight-outcome rules. Serum lithium was kept within a target range (0.6-1.2 mmol/L) rather than reporting an achieved mean/SD, so serum_lithium_mmol_L_mean is left null per rule L5. No lithium salt form was stated anywhere in the text (only 'sustained release preparation'), so lithium_salt is 'unknown' per rule L1. Weight change (3.2 kg, p<0.05) was calculated from the two reported means in Table 1; no SD of the change or exact p-value was given, only 'P<0.05' as a threshold. duration in weeks was calculated from 16.5 months (16.5*30/7=~70.7, using 30.44-day month approx =71.7). No binary weight-gain threshold data or BMI data reported. No other outcomes (renal, etc.) extracted per scope restriction to primary/weight outcomes only — this paper has no distinct 'primary outcome' per se since it is an observational side-effect study; GFR/standard-GFR/creatinine were omitted as they are outside the weight-gain review scope.

summary: This cross-sectional study compared 31 institutionalized chronically psychotic patients receiving lithium (serum levels 0.6-1.2 mEq/L) with 42 similar patients not receiving lithium, measuring weight and urine creatinine (a polyuria marker) twice daily for three weeks. Morning and afternoon body weights did not differ significantly between lithium and non-lithium groups, and the study's main finding was that abnormal diurnal weight gain was driven by polyuria rather than lithium exposure per se. extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: This paper's primary outcome is normalized diurnal weight gain (NDWG, % change from morning to afternoon weight within the same day), not absolute weight or weight change over treatment duration — it is not a treatment-response weight-gain study in the usual sense. I extracted 7am/4pm body weight (Table 3) as the closest available continuous weight outcome since it is the only absolute-weight data reported; NDWG percentages themselves are a same-day physiological fluctuation measure, not a meta-analyzable weight-gain effect for this review, so I did not create a separate outcome for NDWG. Lithium salt form and daily dose in mg were never reported — only mean serum level range (0.6-1.2 mEq/L, treated as equivalent to mmol/L per L3). Per-arm n reflects the two main groups (31 lithium, 42 no-lithium); the additional young-admission-unit controls (n=16, 4 on lithium) and staff normals (n=29) were excluded from arms since they are supplementary comparison groups, not part of the primary lithium/no-lithium contrast of interest to this review. summary: This study followed 37 long-term lithium-treated psychiatric outpatients (mostly postmenopausal women) with serial hand radiographs 2 years apart to assess bone effects, alongside a separate controlled experiment in growing rats given lithium chloride in drinking water. extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: This paper is a bone-morphometry study, not a weight-gain trial. Table I gives baseline human weight (mean ± SD) by sex/menopausal status only — no follow-up or change-in-weight data for humans are reported anywhere in text, tables, or figures, so no weight outcome object could be constructed and reports_weight_outcome is false. Rat body weight is discussed narratively (lithium reduced growth rate/weight gain in growing rats, fig. 2) but presented ONLY as a figure with no numeric table/text values, and rats are an animal model, not the human population this review targets, so these data were not extracted as an outcome. summary: This cross-sectional/prospective study assessed glucose tolerance (oGTT) and body weight in 49 outpatients on long-term lithium maintenance therapy (mean 6.4 years) compared to large German reference populations. The lithium-treated patients showed significantly more pathological oGTT curves and significantly more overweight/obesity than expected from the general population (p<0.01 for weight distribution), though the authors attribute this mainly to weight gain and patient vulnerability rather than a direct pharmacological effect of lithium.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: This paper's primary focus is glucose tolerance, not weight; body weight/BMI data appear only as a categorical distribution (Table III) compared against an expected population distribution (n=1950 reference sample), with no per-patient mean/SD kg or BMI values given, so the weight outcome was extracted as a binary/categorical distribution (proportion overweight/obese: 33/49 = 67.3% observed vs ~32.1% expected) rather than continuous kg or BMI change — there is no baseline/pre-lithium weight measurement (this is a cross-sectional assessment during ongoing treatment, not pre-post). No numeric lithium dose (mg/day) or salt form is given anywhere in the text; only serum lithium concentrations are reported, and only for pathological (0.77 ± 0.25 mEq/1) vs normal (0.66 ± 0.15 mEq/1) oGTT subgroups (not as an overall arm value), so per the schema's arm-level serum_lithium fields these were left null rather than reported as a subgroup comparison — this subgroup contrast (Li plasma level pathological vs normal oGTT, both mEq/L numerically = mmol/L) is present in the results text but excluded here per the narrowed extraction scope (primary outcome only, no secondary oGTT/insulin outcomes). Per the extraction-scope instructions, all *_quote fields are set to null and only the primary (weight) outcome is extracted; the paper's true primary outcome (glucose tolerance/oGTT) was omitted as instructed to focus on weight-related data for this review.

It is NOT a study of lithium as a drug, supplement, or environmental exposure — 'lithium' here refers only to a laboratory reagent used to measure sodium transport kinetics in vitro, and no participant received or was exposed to lithium.
