extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: IRRELEVANT PAPER — NOT A LITHIUM WEIGHT-GAIN STUDY. This is a laboratory/epidemiological study of sodium-lithium countertransport (Na-Li CT), an in-vitro erythrocyte ion-transport assay where lithium chloride is used as a reagent in a cell-washing/incubation protocol to measure sodium efflux kinetics, correlated with body mass index, blood pressure, uric acid, glucose, alcohol intake, etc. No participant ingested or was exposed to lithium as a treatment, supplement, or environmental/drinking-water source. There is no lithium dose, serum lithium level (achieved or target), or weight-gain outcome data of the kind this review requires. The paper's own BMI data (Table 1) reflect the general population sample's baseline anthropometrics, not a lithium-exposure effect, and are not extracted as an outcome. This paper should likely be excluded from the review during screening; flagging for review rather than fabricating any lithium/weight fields.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: This paper is not a weight-gain/metabolic side-effect study — it is a physiology experiment on the effect of strenuous exercise on serum lithium and electrolyte levels in 4 healthy athletes. Per extraction scope, only the primary/final-timepoint outcome was extracted (weight change after 3-5 days of amiloride) and secondary outcomes (urine volume, creatinine clearance, serum potassium, fractional lithium excretion, renal concentrating ability) were omitted. OCR artifacts in the source text (e.g. 'amilonide' for 'amiloride', 'polyunia' for 'polyuria') were normalized only in this notes field, not in quotes (quotes are null per scope rules). extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: This paper's primary outcome is CIMT (carotid atherosclerosis), not weight — no weight, BMI-change, or weight-gain-AE outcome is reported anywhere in the text, tables, or safety data, so the 'outcomes' array is intentionally empty (W1-W7 rules do not apply; there is nothing to extract). BMI (26.47 ± 5.74 kg/m2, whole sample) appears only as a baseline/predictor variable in the CIMT regression models, not as a treatment-related outcome, so it was not extracted as a weight outcome. Lithium salt form is never stated (lithium_salt='unknown'); no serum lithium level was measured/reported. The 'Current daily dosage (mg) Lithium 460.1 (SD 461.3)' and 'Valproate 487.5 (SD 647.7)' figures in Table 1 are averaged across the WHOLE sample (N=106, including non-users presumably coded 0), not restricted to the 58 lithium-users or 43 valproate-users — flagged because the very high SD relative to the mean is consistent with zero-inflation from non-users; treat these as approximate exposure-cohort averages, not per-user dosing. extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: Single-patient case report; weight change reflects surgically-induced weight LOSS (not lithium-induced gain) — included per protocol because lithium salt/dose/serum data and quantitative weight/BMI numbers are present. Lithium dose changed substantially over the case (900 mg/day at baseline -> 600 mg/day -> 300 mg/day final maintenance as 150 mg bid); arm dose fields report the final maintenance dose (300 mg/day) with baseline (900 mg/day) as dose_salt_mg_per_day_max, since this matches the timepoint used for the primary outcome and serum level per extraction scope (final timepoint only). Elemental lithium and mmol/day were calculated from stated salt (carbonate, 18.8% elemental) and the final 300 mg/day dose. Serum lithium ranged from 0.62 to 1.63 mmol/L across the case; serum_lithium_mmol_L_mean/min/max report the reported range, with 'mean' set to the final (1-year) value. Discrepancy noted in source: text states 1-year BMI = 30.26, but the summary table lists 1-year BMI = 31.6 for the same timepoint; text value (30.26) was not used directly (weight in kg was used instead, calculated from 199 lb). Body weight kg values were calculated from pounds (269.6 lb baseline, 199 lb at 1 year; 1 lb = 0.453592 kg). Percent body weight lost (26.2%) is stated verbatim in the text. summary: This case report describes a 17-year-old girl treated with lithium, olanzapine, and benzodiazepines for presumed acute mania that was later found to be anti-NMDAR autoimmune encephalitis with an underlying ovarian teratoma; lithium was discontinued before tumor surgery. No lithium dose, salt form, or numeric serum level was reported (only 'therapeutic levels'), and the sole weight datum (100 kg to 90 kg at 7-month follow-up) was attributed by the authors to prior corticosteroid taper rather than lithium, so this paper contributes essentially no usable quantitative lithium-dose or weight-gain data.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: This is a single-patient case report, not a lithium weight-gain treatment study. No lithium dose (mg/day), salt form, or numeric serum lithium level is ever stated — only the qualitative phrase 'despite therapeutic levels'. Lithium (and olanzapine) were tapered off before ovarian tumor surgery, well before the only weight datum in the paper (a patient-reported drop from 100 kg to 90 kg at the 7-month follow-up visit), which the authors explicitly attribute to 'lingering obesity related to previous cortisone treatment' rather than to lithium. This weight change is therefore flagged as likely NOT attributable to lithium exposure; it is extracted per protocol but should probably be excluded or heavily downweighted in pooling. No between-group comparison exists (single arm, no comparator).

summary: This was an 18-month, open-label continuation study of flexible-dose lurasidone (20-80 mg/day), given as monotherapy or adjunctively with lithium or valproate, in 122 patients with bipolar I depression who had completed prior double-blind and 6-month extension trials. Weight and BMI changes from original baseline were small at both 12 months (+1.8 kg, +0.7 kg/m2) and 24 months of cumulative treatment (+0.8 kg, +0.3 kg/m2); no statistical comparison to a control group was performed since this was a single-arm study. Lithium was only a concomitant medication in a subset of patients (35/122) with no dose or serum level data reported, so this paper contributes little lithium-specific dosing information despite reporting favorable weight/metabolic outcomes overall.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: This paper's primary intervention is lurasidone (an antipsychotic), not lithium; lithium was only an adjunctive/concomitant medication in a subset of patients (35/122, 28.7%) with no lithium dose, salt form, or serum level data reported anywhere in the text, so no dedicated lithium arm could be constructed and all lithium-specific dose/serum fields are null. Per the extraction scope, only the primary continuous weight-change outcome at the final available timepoint (Month 24, observed-case, N=55) was extracted; the paper also reports a 12-month weight-change timepoint (N=118, +1.8 kg) and binary ≥7% weight gain/loss proportions (16.1% gained ≥7%, 5.9% lost ≥7% at 12 months) which were omitted per the primary-outcome-only scope restriction. BMI rose modestly from a baseline mean of 25.9 to 26.6 kg/m2 in the longest-exposure stratum (≥31 years), a small but statistically significant increase (~0.16%/year, p=0.04), though there was no unexposed comparison group to isolate the lithium-specific contribution from aging.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: Single-arm observational cohort; no non-lithium comparator, so between_group_effects is empty. Primary review outcome (BMI) extracted at baseline and at the longest-exposure stratum (≥31 years, n=201) as the closest analog to an 'end of treatment' timepoint, per the paper's own exposure-duration binning in Table 3; six intermediate exposure bins (1, 2-5, 6-10, 11-15, 16-20, 21-30 years) were skipped per extraction scope. change_mean (0.7) was calculated as final-minus-baseline BMI from two verbatim values; the accompanying p-value (0.04) is from the paper's %/year change-over-time ANOVA test for BMI, not a direct paired baseline-vs-final test. dose_elemental_mg_per_day_mean and dose_mmol_per_day_mean were calculated from the verbatim salt dose (833 mg/day lithium carbonate) using standard elemental fraction (18.8%) and atomic weight (6.94), per rule L2. extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: This is fundamentally a lurasidone (antipsychotic) long-term safety study, not a lithium trial. Lithium was a mandatory (non-depressed group) or optional (depressed group) concomitant medication for only a subset of patients (23/44 of mood-stabilizer users at baseline were on lithium, 19/44 VPA, 2/44 both); no lithium salt, dose in mg/day, or serum lithium level was ever reported, and weight/metabolic outcomes were only broken out by episode-type subgroup (depressed vs non-depressed), which mixes lithium, VPA, and no-mood-stabilizer patients together, and also mixes lurasidone dose/route history. Therefore no arm can be classified as a clean lithium exposure arm and lithium_arm_ids is empty. Body weight change (kg) at week 52 (observed case) was extracted as the primary weight outcome per this review's scope. Additional weight-related data not extracted per EXTRACTION SCOPE restriction to primary outcome only: 'weight increased' as a coded adverse event (17/199 overall, 8/117 depressed, 9/82 non-depressed — mirrored into adverse_events above), and a ≥7% weight-gain/loss threshold reported only for the full sample (17.7% gained ≥7%, n=35/199; 14.5% lost ≥7%, n=29/199), not split by subgroup. Baseline body weight/BMI were not reported anywhere in the text. Non-depressed arm weight-change mean of 1.0 kg was taken from prose text (Discussion/Results) because Table 3's cell for that value appears to have lost its numeric mean (only the SD '(5.5)' is legible), consistent with the stated 'Overall mean change in body weight to week 52 was 0 kg (-0.8 kg in the depressed group; + 1.0 kg in the non-depressed group).'

summary: This retrospective single-center cohort compared 657 bipolar-1 and 720 bipolar-2 outpatients followed an average of 18.5 years, reporting lower BMI (25.0 vs 24.3 kg/m2, p=0.04) and less obesity (21.7% vs 10.7%, p=0.007) in bipolar-2 subjects, who also received lithium less often (49.6% vs 65.0%) and at lower doses (609 vs 828 mg/day) with similar achieved serum levels (0.56 vs 0.61 mEq/L, p=0.11). Because BMI/obesity was assessed in the whole diagnostic cohort rather than only the lithium-treated subgroup, the study does not directly link individual lithium exposure to weight outcome.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: This paper is fundamentally a comparison of DSM-5 diagnostic subgroups (BD-1 vs BD-2), not a lithium-exposure-vs-comparator design. Table 4 lithium dose (mg/day) and mean serum level (mEq/L, copied unchanged to mmol/L per L3) reflect only the lithium-treated fraction of each diagnostic group (65.0% of BD-1, 49.6% of BD-2), while Table 1 BMI/obesity data reflect the ENTIRE diagnostic cohort (n=657/720), not just lithium users — these two datasets are not individually linked, so the BMI difference should not be interpreted as a lithium dose-response effect for meta-analysis; flagged as high confounding risk. Lithium salt form is never specified in the text (set to 'unknown'). Obesity event counts (143/657, 77/720) were back-calculated from the reported percentages (21.7%, 10.7%) and are approximate. Table 1 BMI CI for BD-2 has an apparent typo '[23.8–247]', interpreted as 23.8-24.7 based on context. Follow-up duration (18.5 years, range 1-46) converted to ~964 weeks. Secondary outcomes (HDRS items, morbidity, treatment-type comparisons, suicide risk, etc.) were omitted per extraction scope (primary-outcome-only). All *_quote fields set to null per extraction scope instructions.

summary: This retrospective Swedish cohort study followed 25 mother-infant dyads exposed to maternal lithium treatment during late pregnancy and breastfeeding, comparing infants with high (>=0.6 meq/l) versus low (<0.6 meq/l) serum lithium concentrations at birth. Higher intrauterine lithium exposure (driven by higher maternal lithium sulfate doses, ~274 vs 180 mg/day at delivery) was associated with a non-statistically-significant trend toward more neonatal symptoms (85.7% vs 41.2%, p=0.08) and slower infant lithium clearance, but the study reports neonatal clinical/biochemical outcomes rather than weight gain or metabolic side effects in the lithium-treated individual, so it contributes no data to this review's primary weight-gain outcome.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: This paper is a perinatal/neonatal cohort study of infants exposed to maternal lithium in utero and via breastfeeding, not a study of weight gain or metabolic side effects in the lithium-treated adult. No maternal or infant weight/BMI/metabolic outcome data are reported (only 'poor infant growth', a failure-to-thrive/growth-failure symptom used as a marker of possible neonatal lithium toxicity, which is not a weight-gain adverse effect and was not extracted as an outcome per the review's scope). 'Arms' (HEG/LEG) reflect infant serum lithium exposure strata, not randomized maternal treatment arms; maternal dose/serum values are used as the arm-level lithium exposure metric since mothers are the lithium-treated individuals. All but 4/23 mothers used lithium sulfate (Lithionit); the 4 on lithium carbonate had doses converted to lithium sulfate-equivalent mg for all reported dose figures, so dose_salt_mg_per_day values are sulfate-equivalent for the whole cohort, not pure per-salt raw doses. The paper also reports a carbonate-equivalent conversion (e.g. 1468 vs 964 mg/day 'lithium carbonate' equivalent) which was not entered into dose_elemental_mg_per_day because it is a converted salt-equivalent mass, not elemental lithium content. No between-group weight/BMI effect sizes exist to calculate. Percent female in baseline_demographics per_arm/overall was left null because the only 'female' proportions reported (Table 1) are infant sex, not maternal, and were judged not applicable to this field.

summary: This descriptive feasibility study compared pre-treatment (lithium-naive) NMR-based serum metabolomic/lipoprotein profiles in 10 individuals with bipolar disorder from the BIPLONG cohort, 5 of whom later gained ≥5 kg during lithium treatment and 5 who remained weight-stable, with weight status and lithium history ascertained retrospectively. Several lipoprotein parameters (e.g., HDL and LDL free cholesterol, total particle cholesterol, total particle number, apolipoprotein B) were significantly higher pre-treatment in the future weight-gain group on univariate testing, but the overall multivariate model was not statistically significant, and no lithium dose or serum level data were available for either group.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: This is a metabolomics feasibility study, not a treatment trial: blood samples were drawn from both groups BEFORE lithium initiation (participants were lithium-naive at sampling), and the two 'arms' were retrospectively defined purely by whether ≥5 kg weight gain later occurred during subsequent lithium treatment (a matched, outcome-based case-control design nested in the BIPLONG cohort). The paper explicitly states lithium dosage, salt form, serum levels, and exact exposure duration were 'not consistently available' for these participants, so all dose/serum fields are null/not_reported. The binary weight-gain counts (5/5 vs 0/5) are an artifact of the selection criteria, not a measured treatment effect/incidence — this should NOT be pooled as an event-rate/OR in meta-analysis; it is reported here only because the review schema requires capturing the binary weight-gain classification. Baseline weight/BMI/age differ substantially between groups (unadjusted, matched only informally on sex/age) and reflect pre-lithium characteristics, not lithium-induced change. Primary metabolomic/lipoprotein outcomes (the paper's actual focus) were omitted per this review's scope, which restricts extraction to the weight-gain outcome only.

summary: This case report describes a 26-year-old woman on 8 years of lithium carbonate (900 mg/day) plus quetiapine and aripiprazole for bipolar affective disorder who developed weight gain (65 to 70 kg, BMI 30.9 to 33.25 kg/m2 over one year), amenorrhea, and unusually large bilateral multiloculated polycystic ovaries mimicking an ovarian tumor. summary: This is a two-patient case report (not a controlled study) of individuals with manic-depressive psychosis maintained on lithium carbonate who developed thyrotoxicosis; one patient had an episode of apparent weight gain attributed to fluid retention (which masked underlying thyrotoxic weight loss), and the other gained roughly 2 stones over 3 months after starting carbimazole plus lithium for thyrotoxicosis. extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: Two-case anecdotal case report from 1975, focused on lithium-thyrotoxicosis interaction, not a lithium weight-gain trial. Weight changes are narrative only (14 lb gain in case 1 attributed to fluid retention/cardiac failure, not true weight gain; 2 stone gain in case 2 over 3 months coincident with starting carbimazole 15mg qid + lithium 500mg tid for thyrotoxicosis) — no baseline weights, no SDs, no systematic measurement protocol, so no usable continuous or binary numeric outcome could be extracted into arm_results. Serum lithium values mentioned in text (e.g. 0.6-1.5 mmol/L therapeutic range, 2.4 mmol/L toxic level, 0.8 mmol/L) are anecdotal single readings tied to clinical crises, not a defined dosing exposure metric for an arm, so left null per instructions rather than fabricating an arm-level mean. Lithium salt inferred as carbonate from brand name Priadel per L1 rule. OCR/text quality is poor (garbled diacritics, broken table, misrecognized characters throughout) — table I is a corrupted timeline table not usable for structured extraction. No between-group or within-group quantitative effect sizes are calculable from this paper.

summary: This cross-sectional study measured plasma folate in 107 outpatients on long-term lithium carbonate (titrated to plasma levels of 0.8-1.2 mmol/L) and found that patients with the lowest folate had significantly higher affective morbidity than those with higher folate; a secondary comparison of weight change between low- and high-folate subgroups showed a non-significant difference (low-folate group gained 0.4±0.3 kg vs high-folate group 0.68±0.5 kg). The study was not designed to assess lithium-induced weight gain and provides only indirect, underpowered weight data.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: This paper's primary focus is plasma folate and affective morbidity in lithium patients, not lithium weight gain. Weight data is limited to a single sentence comparing mean weight change (kg) between low-folate and high-folate subgroups of the same lithium cohort (not a dose-response or exposure contrast); no SDs, no n per subgroup, and the paper states only that the difference 'was not significant' with no exact p-value or CI. The between-group effect_value (-0.28 kg) was calculated as the difference of the two reported group means (0.4 - 0.68); no SE could be computed since neither group's n nor a usable SD was given, so per instructions in rule 4 a mean_difference without se/CI would normally be discarded — it is reported here for completeness but downstream pooling should treat it as unusable. OCR artifacts throughout (e.g. 'Â±' for ±, garbled table cells) made some numeric table content (Table I stats, Table II group stats) unreliable to parse with confidence, so only the clearly legible weight-change sentence was extracted. Lithium dose in mg/day was never stated; only the target serum range (0.8-1.2 mmol/L) was given, and achieved serum levels for this weight comparison were not reported. Percent female was calculated as 71/107 = 66.4%.

summary: This cross-sectional study assessed subjective side-effects, including self-reported weight gain, in 94 outpatients on long-term lithium carbonate maintenance therapy (mean 5.9 years, target plasma levels 0.8-1.2 mmol/l), compared with 258 healthy controls and 65 drug-free depressed in-patients. extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: Text is OCR-garbled (Table I-VII cell values fragmented/misaligned due to column merging). Table IV gives 'Weight gain 26' for male lithium-treated patients and 'Weight gain 34' for female lithium-treated patients (percentages, denominators 30 males and 64 females respectively); combined estimate ~34% used as the pooled endpoint quote is unreliable due to OCR corruption so events/n per sex were not separately extracted with confidence — only the overall study n=94 and an approximate combined percent are reported. No dose in mg/day, no elemental lithium content, and no achieved serum lithium level (only the target range 0.8-1.2 mmol/l) were reported. This is not a treatment-outcome trial but a cross-sectional side-effects survey; no between-group effect size for weight gain (e.g., OR) was computable because raw event counts by group were not cleanly recoverable from the garbled table text. summary: This was a cross-sectional point-prevalence survey of 99 psychiatric patients receiving maintenance lithium carbonate (mostly slow-release 'Priadel', doses ranging 200-1500+ mg/day) in routine community care in South-west Scotland. extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: Cross-sectional prevalence survey, not a treatment trial with pre/post weight measures — no baseline or follow-up weight data exist to extract. The 43% weight-gain figure (Table III, 'Weight gain 43') is from the subgroup of n=40 patients receiving lithium ONLY (no antidepressants/major tranquillisers), used here to avoid confounding by other psychotropics; n=17 events back-calculated as round(0.43*40)=17. Serum lithium levels are reported only as banded percentages (e.g. '60% 0.4-0.8 mmol/l') for the whole sample, not as a mean/SD, so serum fields are left null per rule L5 (no imputation from bins). Dose is reported as percentage-of-sample bins by mg/day range for the whole sample (not per-arm mean), so only min/max of the reported range bins are given; no mean/SD dose is calculable. Lithium salt inferred as carbonate from brand name 'Priadel' per L1 brand-mapping table (73% of patients on slow-release Priadel; remainder unspecified formulation). This is Part I of a linked two-part paper (Part II is a longitudinal study of the same cohort, appended but truncated in the provided text with no additional weight data).

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: Single-arm retrospective long-term follow-up with no comparator; weight gain reported only as a count of patients (21/59) among a list of side-effects, with no threshold specified, no timepoint precision, and no measured vs self-reported distinction — treated as a binary AE-table outcome per W3. Lithium salt form stated verbatim as 'lithium carbonate' in the title/text. Serum level range/mean given but no SD. Duration on lithium given as total patient-years (957) and 'most had taken it for more than 13 years' rather than a per-patient mean; total_duration_weeks calculated loosely from the ~17-year study span (1966-1983), not a precise per-patient treatment duration. summary: This cross-sectional study of 121 adults with bipolar disorder examined whether laboratory-confirmed insulin resistance or type 2 diabetes was associated with clinical course and response to prophylactic lithium treatment, but it did not measure or report weight, BMI change, or any weight-gain outcome as a result of lithium treatment. Patients with insulin resistance or type 2 diabetes had significantly higher odds of a chronic course, rapid cycling, and non-response to lithium than euglycaemic patients (all p<0.05), independent of BMI and antipsychotic use. extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: This paper's focus is insulin resistance/type 2 diabetes as predictors of bipolar illness course and lithium treatment response — it reports NO weight, BMI-change, or weight-gain-adverse-event outcome as a consequence of lithium treatment, so the outcomes array is empty per extraction scope (primary outcomes only, and none are weight-related). Baseline BMI (Table 1) is reported only as a cross-sectional characteristic stratified by glucose-metabolism status (euglycaemic/insulin resistant/type 2 diabetic), not as a treatment outcome, so it was not extracted into baseline_demographics.per_arm (which would need to align to the lithium arm). Lithium dose, salt form, and achieved serum level are not reported anywhere in the text beyond the qualitative phrase 'adequate trial of lithium (at least 6 months' duration at therapeutic blood levels)' — all corresponding dose/serum fields are null with source 'not_reported'. Only 80 of 121 patients had an adequate lithium trial and were used in the lithium-response analysis; the remaining analyses (chronic course, rapid cycling) used the full n=121 sample or subsets with available data ('Not all data available for all patients' per Table 1 footnote).

summary: This open-label, historically-controlled phase II trial tested lithium carbonate (titrated to serum levels 0.3-0.8 mEq/L, mean dose 375 mg/day) in 107 patients with ALS, compared with 249 historical placebo controls from the MINO trial. Contrary to the hypothesis that lithium would slow disease progression, patients on lithium declined significantly faster on the ALSFRS-R (slope -1.20/month vs -1.01/month, difference 0.19/month, p=0.04); secondary outcomes (FVC decline, weight loss, QOL, survival) did not differ significantly between groups, and lithium was associated with more serious adverse events and falls than expected.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: This is an ALS trial, not a psychiatric/bipolar population; lithium was used experimentally as a neuroprotective agent, not for mood disorder. summary: This cross-sectional biomonitoring study measured urinary lithium as a biomarker of chronic environmental drinking-water lithium exposure (water concentrations 8–1,005 μg/L) in 202 women from four Andean Puna villages in Argentina, and examined its association with thyroid markers and BMI. Urinary lithium was inversely associated with free T4 and positively associated with TSH (both statistically significant, p=0.032 and p=0.007 adjusted), consistent with lithium-induced hypothyroidism, but the association between urinary lithium and BMI was small and not statistically significant (adjusted β=0.14 per 1,000 μg/L increase; 95% CI −0.059 to 0.35; p=0.16).

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: This is an ecological/environmental biomonitoring cross-sectional study, NOT a lithium treatment trial — there are no discrete treatment arms; urinary lithium concentration was used as a continuous exposure biomarker in linear regression against BMI, T4, and TSH, so the 'between_group_effects' entries represent per-1,000-μg/L regression slope coefficients (β) rather than discrete-group mean differences (mapped to mean_difference/adjusted_mean_difference as the closest schema fit). No serum lithium was measured (only urinary); urinary lithium concentration itself (mean 4,404 μg/L, median 3,914 μg/L, range 117–14,343 μg/L, n=202, Table 1) has no dedicated schema field and is recorded here rather than lost. Drinking water lithium concentration (verbatim range 8–1,005 μg/L) was placed in the arm 'dose' field per the ecological-study extraction rule. No absolute body weight (kg) was reported, only BMI; no binary weight-gain threshold outcome was used. Only the BMI outcome was extracted per the review's primary-outcome-only scope; thyroid (T4/TSH) associations, though reported with full quantitative detail in the paper, were omitted as secondary per instructions. duration_value/duration_unit (25 years) represents the median years participants had lived in the exposure area (a proxy for chronic exposure duration), not a treatment protocol duration.

summary: This UK primary-care electronic health record cohort study compared rates of weight gain (>7% and >15% of baseline weight) among 6,671 bipolar disorder patients newly started on lithium, valproate, olanzapine, or quetiapine as maintenance mood stabilizers. After propensity-score adjustment, patients on valproate, olanzapine, and quetiapine all had significantly higher hazards of both >7% and >15% weight gain compared to lithium (all adjusted HRs 1.37-1.84, p<0.001), indicating lithium was associated with the lowest risk of clinically significant weight gain among the four drugs studied.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: This is a 4-arm active-comparator retrospective THIN EHR cohort (lithium vs valproate vs olanzapine vs quetiapine) reporting weight gain as two binary/time-to-event thresholds (>7% and >15% of baseline weight) analyzed by Cox regression with propensity-score adjustment; no continuous kg/BMI change data were reported. Per-arm denominators (total) for the weight-gain outcome subset (overall n=4,458) were not broken out by arm in the text/tables (only events and PYAR in 100s were given), so 'total' is left null in arm_results; PS-adjusted HRs with p-values are extracted per the reporting-scope rule allowing omission of full arm_results. Lithium salt form, dose, and serum levels were explicitly NOT captured by this study ('we were unable to consider dosage differences across the different treatment groups'), so all lithium dose/serum fields are null/unknown. Per extraction-scope instructions, only the weight-gain outcomes were extracted (other reported outcomes — CKD stage 3/4, hypo/hyperthyroidism, hypercalcemia, T2DM, CVD, hypertension, hepatotoxicity — were omitted), intermediate timepoints were skipped, sample_sizes.per_arm was limited to n_enrolled only, subgroup_analyses left empty, and all *_quote fields were set to null as instructed.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: This paper is a case report about an adverse skin reaction (rash) attributed primarily to olanzapine, potentiated by pravastatin and lithium — it is NOT a study of lithium-induced weight gain or metabolic outcomes. No weight, BMI, or serum lithium level data are reported anywhere in the text; the outcomes array is empty because no primary weight/metabolic outcome exists in this paper. Lithium dose (625→900 mg/day carbonate, salt form stated verbatim as 'lithium carbonate') was extracted for completeness since dose/salt data are always high priority, but this paper likely does not belong in a weight-gain meta-analysis pool. risk_of_bias.key_concern: This is not a lithium weight-gain study at all — it is an HIV drug trial of an iodine-lithium-dextrin antimicrobial complex with a trivial, non-therapeutic lithium chloride content (0.004 g per 20 mL), no comparator arm, no dose or serum lithium data, and body weight reported only incidentally as a pooled overall figure with no per-arm breakdown or denominator.

summary: This was a double-blind, uncontrolled, dose-ranging trial of intravenous Iodine-Lithium-alpha-Dextrin (Armenicum), an experimental antimicrobial/immunomodulatory infusion containing a trace amount of lithium chloride (0.004 g per 20 mL dose), given to 56 antiretroviral-naive HIV-infected patients across three dose groups (0.1, 0.2, 0.3 ml/kg) over 48 weeks. The drug reduced viral load and immune activation markers in symptomatic/AIDS patients and improved quality of life, with body weight (reported only as a pooled overall mean, not per-arm) rising from a baseline of ~65-73 kg to 69.5 ± 4.4 kg at week 48 with no statistical test reported. This paper is not informative for lithium-induced weight gain given the negligible lithium content and near-total absence of lithium dose/serum data.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: This paper is almost certainly a false-positive hit for the lithium weight-gain review. IL-alpha-D (Armenicum) is a multi-component iodine/polyvinyl-alcohol/dextrin antimicrobial infusion whose lithium chloride content is trivial (0.004 g = 4 mg lithium chloride per 20 mL dose, i.e. ~0.66 mg elemental lithium at 0.1-0.3 ml/kg, roughly 3-10 mg total per infusion) — far below any pharmacologic/psychiatric lithium exposure, and lithium is not the intended active agent (iodine is). No lithium dose-per-day, serum lithium, or dose-response-by-lithium data are reported; the 3 'dose' arms refer to the whole IL-alpha-D formulation volume, not lithium dose per se, so dose_contrast_within_trial is set to false despite 3 nominal arms. Body weight is reported only as a single pooled value across all 56 patients/doses (not broken out per arm), given as 68.2±2.8 kg (wk12), 70.3±3.2 kg (wk24), 72.4±3.7 kg (wk36), 69.5±4.4 kg (wk48); only the final timepoint was extracted per protocol and could not be assigned to a specific dose arm, so it is reported as a single arm_results entry without an arm_id link to a specific dose group (approximated as arm_id 1, but this is a pooled figure, not arm-1-specific — flagging for reviewer). No baseline (week 0) weight was given for the pooled group (only per-arm baseline weights in Table 1). No between-group statistical comparison of weight was reported. lithium_salt set to 'chloride' per the verbatim formulation ('lithium chloride - 0.004 g') though this is not an oral lithium salt for psychiatric use. Given the exposure stratum, this maps most closely to 'drinking_water' (trace/incidental environmental-level lithium exposure) rather than any clinical dosing stratum, though the O1 ecological-water framework does not perfectly fit an IV infusion context either. Recommend excluding this paper from the lithium weight-gain meta-analysis given lack of relevance to therapeutic lithium exposure.

summary: This case report describes a 47-year-old man with schizoaffective disorder on lithium carbonate (also taking paliperidone) who gained about 40 lbs (~18 kg) over 8 months from compulsive overeating; topiramate was then added for weight management and appetite control. Within 4 days, the patient developed lithium toxicity (serum lithium rising from 0.47 to 1.46 mEq/L) with acute renal insufficiency, attributed to a pharmacokinetic interaction reducing lithium renal clearance, and lost about 6 lbs before topiramate was stopped. No formal statistical testing of weight change was performed; findings are anecdotal from a single patient.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: Single-patient case report; no numeric lithium dose (mg/day) ever stated, only serum levels from three lab tables. Weight is reported only as narrative pound deltas (40 lb gain over 8 months pre-topiramate; 6 lb loss during the 4-day topiramate trial) — converted to kg (source='calculated'); no absolute weight, BMI, or waist circumference given. Table 1's own 'Weight no increase' label appears to describe short-term stability at the point topiramate was started, distinct from the preceding 8-month 40-lb gain narrated in the text and abstract; the 8-month gain was used as arm 1's within-group change since it is the only quantifiable pre-topiramate weight figure. Table 3 (lithium reintroduced after topiramate stopped) reports no weight value, so no third arm was created. Per extraction scope, only the primary weight outcome was extracted at its endpoint timepoint; secondary outcomes (renal function, electrolytes, thyroid, polydipsia detail) and all verbatim quotes were omitted as instructed. This paper's primary focus is a topiramate-lithium pharmacokinetic interaction/toxicity case, not a lithium weight-gain study per se, so all extracted weight data are incidental and heavily confounded (concomitant antipsychotic, comorbid binge-eating behavior, very short exposure window for arm 2).

summary: This retrospective nested case-control study used a multistate Medicaid managed care claims database (1998-2002) to examine diabetes risk among 283 bipolar disorder patients who developed diabetes versus 1134 matched controls. This is not a lithium weight-gain treatment study — lithium appears only as a covariate, and no lithium dose, serum level, or weight outcome data are reported; after adjustment, lithium use itself was not significantly associated with diabetes risk (HR 1.02, 95% CI 0.73-1.42), while atypical antipsychotics (risperidone, olanzapine, quetiapine), weight gain, and hypertension were significant risk factors for diabetes.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: This paper is not a lithium weight-gain treatment study — it is a diabetes-risk case-control study in which lithium use is merely one of several covariates in a Cox regression, with no lithium dose, salt, serum level, or arm-level weight data reported. 'Weight gain' appears only as an ICD-9-coded comorbidity/covariate (a binary yes/no medical comorbidity used as a risk factor for diabetes: HR 2.516, 95% CI 1.876-3.375), not as a measured outcome of lithium exposure, so no outcome object was created per the weight-outcome rules (no arm-level weight measurements, thresholds, or lithium-specific comparison exist). No lithium arms could be constructed since dose/salt/serum data for lithium users are entirely absent from the text; lithium_arm_ids is left empty and arms is empty rather than fabricating an arm with no dose information. Sample size arms are the overall case (n=283) and control (n=1134) groups, not lithium-specific arms, since the paper does not stratify baseline demographics or weight by lithium exposure.

summary: This naturalistic retrospective cohort study compared 25 elderly patients (≥75 years) treated with lithium for mood disorders (mean dose 390 ± 178.5 mg/day, mean minimal plasma level 0.32 ± 0.14 mEq/L) to 138 age- and sex-similar patients treated with other psychotropic medications, over a mean lithium treatment duration of 31.3 months. Lithium-treated patients showed greater clinical improvement (higher CGI-I scores) than every other drug class despite more severe baseline illness; five of 25 (20%) lithium-treated patients had a >7% increase in body weight from baseline, but there was no non-lithium comparator data or statistical test reported for this weight-gain outcome. Hypothyroidism and renal failure were not significant problems in this cohort, though 6 patients (24%) experienced acute lithium intoxication and 6 (24%) discontinued lithium for various reasons.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: Lithium salt form is never stated in the paper (Italian naturalistic study); left as 'unknown' per L1 rather than assuming carbonate. No baseline weight, BMI, or continuous weight change values are reported — only the single binary count of patients with >7% weight increase from baseline in the lithium group (n=5/25), with no comparable figure given for the no-Li group, so no between-group effect could be extracted or calculated. Percent female per arm was calculated from raw counts (Li: 17/25 women = 68%; no-Li: 98/138 women = 71%). Treatment duration in weeks was calculated from the stated 31.3 months (31.3 × 4.345 ≈ 135.9 weeks). Excluded secondary outcomes per extraction scope: CGI-I comparison table (Table 1), GAF score, CGI score, suicidality/suicide attempt data, drop-out rates, thyroxine prescription rate, renal function, and the six individual case narratives — all are non-primary/narrative or lack a comparator arm for the weight outcome specifically.

summary: This retrospective single-center study developed and internally validated a machine-learning (XGBoost) model to predict whether adolescent inpatients on lithium carbonate reach the minimum therapeutic serum concentration (≥0.5 mmol/L), using 406 observations from 279 patients. Daily dose and body weight were the two dominant predictors (weight negatively associated with target attainment), with the final model achieving AUC 0.846 in the held-out test set. The study reports no weight-gain, BMI, or metabolic outcome data — weight is used only as a baseline predictor variable, not as a treatment outcome, so it does not contribute quantitative data to a lithium weight-gain meta-analysis.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: This paper is a PK/machine-learning modeling study of lithium serum-level therapeutic target attainment in adolescents, not a weight-gain trial. Body weight (and height, daily dose, ALB, ALP) are used only as baseline predictor variables in the ML model (reported as median [IQR], not mean/SD, so they could not be populated into the mean/SD baseline_demographics or dose fields per the schema's numeric-format requirements). No weight, BMI, or metabolic outcome data (continuous or binary) are reported anywhere in the paper — weight appears only in SHAP dependence/force plots as a model input, with example patient-level values (e.g. weight 79.0 kg, 53.0 kg) embedded in Figure 5's alt-text, not as a study outcome. Achieved serum lithium concentration is reported only as a binary attainment rate (79.8% ≥0.5 mmol/L overall; 19.2% >0.8 mmol/L; 1.48% >1.2 mmol/L), not as a continuous mean/SD, so serum_lithium_mmol_L_mean was left null per the achieved-vs-target distinction rule. Consequently no quantitative data from this paper feeds the lithium weight-gain meta-analysis; outcomes array is intentionally empty.

summary: This naturalistic, uncontrolled prospective study followed 30 adolescents (mean age 14.2 years) with bipolar disorder treated with lithium carbonate (mean dose ~843–858 mg/day, serum level ~0.69–0.70 mEq/L) for 8 months. CGI-S and C-GAS scores improved significantly and treatment was generally well tolerated (mild GI symptoms, tremor, sedation, modest TSH/calcium/WBC increases); in a subset with BMI data, mean BMI rose slightly from 18.7 to 19.7 kg/m² over 8 months, a change reported as not statistically significant, and no patient discontinued lithium for excessive weight gain.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: Single-arm naturalistic follow-up, no comparator; used the 8-month (T2, endpoint) dose and serum level for arm-level dose fields (4-month/T1 values: 843±176.6 mg/day, serum 0.69±0.20 mEq/L, also reported in text but treated as an intermediate timepoint per extraction scope). Elemental lithium (mg) and mmol/day were calculated from the stated carbonate salt dose using the standard 18.8% elemental fraction and 6.94 g/mol molar mass, since salt form (carbonate) was explicitly verbatim. The 0.4–0.8 mEq/L range in the Discussion ('effective lithium blood levels were relatively low, ranging from 0.4 mEq/L to 0.8 mEq/L') was treated as a stated therapeutic/target range rather than an achieved value, per extraction rules. BMI data were collected only 'in a subset of patients' whose size is not reported, so n_analyzed is null for the BMI outcome. Only the primary weight-relevant outcome (BMI) was extracted per review scope; the study's own stated primary outcome (CGI-S) and secondary outcomes (C-GAS, thyroid function, renal function, QTc, WBC, calcium) were omitted per extraction scope. All *_quote fields set to null per instructions.

summary: This retrospective, single-center study measured steady-state serum lithium concentrations in 186 Chinese Han patients with bipolar disorder after one week of oral lithium carbonate 1.0 g/day, then correlated the level with routine biochemical and hematologic parameters. Serum lithium was positively correlated with creatinine, magnesium, and neutrophil percentage, and negatively correlated with HDL, apolipoprotein A1, and sodium; only sodium and neutrophil percentage remained significant predictors in multivariable regression. No weight, BMI, or other body-composition/metabolic outcomes were reported.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: This paper reports NO weight, BMI, waist circumference, or other metabolic/body-composition outcomes; it is a correlational analysis of serum lithium concentration vs biochemical/hematologic markers only, so the outcomes array is empty. All 186 patients received a single standardized dose (lithium carbonate 1.0 g/d for 1 week) purely to standardize steady-state serum sampling; this may not reflect their usual long-term maintenance dose, and dose_strategy was coded fixed_dose on that basis. dose_elemental_mg_per_day (188 mg) and dose_mmol_per_day (27.1 mmol) were calculated from the stated salt (carbonate, 18.8% elemental fraction) and stated salt dose (1000 mg/day), per rule L2. Weight_kg was not reported individually, only BMI (mean 24.21, SD 4.41 kg/m2, range 19.14-37.87). percent_female and percent_on_antipsychotics were not numerically reported despite antipsychotic use being an exclusion criterion at baseline.

All secondary outcomes (HAM-D-17 depression response, YMRS, PSQI sleep quality, CGI-BP) were omitted per the review's extraction scope. summary: This 12-week, open-label, single-arm trial let 30 poorly adherent bipolar disorder patients self-select which of their maintenance medications they believed caused weight gain, discontinue it, and switch to ziprasidone; lithium was the self-identified offending agent in only 3/30 (10%) participants, with 2/30 (7%) continuing lithium concomitantly (no dose or serum level reported). extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: This paper is NOT a lithium dosing/treatment study: it is a single-arm, open-label trial of patient-driven switching from a self-identified weight-causing BD medication to ziprasidone. Lithium was the 'offending' agent for only 3/30 (10%) participants (who then discontinued it) and remained a stable concomitant medication for 2/30 (7%) throughout the trial; no lithium salt form, dose, or serum level is reported anywhere in the text, so all lithium dose/serum fields are null/not_applicable and derived.lithium_arm_ids is empty. The extracted BMI outcome (Table 2, 'Physical parameters') reflects the whole mixed-medication cohort (mostly patients who had identified antipsychotics as the offending agent, 18/30), not a lithium-attributable effect, and cannot be used as a lithium-exposure comparison. Per the extraction scope instructions, only the weight-relevant outcome (BMI) was extracted rather than the trial's own designated primary endpoint (TRQ adherence), which is not a weight measure and was therefore omitted. Diagnostic criteria were based on the MINI structured interview; no explicit DSM edition was stated. All *_quote fields were set to null per instructions.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: This is an n-of-1 case report, not a controlled treatment/weight-gain trial: it uses daily weight gain solely as a proxy for water intake/polydipsia, not as a body-weight-change outcome. Numeric weight-difference data exist only in Fig. 1 (a bar/line chart), with no table or in-text per-protocol means/SDs — result_source set to not_reported per rule 10. summary: This prospective observational cohort compared body composition changes in 28 adults with bipolar I disorder newly started on lithium (n=14) versus sodium valproate (n=14) monotherapy over six months. Lithium was associated with minimal weight gain at 6 months (mean change +0.6 kg) compared to a much larger gain with valproate (+4.3 kg), a statistically significant between-group difference (p<0.001), with lithium showing an initial rise in the first month that then plateaued.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: Lithium salt form was never specified in the text (only 'lithium', dosage range 600-1200 mg/day) — set to unknown per protocol rather than assuming carbonate. No serum lithium levels were reported anywhere in the paper. Per extraction scope, only the primary weight outcome (body weight, kg) was extracted at the final (6-month) timepoint; BMI, PBF, SLM, and TBW outcomes and the 1-month intermediate timepoint were omitted along with all *_quote fields, per the narrowed extraction scope for this review. Between-group mean difference at 6 months was calculated from the per-arm change means/SDs in Table 3 (0.6±1.6 kg lithium vs 4.3±2.6 kg valproate, n=14 each); the paper itself only reports p<0.001 for this comparison, not a numeric mean difference or CI.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: Single-patient case report about scurvy (vitamin C deficiency) altering lithium pharmacokinetics in an ASD/intellectual disability patient — not a weight-gain study; no weight-change or BMI-change data are reported over the treatment course (weight 69.2 kg / BMI 27.03 kg/m2 was recorded only once, at the baseline admission physical exam, before/independent of the lithium titration, so no outcome object was created and reports_weight_outcome=false). Lithium salt form is never specified anywhere in the text (dose is given only in mmol/day of lithium), so lithium_salt='unknown' throughout and no salt-mg or elemental-mg conversion was attempted (per L1/L2). The three 'arms' are not parallel groups but sequential temporal phases in the same single patient: (1) pre-vitamin-C dosing up to 38 mmol/day with subtherapeutic levels, (2) a transient serum surge (0.8-1.1 mmol/L, isolated peak 1.4 mmol/L) shortly after vitamin C 1 g/day was started, and (3) the post-dose-halving stabilized maintenance phase (25 mmol/day, ~0.6 mmol/L), reported per L6 as a within-patient dose/level contrast. The paper also reports a 'mean serum lithium-to-oral dose ratio' increasing from 0.0165 to 0.0264 after vitamin C, but this composite ratio (not a raw serum level or dose) was not mapped into any single schema field. Figures 1 and 2 contain additional longitudinal ABC-score and lithium-level/dose data only in graphical form with no accompanying numeric table, so those trends were not extracted (data only in figures).

summary: In a naturalistic, real-world cohort of 127 mostly anorexia nervosa inpatients undergoing a structured 10-week nutritional/psychotherapeutic program, lithium (carbonate in 6 patients, sulfate in 5 patients) was one of several mood stabilizers examined for association with BMI change (ΔBMI). Unadjusted mean ΔBMI was +3.47 for lithium carbonate and +2.10 for lithium sulfate; in an adjusted GLM, lithium sulfate exposure was significantly associated with a SMALLER BMI increase relative to the model reference (coefficient -1.70, 95% CI -3.17 to -0.23, p=0.023), while lithium carbonate showed no significant coefficient reported. Because this is an underweight AN population in which BMI gain is the desired therapeutic goal (not an adverse weight-gain outcome), and dosing/serum lithium levels were not reported, direct comparability to lithium weight-gain literature in mood-disorder populations is limited.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: This is NOT a lithium-focused trial: it is a naturalistic ED-inpatient (predominantly anorexia nervosa) cohort study examining associations between many psychotropic classes/compounds and BMI change, with lithium carbonate and lithium sulfate as two of many exposure groups. Patients are underweight (baseline BMI 16.3) and BMI GAIN is the intended therapeutic outcome here, not an adverse effect, so this population/context differs substantially from typical lithium-weight-gain literature; no dose (mg/day) or serum lithium levels were reported for either lithium group. Table 1 (Section B) and Table 2 report conflicting N's for the same compounds (e.g., Lithium Carbonate N=6 in Table 1 vs N=2 in Table 2; Lithium Sulfate N=5 vs N=6); Table 2 appears internally corrupted/misaligned (e.g., Quetiapine listed as 91/71.7% despite total antipsychotic class N=95/74.8%, and benzodiazepine compound N's are inconsistent with Table 1). Table 1 was used as authoritative because its individual compound N's for mood stabilizers sum exactly to the Section A mood-stabilizer class total (28+2+6+5+1+2+1=45). No dose_strategy, route, or duration details for lithium specifically were stated in text (route inferred as oral; duration left null because exposure windows for individual compounds could be shorter than the full 10-week program). AMI (a psychopathology outcome) was excluded per this review's scope, which restricts extraction to the primary weight/BMI outcome. No between-group GLM coefficient for Lithium Carbonate on ΔBMI was reported in Table 3 (likely because it was not significant/not selected for the displayed model output), so between_group_effects for arm 1 was left empty rather than inferred. Concomitant antipsychotic/valproate/antidepressant use was not reported specifically for the lithium subgroups (only class-level percentages for the whole sample), so these fields were left null rather than assumed.

summary: This is a single-patient case report of a 25-year-old woman with bipolar I disorder on stable long-term lithium carbonate (1,200 mg/day, sustained-release) who developed severe lithium intoxication (serum level 4.16 mmol/L) with profound sinus bradycardia (27 bpm) and acute kidney injury about 7 weeks after sleeve gastrectomy, precipitated by rapid post-surgical weight loss, vomiting, and reduced fluid intake. She fully recovered after lithium withdrawal, supportive care, and three CRRT sessions, and continued to lose weight (to 62 kg, -21.2 kg from baseline) over 4 months of follow-up while switched to lamotrigine; there is no comparison group and no statistical testing, so no formal significance can be attributed to any weight change.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: This is a case report of lithium TOXICITY after bariatric surgery, not a weight-gain treatment study; the weight changes reported (83.2 kg -> 62 kg) are progressive WEIGHT LOSS driven by sleeve gastrectomy and post-op vomiting/poor intake, confounded with (and a precipitant of) the lithium intoxication itself, not a measure of lithium-induced weight gain. dose_elemental_mg_per_day and dose_mmol_per_day were calculated from the verbatim stated salt (carbonate) and salt dose (1,200 mg/day sustained-release) using elemental fraction 18.8%; not stated directly in the paper. The 4.16 mmol/L value is the toxic/intoxication level, not an achieved therapeutic level, so it was NOT used for serum_lithium_mmol_L_mean; the last stable preoperative level (0.65 mmol/L) was used instead as the achieved maintenance-therapy exposure. Table 2 (literature review of 9 other published cases) was not extracted as separate arms/outcomes because those are secondary-source summaries from other papers, not this study's own measured data, and the extraction scope excludes secondary outcomes/data. No control/comparator arm exists in this single-patient report.

summary: This retrospective study used a large Taiwanese EMR/claims database (Chang Gung Research Database, N=1709 inpatients on lithium) to build machine-learning models (logistic/linear regression, SVM, random forest, XGBoost) predicting serum lithium concentrations from clinical features including daily dose, age, weight, and concomitant medications. The study reports no weight-gain treatment outcome — baseline weight was used only as a static predictor feature, not as a pre/post or between-group outcome, so it is not usable for this meta-analysis's weight-gain endpoints, though its dose/serum-level data are relevant background.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: This paper is a machine-learning prediction-model study (predicting serum lithium levels from EMR data), not a weight-gain treatment/outcome study. Weight (69.64±14.73 kg development; 70.35±14.54 kg test) appears only as a baseline predictor feature in Table 1, never as a pre/post or between-group outcome, so 'outcomes' was left empty per review scope (primary outcomes only) and there is no weight-gain endpoint to extract. Lithium salt form is never specified anywhere in the text, so lithium_salt is 'unknown' per rule L1 rather than assumed carbonate. Dose and serum-level values are reported separately for the 'development' (n=1505) and 'inpatient test' (n=204) subsets (a train/test split for model validation, not distinct clinical exposure arms); development-set values were used as representative for the single lithium arm since no combined/pooled summary across both subsets was given in the text. A third 'outpatient test' set (n=7) exists but its demographic/dose values are only in Supplementary Table S3, not in the main text provided. No adverse events, weight-change, or follow-up outcome data are reported anywhere in this paper.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: This paper is fundamentally about pulse methylprednisolone for amiodarone-induced thyrotoxicosis (AIT), not about lithium or weight gain. Lithium carbonate appears only as a brief adjunct drug in 2 of 5 cases (Case I: 250 mg tds; Case V: 250 mg bd), given for at most a few weeks alongside thionamides and glucocorticoids, with no serum lithium level ever reported and no weight, BMI, or metabolic outcome tied to lithium exposure anywhere in the text. Elemental lithium (mg) and mmol/day were CALCULATED from the stated carbonate salt dose using the standard 18.8% elemental fraction and molar mass 6.94 g/mol, since the paper itself gives only the salt dose. The weight loss discussed in the paper (e.g. Case II lost ~25 kg, Case V lost ~20 kg) is a pre-treatment symptom of thyrotoxicosis, not a lithium-attributable weight change, and was therefore NOT extracted as an outcome. extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: This study's own primary outcome was YBOCS (OCD symptom) change, not weight; per this review's scope, the weight (kg) and BMI outcomes were extracted instead as the primary outcomes of interest. Critically, the two study arms are defined by ANTIPSYCHOTIC type (paliperidone LAI vs. aripiprazole LAI), NOT by lithium exposure: within each arm, patients received either lithium (62.5% of PP-LAI arm, 72.7% of ARI-LAI arm) or sodium valproate as background mood stabilizer, and weight/BMI results are not stratified by which mood stabilizer was used. Lithium salt form, mg/day dose, and achieved serum level are never reported; only a monitored THERAPEUTIC TARGET range (0.5-0.8 mmol/L) is given, which per protocol must not be imputed as an achieved level. Because lithium exposure is a mixed background covariate rather than the arm-defining exposure, this paper cannot cleanly isolate lithium's contribution to the observed weight/BMI differences and should be treated with caution in the lithium-weight-gain pooled analysis (confounded by mood-stabilizer type and antipsychotic type together). Percent-change weight (5.6±2.7% PP-LAI vs. 1.6±6.2% ARI-LAI, p=0.029) and percent-change BMI (5.5±2.8% vs. 1.7±6.1%, p=0.036) are also reported in Table 3 but were not extracted as separate outcome objects given the scope restriction to primary outcomes only. The safety-tolerability side-effect percentages reported in the Discussion (9.1% PP-LAI vs. 31.2% ARI-LAI with 'no side effects') appear internally inconsistent with the group sizes (9.1%≈1/11 matches the ARI-LAI n=11 group and 31.2%≈5/16 matches the PP-LAI n=16 group), suggesting a possible group-label swap in the source text; counts were not force-fit into adverse_events for this reason.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: This is not a lithium treatment trial but a cross-sectional, multi-site harmonized-database (GAGE-BD) analysis of correlates of BMI in older adults with bipolar disorder, in which current lithium use is one of several covariates examined via regression. No lithium dose, salt form, formulation, or serum level data are reported anywhere in the text. Per extraction-scope instructions, all *_quote fields were set to null; per-arm ns for lithium vs. non-lithium (299 vs. 927 of 1226) were derived from the 'Lithium' row of Table 1's 'All Cases' column, not from a dedicated lithium-exposure comparison table. Two primary-outcome representations were extracted per the weight-outcome rules: (1) BMI as a continuous variable (Table 2, Model 5, adjusted linear regression coefficient for lithium), and (2) BMI weight category as a categorical/'binary-like' outcome (Table 3, multinomial logistic regression ORs for lithium, overweight and obese vs. underweight/healthy-weight reference). No per-arm mean/SD BMI values split by lithium-use status are reported anywhere in the paper (Table 1 stratifies by BMI category, not by lithium exposure), so arm_results were left empty and only the adjusted between-group effects could be extracted. Geographic sites are reported only as broad World Bank-style regions (East Asia and Pacific, Europe and Central Asia, Latin America and the Caribbean, North America, Sub-Saharan Africa), not individual countries. Despite hemodialysis and intensive care she died on hospital day 5; the authors attribute the toxicity to declining renal clearance rather than a dosing error, and no comparative statistics apply as this is a single-patient case.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: Single case report (n=1), not a comparative or interventional weight-gain study. The only weight datum is ~25 kg of WEIGHT LOSS (cachexia) over the year before admission, attributed by the authors to advanced, previously undiagnosed polycystic kidney disease and/or psychiatric decompensation — NOT lithium-induced weight gain; flag for reviewers before pooling. Serum lithium of 3.79 mmol/L is a toxic level captured at acute presentation, not a stable achieved therapeutic level from routine monitoring (patient had refused lithium-level checks for the preceding 18 years); subsequent post-hemodialysis levels (0.85, 0.93, 1.12 mmol/L) are given in a table spanning hospital days 1-3 and are summarized in serum_lithium_min/max rather than as a single mean. Salt form (carbonate) is stated verbatim throughout (title and text); salt dose (1000 mg/day = 0.25 g x 4 tablets/day, verbatim) and elemental (~188 mg/day) / mmol (~27.1 mmol/day) figures were calculated using the 18.8% elemental fraction for lithium carbonate, since the paper does not state elemental content directly. Duration of lithium therapy (~30 years) was converted to ~360 months because the duration_unit enum has no 'years' option. In-hospital haloperidol/clonazepam and hemodialysis/vasopressor/antiarrhythmic treatment occurred only during the terminal 5-day admission, after the weight-loss period being reported, so concomitant_antipsychotic is coded false for the chronic outpatient regimen (clomipramine only). Per review scope, all *_quote fields are set to null, only the primary/weight-relevant outcome is extracted in 'outcomes' (renal function trajectory, electrolyte, and arrhythmia detail are captured only under adverse_events), and subgroup_analyses is left empty.

summary: This case report describes a 33-year-old woman with treatment-resistant bipolar disorder maintained on lithium carbonate 900 mg/day continuously across several years, with adjunctive agents changing over time (antipsychotics, valproate, and finally clozapine). The only quantified weight change was an 8 kg gain over 6 months while lithium was combined with valproate and quetiapine; a further unquantified 'weight gain' adverse effect was noted after clozapine was added, alongside sialorrhea and sedation, none severe enough to cause discontinuation. No statistical testing was performed (single-patient case report), and weight gain cannot be attributed to lithium alone given the confounding co-medications.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: Single-patient case report spanning ~7 years (age 26 to 33); lithium carbonate 900 mg/day was reported identically at every mention and appears constant throughout, so it is modeled as one arm rather than dose-contrast arms per L6 (only adjunctive agents changed: haloperidol -> paliperidone palmitate -> valproate+quetiapine -> clozapine). No serum lithium level, lithium formulation (IR/SR), baseline weight, or BMI was reported. The only numeric weight-change value is the stated 'gained eight kilos in six months' during the lithium+valproate+quetiapine phase; a separate 'weight gain' adverse event during the later clozapine+lithium phase was mentioned only qualitatively (no kg value, no percent), so it was not extracted as a second outcome (per binary-outcome rule W3 this would need events/total, unavailable for n=1 with no denominator) and is instead listed under adverse_events.notable_aes. Age (33) reflects the patient's age at time of report/last follow-up, not at lithium initiation (age 26); total duration (338 weeks / ~6.5 years) was calculated by summing the stated intervals between episodes (3 years + ~1 year + 1 year + 18 months) and is approximate. Country (Italy) was inferred from the patient having been 'raised in Italy' and the authors' Italian affiliation/names; treatment location is not explicitly stated. Diagnosis of 'bipolar I' and lithium-naive status at first lithium exposure are inferred, not verbatim. All *_quote fields were set to null per extraction-scope instructions.

summary: This case report describes a 22-year-old man with bipolar disorder who gained 25 kg (BMI rising from 22.7 to 31.1) over roughly three years while maintained on lithium carbonate 1,200 mg/day (serum level 1 mEq/L), with quetiapine co-administered only briefly early in treatment. After metformin 500 mg twice daily was added for the weight gain, he lost 8 kg over six months without adverse effects. As an uncontrolled single-patient observation there is no formal statistical test, but a Naranjo score of 7 supported a probable causal link between lithium and the weight gain.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: Single case report (n=1). Elemental lithium dose (225.6 mg/day) and mmol/day (32.5) were CALCULATED from the stated salt (carbonate) and dose (1,200 mg/day) using the 18.8% elemental fraction for carbonate, per rule L2. Serum level reported as '1 meq/L' was copied unchanged as mmol/L (valence 1) per rule L3; no exact timepoint or target range was stated. Per the extraction scope (primary outcome only, final timepoint only), the extracted outcome is the cumulative lithium-attributable weight gain (68 kg to 93 kg, +25 kg over ~33 months, as stated verbatim in the discussion: 'gained 25 kg over three years while on lithium maintenance therapy'). The subsequent metformin-associated weight loss (93 kg to 85 kg over 6 months) is a secondary treatment-response finding and was omitted per the 'omit secondary outcomes entirely' scope rule. Concomitant quetiapine (400 mg/day) was given for the first ~2 months at full dose then tapered over 6 months, before the major weight gain was reported at 9 months; monotherapy was therefore not continuous across the full observation window. Follow-up durations in weeks were calculated from the paper's stated months/years (~4.345 weeks/month). Country of the case was not stated in the provided text.

summary: This case report describes a 36-year-old man with bipolar II disorder maintained on lithium ER 300 mg three times daily who developed lithium toxicity (serum level 2.2 mmol/L) with neurologic and gastric symptoms 41 days after Roux-en-Y gastric bypass, coinciding with 27 kg of rapid postoperative weight loss and dehydration. Lithium was held and the patient treated with IV hydration, after which levels normalized and lithium was cautiously restarted at a lower dose. The paper also tabulates 11 previously published cases of lithium toxicity after bariatric surgery but does not report lithium-induced weight GAIN; its weight data instead concern surgical weight LOSS as a risk factor for lithium toxicity, the opposite causal direction from this review's core question.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: This is a case report/mini-review, not a comparative study: only Mr A (the illustrative case) was extracted as arm 1; the Table's 11 additional literature-derived cases (each from a separately published source, with heterogeneous doses, salts — several explicitly lithium carbonate — and serum levels) were NOT extracted as separate arms since they are secondary summaries of other papers, not this paper's own primary data. Lithium salt form was never stated for Mr A ('Li extended-release'), so lithium_salt=unknown per protocol (never inferred as carbonate). The case narrative reports a serum-lithium trajectory (0.63 preop -> 0.93 mmol/L on postop day 28 -> 2.2 mmol/L toxic at ED presentation -> 0.21 mmol/L after treatment -> restarted at 300 mg once daily, later retitrated to 300 mg BID then TID); only the preoperative baseline/trough (0.63 mmol/L) was used as the arm's steady-state serum level and dose fields, since these are not distinct dosing arms but one patient's chronology. The paper's weight data reflect bariatric-surgery-induced weight LOSS (113 kg -> 85.7 kg) as a driver of altered lithium pharmacokinetics/toxicity, not lithium-induced weight gain, so relevance to this review's core question is limited; included here for completeness since it was in the corpus. Total/treatment follow-up duration was left not_reported because the timeline is fragmented across several stated intervals (28 days, +10 days, +3 days, 6-day admission, 2 weeks, then '6 months') that do not sum to one unambiguous total; only the explicitly stated final 6-month stable-dose follow-up period was captured (post_treatment_followup_weeks=26). All *_quote fields were set to null per this task's extraction-scope override.
